We saw an example of this in al-Shahrastānī’s earlier remarks, when he doubted that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī had written the letter attributed to him and addressed to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

There, al-Shahrastānī clearly treats Qadarite doctrine as something opposed to the position of the early Muslim authorities, who, in his words, believed that divine decree, “both its good and its evil,” comes from God.

So do we find anything in the lives of these three Qadarites, all of whom died while holding their doctrine, that could be used to cast doubt on their commitment to Islam?

Would there be any basis for concluding that their Qadarite preaching was really aimed against Islam itself?

I wanted to investigate this question in the historical sources for the period.

What I found was the opposite.

The historians’ accounts of all three men show not only that they were sincere Muslims, but that they were known for serious religious devotion and trusted for it.

I found no historian of Islamic sects—not al-Shahrastānī, al-Baghdādī or al-Isfarāyīnī—who attacked the personal religious commitment of any of the three.

As for Maʿbad al-Juhanī, al-Isfarāyīnī speaks of him in a way that shows he was a transmitter of sayings from the Prophet.[^V2-106]

That alone gave him a respected religious standing and makes it difficult to accuse him of hostility toward Islam.

It was even said that Ibn Mājah, one of the well-known transmitters of hadith, narrated some reports from him.[^V2-107]

If Maʿbad had not possessed this kind of Islamic religious standing, he could hardly have exercised the wide influence we have already described in major centers of Islamic learning such as Basra, Medina and Syria.

Nor would one of the great historians of Islamic sects, al-Dhahabī, have described him in his *Mīzān al-Dhahab* as a truthful member of the generation of the Successors.

The Successors ranked immediately after the Companions as trusted sources for reports from the Prophet used in Islamic law.

Even a modern Ashʿarite researcher[^V2-108] admits that Maʿbad “was deeply religious,” despite the fact that Ashʿarites were among the strongest opponents of the Qadarites and of their later Muʿtazilite successors.

As for ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ, the fact that he was chosen to teach one of the sons of the Umayyad caliphs—Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd—about religion shows that he was known as a religious scholar and teacher whose faith and knowledge were not in doubt.

The later accusation by the Umayyads that he had “corrupted” his student Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd came only after the political crisis.

Their anger came from the fact that ʿAmr had taught one of their own sons an ideology opposed to the ideology of Umayyad rule.

As a result, one member of the Umayyad family publicly exposed the wrongs of their political system.

The issue here was therefore political.

The killing of ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ was a political killing.

As for Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, it is enough to note the trust placed in him by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

The caliph asked Ghaylān to help him reform Muslim affairs and placed him in charge of selling the Umayyad treasures.

He did this even though he knew Ghaylān was a Qadarite and disagreed with him over the problem of human freedom.

And we know that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz followed a religious path very different from that of the earlier Umayyad caliphs.

Al-Baghdādī[^V2-109] also reports that al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya used to say of Ghaylān:

> “He is God’s proof against the people of Syria, but the young man will be killed.”

This is the testimony of an important Muslim figure to Ghaylān’s high religious standing.

There is something especially striking about Ghaylān.

He grew up in Damascus, in an environment shaped by the pro-ʿUthmān party and by the Umayyads themselves.

In other words, he grew up in an environment dominated by the ideology of divine compulsion, which worked hard to spread the claim that everything done by the Umayyads, good or bad, happened by God’s decree.

Yet Ghaylān was not absorbed into this environment or its ideology.

Instead, he openly opposed it with great passion and was eventually killed because of that opposition.

Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya had predicted this fate.

Perhaps that prediction came from what was already known in Iraq and the Hijaz about Ghaylān’s passionate opposition to Umayyad determinism.

He openly taught the opposite view: good deeds and goodness come from God, while evil deeds and wrongdoing come from human beings themselves.

There is another historical point that supports our conclusion that these three Qadarites were not opposing Islam through their doctrine.

Rather, they were opposing the Umayyad rulers’ use of the doctrine of compulsion to hide their injustice by claiming that this injustice had been decreed by God.

No historian tells us that the religious scholars of the time declared the killing of these Qadarites lawful, with one exception: al-Awzāʿī.

He is said to have given Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik a legal opinion allowing him to kill Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

If these Qadarites had really been regarded as unbelievers or apostates from Islam, religious scholars would have permitted their killing under the rules of Islamic law.

In fact, the attitudes of several major conservative Muslim authorities show that the Qadarites were trusted in religious matters.

Many Qadarites are known from the books of hadith as transmitters of reports from the Prophet.

The great Sunni collections, including Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, transmit hadith from a number of Qadarites just as they do from other trusted transmitters.

Even Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, founder of one of the four major Sunni schools of law, said:

> “If we stopped accepting reports from the Qadarites, we would have to abandon most of the people of Basra.”

This statement also tells us how widely Qadarite doctrine had spread among the educated people and intellectuals of Basra.

From all these views about the Qadarites, we can draw one final conclusion.

We are **not** claiming that Qadarite doctrine developed outside the framework of religious thought.

What we are saying is that it made an important positive contribution to the development of opposition to Umayyad rule.

It gave the opponents of that rule—especially the social groups suffering under Umayyad injustice—an ideology that could stand against the ideology of the Umayyad ruling class.

Its theoretical foundation was the idea that human beings possess freedom of will and are responsible for their own actions.

That principle later became one of the foundations on which Muʿtazilite rational thought was built, as we will see in the next chapter.

###### Qurʾānic Sources for the Question of Human Freedom

We have said that the thinkers who first developed Qadarite doctrine remained within the framework of religious thought.

They therefore needed an Islamic religious basis for their theory of human freedom.

The Qurʾān, as the primary source of Islamic ideas, naturally became their main point of reference.

And they did in fact find strong support in the Qurʾān for the ideas of free will and human responsibility.

Through their own interpretation of certain Qurʾānic verses, especially verses from the Meccan period, they found what they regarded as a foundation for this position.

One account tells us about a debate between Ghaylān al-Dimashqī and the Umayyad caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz over Qadarite doctrine.

During the discussion, Ghaylān turned to the meaning of the verse:

> “We have shown him the way, whether he chooses gratitude or ingratitude.”

(Qurʾān, Sūrat al-Dahr, 76:3).[^V2-110]

Ghaylān understood this verse to mean that God’s role is to make the path of guidance clear.

After that, the choice belongs to the human being: either gratitude—that is, faith in this context—or unbelief.

Ghaylān therefore understood the verse as affirming that human beings have a choice in their actions and are responsible for what they choose to do.

Ghaylān, however, does not rely on Qurʾanic quotations alone. In another discussion with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, he gives a theoretical defense of free choice based on the idea of justice. And when he applies justice to God, he treats it in a down-to-earth rather than metaphysical way, beginning with what justice means between human beings. Addressing the caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Ghaylān says:

> “...So consider which kind of leader you are. God does not say, ‘Come to the Fire,’ because then no one would follow Him. Those who call people to the Fire are those who call them to disobey God. Tell me, ʿUmar: have you ever known a wise man to condemn what he himself does, or to do what he condemns, or to punish people for what he has decreed, or to decree the very thing for which he punishes them? Have you ever known a merciful person to demand more of people than they are capable of, or to punish them for obeying? Have you ever known a just person to force people into injustice and wrongdoing against one another? Or a truthful person to make people lie, or make them accuse one another of lying? That should be clear enough. If someone cannot see it, that is blindness indeed.”[^V2-111]

The Qadarites also relied on many other Qurʾanic verses that seem clearly to support human freedom. For example:

> “Say: The truth is from your Lord. Whoever wishes may believe, and whoever wishes may disbelieve.”
> — Sūrat al-Kahf, 18:29

And:

> “There is no compulsion in religion. Right guidance has become clear from error.”
> — Sūrat al-Baqara, 2:256

And:

> “Every soul is held to what it has earned.”
> — Sūrat al-Muddaththir, 74:38

And:

> “Whoever follows guidance does so for his own benefit, and whoever goes astray does so to his own harm.”
> — Sūrat al-Isrāʾ, 17:15

And so on.

The Qadarites understood these and similar verses in a way that supported their theory of human free will, and they used them as evidence that the theory was correct.

Their reasoning was that verses of this kind contain actions, and these actions are attributed directly to human beings. In many verses, verbs such as **wills**, **earns**, **follows guidance**, **goes astray**, **strives**, and **acts** are all attributed to people themselves. The Qadarites argued that an action cannot properly be attributed to someone who had no choice in doing it. These verses must therefore point to freedom of choice.

But the Qadarites also found other passages in the Qurʾan that seemed to point in the opposite direction. Some verses, at least on the surface, seem to support absolute predestination.

One example appears in the discussion between ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī mentioned above. According to Ibn Nubāta’s account,[^V2-112] Ghaylān quoted the verse:

> “We showed him the way, whether he chooses to be grateful or ungrateful.”

ʿUmar then told him to keep reading. Ghaylān continued until he reached the words:

> “This is a reminder. Whoever wishes may take a path to his Lord. But you will only if God wills.”[^V2-113]

The last part of this verse seems to deny that human beings possess a will independent of God’s will. On the surface, then, it supports absolute predestination.

Nor is it surprising that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz should accept such a view, even though he was the only Umayyad caliph commonly described as righteous or just. Good intentions alone could not naturally free him from the ideology of his family and his predecessors. That ideology was bound to shape his thinking, and perhaps his behavior as well, automatically and without any conscious intention on his part.

The Qadarites ran into many Qurʾanic verses like the one ʿUmar quoted in his discussion with Ghaylān. These same verses were used by the supporters of predestination as evidence for their own position.

Examples include:

> “God is the creator of everything.”[^V2-114]

> “God has sealed their hearts.”[^V2-115]

> “Whomever He wishes to lead astray, He makes his chest tight and constricted.”[^V2-116]

> “God created you and what you do.”[^V2-117]

Each of these verses has its own apparent meaning.

“God is the creator of everything” would seem, by its general wording, to include human actions. A human action is itself a “thing,” so it too must have been created by God, like everything else, rather than by the human being.

“God has sealed their hearts” seems to deny freedom of the human will, because God’s will has placed its seal and its power over human hearts.

“Whomever He wishes to lead astray, He makes his chest tight and constricted” seems to say that a person goes astray because God wills it.

And “God created you and what you do” states quite directly that God created both human beings and their actions. Everything a person does would therefore ultimately be God’s doing.

These verses, and many others like them, clearly seem on the surface to support predestination.

What did the Qadarites do when faced with Qurʾanic passages of this kind?

Their answer was to try to reconcile the different verses.

They had to interpret the verses that seemed to support predestination in a way that moved beyond their surface meaning, so that they would no longer contradict the other verses they used as evidence for human free will.

Perhaps the earliest roughly systematic example of this approach appears in the letter attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and said to have been written to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. We discussed earlier al-Shahrastānī’s doubts about whether al-Ḥasan really wrote it. But whether its author was al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, or someone else, the letter is clearly written from a Qadarite point of view. It therefore shows us how the Qadarites tried to reconcile Qurʾanic verses that seemed to contradict one another on predestination and human freedom.

The letter responds to the determinists’ use of the verse:

> “God leads astray whomever He wills and guides whomever He wills.”[^V2-118]

Both actions in this verse—leading astray and guiding—are attributed to God.

According to the letter, as quoted by Ibn al-Murtaḍā in *al-Munya wa-l-Amal* (pp. 12–15), those who say that God Himself leads astray whomever He wishes and guides whomever He wishes would understand the matter differently if they looked at the verses before and after this one.

They would then see that God leads astray only people who were already astray before God “led them astray.” The letter supports this reading with another verse:

> “God leads the wrongdoers astray.”[^V2-119]

This verse says that God’s act of “leading astray” applies to **wrongdoers**—people who were already doing wrong beforehand. They had wronged themselves by their own choice when they chose disobedience or unbelief.

This means that when God saw that they had gone astray, He judged them according to the state they had already brought upon themselves.

The letter supports this interpretation with another verse:

> “When they went astray, God made their hearts go astray.”[^V2-120]

The point here is that “God made their hearts go astray” comes **after** “they went astray.” The second action is presented as the result of the first.

The phrase “when they went astray” refers to something that had already happened. Their own act of going astray therefore came first in time, while God’s act of making their hearts go astray came afterward.

Their going astray was therefore the cause of God making their hearts go astray.

From this explanation, we can see that the Qadarites’ method of reconciling Qurʾanic verses on predestination and free will rested on two principles.

First, God leads astray only those who have already gone astray by themselves and through their own choice.

Second, when the Qurʾan says that God “leads these people astray,” this does not mean that God creates their misguidance in them. Their misguidance already exists through their own will. How could God bring into existence something that already exists? That would be impossible.

Rather, phrases such as “God leads astray” and “God made their hearts go astray” mean that God **judges** these people to be astray. He declares the reality that already exists, and in doing so establishes the reason why they deserve punishment for what they themselves chose to do.

We do not have other historical texts showing how the earliest founders of the Qadarite movement applied this method.

We have found no statement from Maʿbad al-Juhanī explaining how he reconciled Qurʾanic verses that seemed to point in opposite directions on this question.

Nor do we have a clear statement from Ghaylān al-Dimashqī applying this method. What survives of his discussions goes little beyond setting out the general theoretical principles of the Qadarite position.

Two aims stand out in Ghaylān’s arguments.

The first is political. He wants to expose the abuses committed by the rulers of his time—that is, the Umayyads.

The second is theoretical. He wants to defend the justice of religious obligations: God’s right to command people to do certain things and forbid them from doing others.

This defense rests on the principle of justice.

For Ghaylān, if God is just, He can only command people to do something, or forbid them from doing it, if they genuinely have the power either to act or not to act. In other words, they must be capable of choosing.

Predestination denies them this ability. But if people have no real power either to act or to refrain from acting, then commanding them and punishing them becomes unjust.

Both sides of Ghaylān’s argument—the political and the theoretical—can be seen clearly in his discussion with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz quoted earlier.

The political side appears when he tells ʿUmar:

> “You have begun to see, ʿUmar, though only just. You have begun to look, though only just. Know, ʿUmar, that you have found Islam reduced to a worn-out garment and a fading trace among the dead. You see no path left for us to follow, and hear no voice from which we can benefit. The Sunna has been pushed aside, and religious innovation has spread. The learned man is frightened into silence, while the ignorant man is not even allowed to ask about what he does not know. Sometimes a community may be saved by its leader. So consider which kind of leader you are: the just leader or the unjust one. God does not say, ‘Come to the Fire,’ because then no one would follow Him. Those who call people to the Fire are those who call them to disobey God...”

Here Ghaylān points to the social and religious corruption of his time, and argues that this corruption has grown out of the rulers’ intimidation of the people and their encouragement of wrongdoing.

The second, theoretical part appears in the rest of the discussion, when Ghaylān says:

> “Tell me, ʿUmar: have you ever known a wise man to condemn what he himself does...”

and continues with the passage quoted earlier, whose theoretical meaning we have already explained.

The only surviving practical example of this method of reconciling conflicting Qurʾanic verses on predestination and free will among the earliest founders of the Qadarite movement is therefore the letter attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.

The Muʿtazilites, however, began from the Qadarite position, developed it further, and built its theoretical foundations on philosophical reasoning. In doing so, they made the method much clearer. They applied rational interpretation to Islamic texts from both the Qurʾan and the Sunna.

We will examine this when we come to the Muʿtazila.

###### The Social Ground of the Problem of Predestination

When we examined the history of the problem of predestination earlier in this chapter, we saw that it had already been raised during the earliest period of Islam, before al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Maʿbad al-Juhanī, and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

From this we concluded that the problem did not arise because of foreign influence. Nor did it arise from some purely philosophical need, detached from the realities of life.

There is a striking feature of the Qurʾan that deserves some attention here.

Most of the verses that seem to support human freedom of action are Meccan verses, while most of those that seem to support predestination are Medinan.

De Boer[^V2-121] discusses this only indirectly, as part of the wider problem of apparent contradictions in the Qurʾan over “predestination and free choice.”

He explains these differences by pointing to the changing circumstances of the Prophet’s life and to changes in his psychological state.

We find a similar explanation among some Orientalists, such as H. Grimme in his book on the life and teachings of Muḥammad. Grimme argues that contradictions between Qurʾanic passages came from changes in the Prophet’s psychological state and from the different stages of his mission.[^V2-122]

The explanation shared by De Boer and Grimme clearly relies on a psychological method for understanding religious and historical events.

This is a subjective idealist method. It treats psychological states as the decisive cause behind historical developments. The real conditions of life matter only because of the feelings and personal reactions they produce in an individual. Those feelings then become the main force driving and directing historical events.

Applied to our subject, this means explaining the Islamic movement as a whole, with all its different features, primarily through its connection to the Prophet as an individual and through his personal psychological reactions to the circumstances around him.

That begins from a very narrow center.

It does not even fit the Islamic understanding of the Prophet himself, which sees him as the person who delivers a divine message through revelation.

The commentator[^V2-123] on De Boer’s book gives another explanation for the emphasis on freedom of choice in the Meccan verses.

According to him, the general direction of these verses was aimed at “destroying the fatalistic and submissive spirit that had come down to the Arabs from the pre-Islamic period, as shown both by their poetry and by verses of the Qurʾan itself.”

This explanation is closer to historical reality and to the actual development of the Islamic movement.

But the commentator does not explain why the later Medinan verses tend in the opposite, more deterministic direction.

In our view, the reason is that the Medinan verses came at a time when Islam, after the Hijra and after achieving a degree of stability, faced a new situation.

It now needed to work out its theoretical and ideological framework in matters of belief and law. It also needed to put that framework into practice, so that the Islamic movement could advance toward its goals and face the future rather than remain tied only to the relationships of the past.

This helps explain something we already discussed in the first volume of this study: during the period after the Hijra, the Prophet did not welcome arguments over matters of belief. The same was true of the first Rightly Guided Caliphs. They disliked such disputes and called instead for complete religious acceptance of what the Qurʾan taught and what the Prophet decided.

This attitude can be seen clearly in the following Qurʾanic instruction:

> “If they argue with you, say: I have submitted myself to God, and so have those who follow me...”[^V2-124]

This Medinan verse instructed Muslims to answer people who argued with them over matters of belief by saying, in effect: We have submitted ourselves to God, and there is no room for argument about that.

This was the situation during the Prophet’s lifetime and during the first period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs.

But the social and political conflicts that emerged toward the end of the Rightly Guided period, and then became much more intense under the Umayyad state, created a completely different situation.

Under these new conditions, the door to debate could no longer remain closed, even in matters of belief.

The problem of predestination was one of the first issues to become the subject of unavoidable debate.

The reason was that social and political developments had drawn increasingly clear lines between the ruling class and those who benefited from it, on one side, and the groups suffering different forms of injustice under those rulers, on the other.

The ruling class then began to use the idea of predestination for its own purposes. It turned the doctrine into a religious argument for preserving its rule and keeping its authority over the people.

It was natural, under these conditions, for the idea of predestination to become deeply rooted in the minds of most ordinary believers throughout the Umayyad period. They repeatedly heard Qurʾanic passages whose surface meaning seemed to support it.

They must also have heard preachers and mosque speakers explain these verses in ways that reinforced this deterministic reading.

Over time, many came to believe that everything they suffered—the hardships of life and the injustice of rulers alike—had been fixed for them by fate and divine decree. They were left with no choice but to submit to suffering and oppression because these had supposedly been eternally decreed by God.

This is where the idea of predestination began to take its place in the history of Arab-Islamic thought.

It was also here that it began to acquire an **ideological** dimension, expressing the class outlook of the political institution—that is, the state.

Of course, some people do not see, or do not want to see, any direct connection between the idea of predestination as a religious or intellectual doctrine and this ideological role.

It may indeed be true that no direct connection existed.

But that does not mean there was no indirect connection.

There was.

Speaking about the state after it had become a power standing independently over society, Engels writes that once this happened, it “created a new ideological revolution.” He explains that among professional politicians and theorists of state and civil law, the connection with economic realities can disappear almost completely from view.

Engels then says that higher forms of ideology—that is, forms further removed from their material and economic base—take the shape of philosophy and religion. The link between ideas and the material conditions in which people live becomes less and less direct and increasingly hidden behind a chain of intermediate connections.

But the link still exists.[^V2-125]

Basra was the first setting from which the Qadarite movement emerged.

As we saw earlier, it first appeared in the school of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. Maʿbad al-Juhanī then entered the movement and became an active advocate for it, not only in Basra but also in the Ḥijāz. His influence later reached Syria through Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

Why did this happen in Basra?

The answer lies in two features that marked the city throughout the Umayyad period in particular.

The first was that Basra had become a gathering place for many different political forces, parties, and intellectual movements opposed to Umayyad rule.

These included the Shīʿa, the Khārijites, and the *mawālī*, many of whom came from different earlier religious traditions.

Basra was also a major center for large groups of craftsmen, agricultural workers, slaves, and poor small traders who had arrived from many different regions in search of work or while fleeing persecution by landowners.

The second feature followed largely from the first.

Basra was one of the places where Umayyad oppression appeared most openly.

On one side, this oppression was directed against political parties and intellectual movements that opposed Umayyad rule for one reason or another.

On the other, it fell on the weaker groups in society: craftsmen, agricultural workers, slaves, poor small traders, and people with almost nothing.

Their lives were marked by severe exploitation, forced labor, oppression, misery, and poverty.

At the same time, the wealth and power of feudal landowners, major merchants, and other rich groups grew at the expense of these weaker sections of society.

Basra in this period was therefore a political, cultural, and social center full of deep contradictions. It was also a major target of Umayyad pressure and repression.

The response to all this was itself deeply divided.

Among the poor, the exploited, and those forced into labor, despair often led to submission to the idea of fate and divine decree.

The Umayyads strengthened this submission by spreading the idea that their own rule had been ordained by fate and divine decree, and that even the actions that caused people to resent them “happened according to God’s decree,” as Maʿbad al-Juhanī and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār put it when they came to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī to complain about the Umayyads.

Among Basra’s thinkers and educated people, some also gave in to despair.

One group withdrew from society and turned to asceticism.

Another tried to remain neutral in the bitter conflict with the Umayyads, fearing persecution that could go as far as execution.

From what we explained earlier, it seems that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī himself eventually adopted a form of this neutrality out of fear for his own safety, even though the intellectual method of the Qadarite movement had first emerged from his teaching circle in the mosques of Basra.

A third group of intellectuals moved within the deterministic ideology promoted by the Umayyads.

But under conditions like these, it was natural that some thinkers and educated people would emerge who, whether through social awareness or theoretical reflection, gave voice to the anger of oppressed groups and to an ideology opposed to the ideology of an unjust ruling power.

This opposition did in fact begin to find expression in al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī’s religious and scholarly circle.

Maʿbad al-Juhanī then became its courageous public voice. He committed himself to the cause in both its political and its religious-theoretical forms, and devoted himself to spreading it.

It eventually became a broad intellectual current and a widely known school of thought.

Despite severe persecution of its advocates and supporters, the Umayyad state could not destroy it.

Out of this current, the Muʿtazilite movement later emerged.

###### The Historical Importance of the Problem of Predestination

There is something striking here.

The problem of predestination first arose from a particular set of historical conditions at a particular stage in the development of Arab-Islamic thought. But from the beginning, it also contained an intellectual element with a life of its own, at least to some degree.

Because of this, the problem remained alive even after the particular conditions that had first produced it disappeared. Its historical role did not end when the early Islamic period that had brought it into being came to an end.

The intellectual element born with the problem was not something temporary.

If we look broadly at the development of Arab-Islamic thought from the earliest period of Islam all the way to what is called the “modern Arab Renaissance” of the nineteenth century, we can see the problem of predestination returning whenever Arab society faced conditions similar to those that had first brought it to the surface.

But it did not always return in the same form.

Its form changed from one period to another according to the conditions of each age and according to the level reached by intellectual development at that time.

Among the Muʿtazilites, for example, the problem appeared in a more advanced form than it had among the earliest Qadarites, especially in the logical structure of their arguments and proofs.

Later, in Arab-Islamic philosophy, the same problem became connected with the universal law of causality.

In Ibn Rushd, for example, this law comes close to what Marxist dialectical materialism calls the category of **necessity**.

Yet the necessity imposed by causal law takes a metaphysical form in Ibn Rushd, while containing a materialist content within it. We will examine this when we discuss Ibn Rushd.[^V2-126]

We also find the same problem appearing among Islamic reformers such as Shaykh Muḥammad ʿAbduh at the beginning of the modern Arab “Renaissance.” There it takes a new form with an almost directly social content.

The same problem was also discussed in European philosophy by Hobbes, Spinoza, Holbach, Schelling, Hegel, and later philosophical schools all the way to Marxism.

In Marxism, the relationship between freedom and necessity is one of the major philosophical questions.

From a Marxist point of view, however, necessity with no place for chance leads to absolute determinism—*jabr*—which rules out the possibility of freedom.

What matters for us here is that throughout Arab-Islamic history there was repeatedly a need for thinkers capable of giving expression to one or both sides of the struggle between exploiting classes and groups on one side and exploited classes and groups on the other.

Historically, the first of these—the exploiting classes and groups within Arab-Islamic society—repeatedly made use of Islamic religious texts whose surface meaning seemed to support predestination.

They turned these texts into a theoretical, ideological, and political weapon.

With it, they defended their own existence, promoted the idea that their domination should last indefinitely, and at the same time encouraged the exploited classes and groups to submit to fate.

In this way, they tried to dull their revolutionary spirit, suppress their class aspirations, and weaken their willingness to struggle.

###### The Origin of the Name “Qadarites”

One final point remains about the earliest founders of the Qadarite movement: why they were called **Qadarites**, and why their school became known as the **Qadariyya**.

Strictly speaking, the name is inaccurate. In fact, it is the opposite of what these thinkers actually believed.

The name seems to suggest that they believed human will was ruled by divine decree, whereas their position was precisely the reverse.

How, then, did the name “Qadarites” become attached to them—and later to the Muʿtazilites as well?

Most likely, it was their opponents, and later the opponents of the Muʿtazila, who attached the name to them as an insult and a way of discrediting them. They applied to them the saying attributed to the Prophet:

> “The Qadarites are the Magians of this community.”

The Muʿtazilites themselves rejected the name. They argued that the term **Qadarites** should properly be applied to those who say that divine decree, both good and evil, comes entirely from God.

But that belief is different from—and indeed the opposite of—the view held by the earliest “Qadarites” and by their Muʿtazilite successors, as we have already seen and will see again later.

For this reason, names such as **the People of Divine Unity** and **the People of Justice** fit the Muʿtazilites better than any of the other names given to them, even the name “Muʿtazila” itself.

We will explain the meaning of these two names later.

### D — The Jabriyya, or Jahmiyya

#### First — A Rational Logic

The deterministic school, or the theory of *jabr*, holds an important place in the early history of rational thought and in the development that prepared the way for Muʿtazilite thought.

The Jabriyya and the Qadariyya both grew from a common rational logic.

The historical importance of the Jabriyya is not cancelled out by the fact that their theory was the negative opposite of human free will, or by the fact that ruling classes and social groups used it ideologically to defend and preserve their power.

Those two facts remain important and cannot be ignored.

But neither of them removes the major importance of the Jabriyya’s role in helping to lay the foundations of rational inquiry in the history of Arab-Islamic thought.

The Jabriyya were also called the **Jahmiyya**, after Jahm ibn Ṣafwān.

Al-Shahrastānī, however, treats the Jahmiyya as only one of three groups within the wider Jabriyya.

He first defines *jabr* as “denying that the human being truly performs the act and attributing it instead to the Lord.”

He then says that the Jabriyya fall into several groups.

The **pure determinists** deny that human beings possess any action of their own or any power to act at all.

The **moderate determinists** allow that human beings possess a power, but say that this power has no effect on what happens.

As for those who say that the created human capacity has some effect on an action, and call this effect **acquisition** (*kasb*), al-Shahrastānī says that they should not be regarded as Jabriyya.[^V2-127]

He then says that the Jahmiyya were the followers of Jahm ibn Ṣafwān, who belonged to the pure deterministic group. His doctrine first appeared in Tirmidh. Salm ibn Aḥwaz al-Māzinī killed him at Marw[^V2-128] near the end of Umayyad rule.[^V2-129]

#### Second — The Theory of the Jahmiyya

Al-Shahrastānī summarizes Jahm’s position on predestination and on human power as follows:

> “A human being has no power over anything and cannot be described as possessing ability. He is compelled in his actions and has no power, will, or choice. God creates actions in him just as He creates what happens in all other inanimate things. Actions are attributed to the human being only figuratively, not in reality, just as actions are attributed to inanimate things. We say that a tree bore fruit, water flowed, a stone moved, the sun rose and set, the sky became cloudy and rained, and the earth shook and produced plants, and so on. Reward and punishment are also matters of compulsion, just as all actions are. Jahm said: once compulsion is established, religious obligation—the command to do something or refrain from doing it—is itself also a matter of compulsion.”[^V2-130]

In this passage, Jahm appears to take the most extreme possible negative and reactionary position on human freedom of choice.

But another statement attributed to him by Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī may seem to soften this position.

There Jahm says:

> “In reality, no one acts except God alone. He is the true agent. Human actions are attributed to people only figuratively, just as we say that the tree moved, the heavenly sphere turned, or the sun changed position, when in reality God caused all this in the tree, the sphere, and the sun. Human beings, however, differ in some respects from these inanimate things. God created in the human being a power through which the action occurs, and created in him a will for the action and a choice that belongs to him alone.”[^V2-131]

From this second statement, the difference between human beings and inanimate things seems to lie only in the fact that humans possess something called will and choice.

But what is the real meaning or value of this will and choice if Jahm begins by insisting that “in reality, no one acts except God alone,” that God is the true agent, and that actions are attributed to human beings only figuratively?

Once that basic principle is accepted, human will and choice become almost mechanical.

Every particular act of willing that arises in a human being is itself “created by God.” In that case, the one who truly wills is God, not the human being.

The same applies to choice.

So this later statement does not change our earlier judgment of Jahm’s determinism. It remains a completely negative and absolute determinism.

In this respect it resembles the Ashʿarite doctrine they call **acquisition** (*kasb*), which we will discuss when we come to their school.

We agree with Aḥmad Amīn that this idea of “acquisition” adds nothing and changes nothing. In the end, it still comes back to predestination.

Jahm took a very different position, however, on another set of questions.

Here he gave reason a new place in Islamic thought for his time, and used philosophical argument in several areas.

In doing so, he anticipated later rationalist thinkers such as the Muʿtazilites and the scholars of *kalām*, and helped lay the foundations on which they would later build their intellectual system.

We will now examine the main questions in which Jahm took this rational approach before them.

##### 1 — The Attributes of God

On this question, Jahm gives the judgment of reason priority over the surface meaning of Qurʾanic texts.

He does not simply accept their literal wording, as conservatives who insisted on the letter of the text did.

Jahm denied that God has attributes separate from His essence, such as hearing, sight, will, speech, and so on.

His reason was that giving these attributes to God would make God resemble human beings, and, in his view, the Creator cannot be compared with the created.

Hearing, sight, life, and speech are human qualities. Some of them are also found in animals.

What, then, does Jahm do with Qurʾanic passages that attribute all these qualities to God?

He turns to rational interpretation.

Before giving this interpretation, however, he lays down a theoretical principle. In doing so, he places the first stone in what would later become a metaphysical philosophical doctrine on this subject.

Here too he came before the Muʿtazilites and the scholars of *kalām*, placing the question firmly within rational inquiry. The Muʿtazilites and the scholars of *kalām* would later develop Jahm’s theory according to their own methods of reasoning.

Jahm’s basic position was that God is simply an **essence**.

If this is so, then God cannot be described by any attribute that can also be applied to something else—for example, as a thing, as existing, living, knowing, or willing.

He may, however, be described as powerful, as the one who brings things into existence, as the one who acts, creates, gives life, and causes death, because Jahm regarded these descriptions as belonging to God alone.[^V2-132]

Jahm also says:

> “God is not a thing, is not from a thing, and is not in a thing.”

And he says that God:

> “cannot be grasped by any description, nor by knowledge of any thing, nor by imagining any thing. They know God, so they claim, only by conjecture. They apply the name of divinity to Him, but do not describe Him with any quality to which divinity itself could be applied.”[^V2-133]

The last sentence means that they apply the name “God” to Him, but refuse to describe Him with any quality that could itself be treated as divine.

From these statements attributed to Jahm, we can see that he rejects every description of God that would make Him resemble created beings.

He seems to be arguing directly against the school known as the **anthropomorphists**, who gave God physical or sensory qualities.

They were also known as the **corporealists**, because the physical qualities they attributed to God pictured Him as a “thing” with a material body.

Because Jahm denied that God possesses the attribute of **speech**, he also concluded that the Qurʾan was created—that it came into existence in time and was not eternal.

God, in his view, cannot literally speak because speech is a human quality.

The Qurʾan, therefore, cannot be eternal divine speech.

Jahm interprets Qurʾanic verses that describe God as speaking in a non-literal way.

For example:

> “And God spoke to Moses directly.”[^V2-134]

Jahm interprets “spoke” here to mean that God **created speech** in one of His creatures, such as a prophet.

Jahm therefore also preceded the Muʿtazilites in saying that the Qurʾan was created.

This later became the center of a famous historical controversy and a terrible intellectual conflict, one closely associated with the Muʿtazila and one that greatly intensified the hostility between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites.

We will return to this dispute, which became known in the history of Arab-Islamic thought as the **ordeal over the created Qurʾan**.

##### 2 — The Question of Eternity

Jahm also introduced a new idea about eternity into Islamic thought.

Many Qurʾanic verses clearly speak of the afterlife as everlasting. For example:

> “It will be said: Enter the gates of Hell, remaining there forever.”[^V2-135]

And:

> “Because of what they said, gardens beneath which rivers flow, remaining there forever.”[^V2-136]

Despite such verses, Jahm argues:

> “The movements of the inhabitants of the two eternal abodes—Paradise and Hell—will come to an end. Paradise and Hell themselves will cease to exist after their inhabitants have entered them, after the people of Paradise have enjoyed its pleasures and the people of Hell have suffered its fire. For just as we cannot conceive of movements extending infinitely backward without a beginning, neither can we conceive of movements extending infinitely forward without an end.”[^V2-137]

Here we can see a purely philosophical and rational position.

Jahm does not begin with the Qurʾanic text. He begins instead with what he believes philosophical reason requires.

He bases his view of eternity on the idealist philosophical theory that movement cannot have existed without a beginning. From this he concludes that it also cannot continue without an end.

He then applies the same reasoning to the world of the afterlife as he does to this world.

Only after framing the problem philosophically does he return to the Qurʾanic text and interpret it according to his theory.

For example, he interprets the phrase:

> “remaining there forever”

as an expression of emphasis rather than literal endless duration.

It is like saying, “May God make the rule of so-and-so everlasting.”[^V2-138]

Jahm supports this interpretation with the verse:

> “They will remain there as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills.”[^V2-139]

He points out that this verse contains both a condition—“as long as the heavens and the earth endure”—and an exception—“except as your Lord wills.”

But genuine eternity, he argues, can contain neither a condition nor an exception.[^V2-140]

To apply his theory that movement can have neither an infinite past nor an infinite future consistently to Paradise, Jahm also argues that God has not yet created Paradise.

The Paradise of Adam mentioned in the religious texts, he says, was created and later brought to an end.[^V2-141]

In this way, Jahm argues that Paradise is neither beginningless nor everlasting.

But was Jahm really the first Muslim thinker to deny that the world of the afterlife lasts forever?

There are some signs that the question had been raised before him.

Al-Maqdisī[^V2-142] reports that the Companion Ibn Masʿūd said:

> A time will come upon Hell when its doors will flap in the wind and no one will be inside, after its inhabitants have remained there for ages.

He also reports that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said:

> If the people of Hell remained there for as many years as there are grains of sand in ʿĀlij,[^V2-143] they would still have something to hope for.

That is, they could hope for forgiveness and eventual release from Hell.

But neither statement, in our view, amounts to Jahm’s denial of an everlasting afterlife.

Ibn Masʿūd and ʿUmar are speaking only about the possibility that God may eventually forgive the people being punished in Hell.

Neither statement says that Paradise itself will cease to exist.

According to Islamic belief, where would those released from Hell go after being forgiven?

The two statements simply give sinners hope that, after receiving their share of punishment in Hell, they may eventually remain forever in Paradise.

They say nothing beyond that.

This is very different from Jahm’s position.

We can therefore say that Jahm’s view on this subject had no known precedent in Islamic thought.

He was also unique in his own time in the philosophical reasoning he used to defend it.

##### 3 — Good and Evil According to Reason

Al-Shahrastānī summarizes Jahm’s position on this question in a short phrase. While listing Jahm’s views, he writes:

> “...and making knowledge obligatory through reason before the arrival of revelation.”[^V2-144]

What does this mean?

It refers to a question that, after Jahm, became the subject of intense debate between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites, and later became one of the central issues of *kalām*.

As Jahm first understood the problem, it meant that reason could tell what is good or bad in things and in human conduct, requiring us to do what is good and avoid what is bad. Reason can recognize all this and act on it by itself before “hearing”—that is, before people hear what the prophets and messengers bring from divine revelation.

Jahm may not have developed this idea systematically in the way the Muʿtazilites and later scholars of *kalām* would. Over time, they gave it the final philosophical form known in Muʿtazilite and *kalām* literature as “the question of rational good and bad.” What they meant was that reason can decide for itself what is good and what is bad before religious law arrives. Jahm’s importance lies in being the first to identify this question and give it an early theoretical form.

The Ashʿarites later opposed this with their own doctrine of “good and bad as determined by religious law.” They denied that good and bad exist objectively in things themselves. On their view, nothing is good or bad in itself. Something becomes good when religious law commands it, and bad when religious law forbids it.

At first glance, Jahm’s position may seem to have only one side, pointing in a metaphysical direction. After all, the knowledge he believes reason can reach includes knowledge of God and of principles of faith even before religion actually reveals them.

But we also have to see the other, rational side of the argument.

First, it gives reason the power to discover the true nature of things on its own. This introduces an important new element into the theory of knowledge in Islamic thought: reason itself has an independent role in gaining knowledge.

Second, it accepts that the nature of things exists objectively, independently of human awareness and understanding.

In both respects, this second side has a progressive content. It also creates a real dialectical tension with the obvious idealism and metaphysics of the first side.

##### 4 — The Question of Seeing God

Most Muslims, especially the Ashʿarites, believed that God could be seen in the afterlife.

They supported this with what they called a rational argument. Everything that exists, they said, can be seen. Anything that cannot possibly be seen cannot be shown to exist and is therefore as good as nonexistent. Since God’s existence has been established, it follows that seeing Him must also be possible.

Their logical formula therefore rested on two claims they already accepted: first, that God exists; and second, that everything that exists can be seen.

They then supported this argument with a literal, almost crudely materialist reading of Qurʾanic verses. One example was:

> “Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be: Peace.”[^V2-145]

Al-Malaṭī explained this verse by saying that when the word “meeting” is used without qualification, it means seeing, especially when physical meeting and bodily contact are impossible.[^V2-146]

But they also went beyond this literal reading and gave some verses a metaphysical interpretation. One example was:

> “For those who do good is the best reward, and more. Neither darkness nor humiliation will cover their faces. These are the people of Paradise, and there they will remain forever.”[^V2-147]

They said that the “best reward” was eternal life in Paradise, but that the highest pleasure in Paradise was seeing God. In other words, the joy of Paradise would not be complete without that vision.

There is something important here that we should notice.

By this period, members of the religious schools were no longer relying only on religious texts when making their arguments. Before anything else, they were also trying to use reason and formal logic. Their arguments may look weak to us, and the logical formulas they used may have rested on metaphysical assumptions they had already accepted in advance. But the important point is that they were now trying to argue in this way at all.

This was no accident. It grew out of the historical conditions of the period. Religious thinkers were becoming increasingly open to rational and logical ways of thinking, helped by their contact with the philosophical cultures of the ancient world. These methods had become intellectually necessary even for thinkers with conservative views, including those who were extremely conservative in religious matters.

Jahm ibn Ṣafwān took a very different position on the question of seeing God.

He denied completely that God could ever be seen, either in this world or in the afterlife.

His position followed from an earlier claim he had made while denying the attributes of God: that God “is not a thing.” The rule that “everything that exists can be seen” therefore did not apply to God, because an existing thing is precisely that—a “thing.”

Here, just as in his treatment of the divine attributes, Jahm begins from an abstract view of the reality of God. His approach comes close to philosophical thinking in concepts, even though his overall direction remains completely metaphysical.

##### 5 — The Question of God’s Knowledge

In a later period, this question became a major point of disagreement between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites. But here too, Jahm seems to have reached a position before the Muʿtazilites that they would later adopt themselves.

What exactly was the disagreement?

In our discussion of the Qadarites, we saw that some Qurʾanic verses appear on the surface to support predestination. They say that everything that happens in the universe and in human life happens according to a decree from God that is as eternal as God Himself.

This also seems to imply that God knows everything He has decreed will happen, and that His knowledge is therefore eternal as well.

Some verses state this quite directly. For example:

> “Not a leaf falls without His knowing it, nor is there a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry, that is not written in a clear book.”[^V2-148]

Disagreement over verses like this was not limited to the question of free choice and predestination. It also produced a disagreement over God’s knowledge.

Even the Jabriyya took the same position as the Muʿtazilites on this question, despite the deep difference between them over freedom and predestination.

Jahm, whom we have already seen was a leading figure of the Jabriyya, raised the question of “God’s knowledge” before the Muʿtazilites did.

He argued that God’s knowledge is not eternal, despite the apparent meaning of the verses just quoted. Instead, this knowledge comes into being.

Here again, Jahm goes back to the position he had already taken on the divine attributes. Knowledge is an attribute. Since he had denied attributes to God, what could he now say about God’s knowledge?

Could he simply deny that God knows?

He could not accept that conclusion, because denying God knowledge would mean attributing ignorance to Him. Jahm was not prepared to say that.

So how did he solve the problem?

Once again, he used a rational method that comes close to philosophical reasoning.

Ibn Ḥazm reports Jahm as setting out the problem in these terms:

> “If God’s knowledge had always existed, then it must either be God Himself or something other than Him. If God’s knowledge is something other than God and has also existed eternally, then this means associating something with God”—that is, making knowledge a partner alongside God, since there would now be two eternal realities: God and His knowledge—“and giving eternity to something other than God. This is unbelief. But if God’s knowledge is God Himself, then God is knowledge”—meaning that “God” would simply mean “knowledge”—“and this is heresy.”[^V2-149]

What Jahm means in the last part is that if God Himself is simply identical with knowledge, then what truly exists is knowledge, rather than God.

Jahm has now stated the problem in philosophical terms. But how does he solve it?

He chooses a solution that denies the eternity of God’s knowledge without denying knowledge to God altogether. In other words, he says that God’s knowledge arises in time rather than existing eternally.

But this immediately raises more questions.

How does this knowledge arise? How does God come to know something that He did not know before? Does He know a thing before it exists, or only when it comes into existence? And when this new knowledge arises, where does it exist? In what “locus,” or subject, does this newly arising knowledge of God exist?

Historians of the Islamic schools give somewhat different answers to these questions, apart from the last one.

The reason is that no book written by Jahm himself has survived, so we cannot read his views directly. In later centuries, his ideas and the basic principles of his doctrine became known through works describing the different Islamic schools and sects, as well as through historical and literary works from that period.

A number of major historians of Arab-Islamic thought discussed this particular question in their accounts of Jahm, including al-Shahrastānī, al-Ashʿarī, al-Baghdādī, al-Ṣafadī, Ibn Taymiyya, and others.

Al-Shahrastānī answers the questions above by saying that Jahm accepted newly arising instances of knowledge for God that existed in no particular locus.

He then reports Jahm as saying:

> “It is not possible for God to know a thing before creating it. For if He knew it and then created it, would His knowledge remain as it was, or would it not? If it remained as it was, it would become ignorance, because knowing that a thing will exist is different from knowing that it has already come into existence.[^V2-150] But if His knowledge did not remain as it was, then it changed.[^V2-151] And whatever changes is created, not eternal.”[^V2-152]

After quoting this, al-Shahrastānī says that Jahm’s position agrees here with that of Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam.

He then gives the rest of Jahm’s argument:

> “Once it is established that knowledge comes into being, there are only two possibilities. Either God’s knowledge comes into being within His own essence, which would mean that His essence changes and that God becomes a place in which new events occur.[^V2-153] Or it comes into being in some other locus,[^V2-154] in which case that locus would be the thing described as possessing the knowledge, not the Creator Himself.[^V2-155] It therefore follows that this knowledge exists in no locus.”[^V2-156]

Al-Shahrastānī then says that Jahm accepted “newly arising instances of knowledge as numerous as the things known.”[^V2-157]

This account gives us a fairly complete picture of how Jahm tried to solve the problem.

God’s knowledge, on this view, is not eternal but arises in time. This divine knowledge exists in no locus. Nor is it one single, universal knowledge that contains everything. Instead, God has knowledge of individual things, and these instances of knowledge multiply according to the number of individual things that exist and become known to Him.

The question of whether God knows particulars rather than universals would later become one of the major points of disagreement between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites. Here again, Jahm anticipated a later problem in *kalām*.

From al-Shahrastānī’s account, we can understand Jahm to mean that God cannot know a thing before that thing exists.

But al-Ashʿarī reports two different views from Jahm on this part of the question.

According to the first, Jahm allowed that God might know all things before they exist through a kind of knowledge that God brings into being before them.

But al-Ashʿarī then reports another account that says the opposite:

> “Someone else reported the opposite from him, claiming that God knows a thing at the moment it comes into existence. It is impossible for a thing to be known while it does not exist”—that is, before it comes into being—“because for Jahm, a ‘thing’ is an existing body. What does not exist is not a thing, and therefore cannot be known or unknown.”[^V2-158]

When we compare this second account with what al-Shahrastānī reports, and with the similar accounts found in al-Baghdādī[^V2-159] and al-Ṣafadī,[^V2-160] there is good reason to think that Jahm believed God’s knowledge of a thing arises when the thing itself comes into existence, not before.

But our main concern here is not to settle historically which of these two positions Jahm actually held.

What matters most is the way he thought about the problem and tried to solve it.

From the statements attributed to him by the major historians of the Islamic schools, we can see that this determinist thinker relied on a rational method very close to philosophical reasoning. Even when dealing with these metaphysical questions, he worked with abstract concepts.

There is, however, a contradiction in Jahm’s thought.

It appears in the tension between his determinism and his strong insistence on denying knowledge as an eternal attribute of God.

If God has no prior knowledge of human actions that will happen later, then those actions are not known to Him in advance. They therefore cannot be governed in advance by divine will. At that point, determinism falls away and human choice returns.

##### 6 — The Question of Faith

Here we find another development beyond the way the Khārijites had treated this question earlier.

For most Muslims, the usual understanding of faith had two parts: first, belief in God and His messengers; and second, openly declaring that belief.

The Khārijites then added a third element: acting according to that belief. In their view, there could be no true faith unless belief and profession were joined by action.

With Jahm, however, the meaning of faith takes on a new form.

He reduces it to a single new element: **knowledge**.

Faith, in Jahm’s view, means knowing God, His messengers, and everything that comes from God. Nothing else counts as faith.

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī describes Jahm’s doctrine in these words:

> “Faith is knowledge alone. Everything apart from knowledge—professing it with the tongue, submitting and surrendering to God and His Messenger, honoring them, fearing them, and performing acts with the body—is not faith.”[^V2-161]

Al-Shahrastānī gives Jahm’s position in another form:

> “If someone gains knowledge and then denies it with his tongue, that denial does not make him an unbeliever, because knowledge does not disappear through denial. He therefore remains a believer.”[^V2-162]

Al-Shahrastānī adds an important point. Speaking for Jahm, he says:

> “Faith cannot be divided.”

In other words, it cannot be broken down into belief, speech, and action.

He then adds another statement from Jahm:

> “Nor do believers differ in the degree of their faith. The faith of the prophets and the faith of the community are of one kind, because knowledge itself does not differ in degree.”[^V2-163]

Al-Baghdādī gives the same doctrine in essentially the same form.[^V2-164]

Opposite faith stands unbelief.

So what, for Jahm, is unbelief?

Al-Ashʿarī reports him as saying:

> “Unbelief is one single quality. It exists in the heart, and it is ignorance of God.”[^V2-165]

We now have Jahm’s complete formula for faith and its opposite, unbelief.

Faith is **knowledge**. Unbelief is **ignorance**.

This is genuinely a new understanding of faith. It does not simply connect faith with knowledge. It makes the two the same thing.

And if we remember that Jahm believed in knowledge reached through reason, and that he regarded reason as the first path to God even before revelation, then we can see that we are dealing with a new way of thinking.

At this stage in the development of Arab-Islamic thought, we are beginning to reach a turning point. This new approach leads toward the rational and philosophical method later developed by the thinkers of *kalām*, which in turn helped prepare the way for the emergence of philosophy itself.

One strong sign that this really was a turning point is the fierce opposition Jahm’s doctrine provoked among traditionalists.

His rational method, whose main features we have now seen, seems to have been what most disturbed both the traditionalists and the Umayyad authorities.

His determinism itself could fit quite comfortably with the ideology of Umayyad rule. But Jahm’s determinism was inseparable from the rational method he used to deal with the religious questions discussed above. As we have seen, he approached these questions with an unusual degree of independence and intellectual freedom.

This bold rational tendency did not please the men who ruled the Umayyad state. On the contrary, it angered them.

The class position of the Umayyad ruling order required its leaders to oppose firmly any intellectual movement that gave reason a place of its own, even a relatively independent one, outside the conservative “official” view of the state. Jahm had done precisely that.

This may have been one of the factors that led him to answer the call of al-Ḥārith ibn Surayj in Khurasan. Near the end of Umayyad rule, Ibn Surayj called on Jahm to join his war against the Umayyads. Jahm did so, and both men were killed in 128 AH.[^V2-166]

There is another report that supports our interpretation.

The Umayyad caliph Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik wrote to his representative in Khurasan, Naṣr ibn Sayyār:

> “A man named Jahm has appeared in your region, one of the Dahriyya.”[^V2-167]

He then ordered:

> “If you capture him, kill him.”[^V2-168]

Here Hishām accuses Jahm of belonging to the Dahriyya.

Yet we find nothing in Jahm’s doctrine or recorded views that supports this accusation. Nor do we find even his fiercest opponents accusing him of it when they wrote against him.

Tāj al-Dīn al-Subkī, for example, attacked Jahm harshly and strongly condemned his view of faith. Yet even al-Subkī said nothing to suggest that Jahm had left Islam. In fact, he tried to interpret Jahm’s position in a way that would keep him within an Islamic framework.[^V2-169]

Why, then, was the Umayyad ruler Hishām alone in attaching the charge of belonging to the Dahriyya to Jahm, and then using it as grounds for ordering his death?

The answer clearly cannot be Jahm’s determinism.

Determinism was itself one of the religious weapons used by the Umayyads to defend their political and class position.

The more likely reason is that Jahm’s determinism existed alongside an intellectual independence from Umayyad “ideology.” It was also joined to the rational tendency that led him to give reason the leading role in dealing with some of the most sensitive religious questions of his time—questions closely tied to Islamic texts that still held the highest authority as sources of religious belief.

This may be what Aḥmad Amīn meant in the statement we quoted earlier:

> “Although Jahm was a determinist, he nevertheless rebelled alongside those who rose against the Umayyads. He also held views that people strongly objected to. Politics exploited the public hostility toward him and killed him.”[^V2-170]

We should not, however, overlook another factor when trying to understand the conflict between Jahm and the Umayyad authorities that ended in his death.

Jahm was one of the **mawālī**. He grew up in a Persian environment in Khurasan and was attached as a client to a branch of the Arab tribe of Azd that lived there.[^V2-171]

He also spent part of his intellectual life in Kufa.

Kufa was a place where thinkers and educated people from among the *mawālī* found room for political and intellectual activity against Umayyad rule. Their opposition came partly in response to the ethnic arrogance shown toward the *mawālī* by the Umayyad ruling order.

It is quite possible that Jahm was influenced by this atmosphere, both politically and intellectually.

There is another related point.

Historians report that Jahm met al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham in Kufa. Al-Jaʿd was also one of the *mawālī*. They say that he had lived in Damascus, where the Umayyads became angry with him and pursued him, forcing him to flee to Kufa.

According to these accounts, the reason for Umayyad anger was his belief that the Qurʾan was created. Al-Ṭabarī regarded him as the first person to make this claim, sometime after 120 AH.

Taken together, all of this suggests that the environment of Kufa left both political and intellectual marks on Jahm. These influences may have helped shape some of his later positions toward the Umayyad state, as well as the Umayyad attitude toward him.

Alongside this was the rational method that guided his independent thinking to its furthest conclusions.

In the end, his life was brought to a close by political killing.

As we come to the end of our discussion of Jahm ibn Ṣafwān, we should point to one final contradiction. It concerns Jahm’s historical role and the problems we face when trying to place him within the development of Arab-Islamic thought.

The contradiction appears in the position of the traditionalists who opposed Jahm’s determinism.

Most of the traditionalist writers who argued against him correctly identified a basic problem in his doctrine when they described it as “pure suspension.”[^V2-172]

What they meant was that determinism makes religious duties meaningless.

If human beings have no freedom of will in what they do, then there is little sense in commanding them to obey religious duties. Their obedience and disobedience do not come from their own will, but from a force that determines that will for them.

Yet these same traditionalists also opposed the rational tendency on which Jahm’s entire system of thought was built.

This created a contradiction within their own reasoning. From one side, opposing the independent use of reason ultimately leads toward opposing human freedom of will as well.

Jahm fell into the opposite contradiction. His determinism conflicted, from another side, with the demands of the very rational approach on which his thought was based.

## Summary of Chapter Two

### 1

At the beginning of this chapter, we wanted to see how the fierce political struggle between the different Islamic parties and schools gradually became an intellectual struggle as well.

One of the clearest signs of this change appeared in Islamic law. Two main approaches began to take shape: the **school of reasoned judgment** and the **school of hadith**.

This division became increasingly clear and began to develop with some independence from the political conflict itself. The reason was that Islamic law was now facing new conditions created by the Arab conquests. Muslims were entering regions where social relations were very different from those they had known in Arabia when Islam first appeared. The conquests also forced the Islamic state to create new forms of organization.

Islamic law therefore faced a new task. It had to deal with situations that had not existed before and develop new rulings for them, while still preserving the spirit of its general principles.

This historical challenge showed just how necessary it was for law to develop as life itself developed. And it was only natural that people would differ over how far the law should change, just as they differed over change in the wider sense. In every age and every society, people have tended to divide according to their social positions between those who defend what already exists and those who seek to renew it.

This was precisely the basis of the division among those concerned with Islamic law.

The conservatives rejected rulings that had no explicit basis in the Qurʾan or the Sunna. The reformers, by contrast, used their own reasoned judgment to derive new rulings for questions that neither of these two main sources addressed. These questions had not existed in Arabian society when Islamic law first appeared. The reformers therefore used rational reasoning alongside the general principles of the law.

From this division came two schools. The first became known as the **People of Reasoned Judgment** (*Ahl al-Raʾy*), and the second as the **People of Hadith** (*Ahl al-Ḥadīth*).

The second of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, had in practice stood on the side of reasoned judgment during his caliphate. He made a number of rulings on his own judgment, and these later formed some of the earliest foundations of the school of *raʾy*.

By the middle of the first Islamic century, this school had developed a clearer identity. It relied more heavily on independent judgment in matters of law and less heavily on hadith, especially after doubts had spread about the authenticity of many reports attributed to the Prophet.

The other, more conservative school reacted strongly against this position. Some of its members went beyond simply rejecting reasoned judgment and independent legal interpretation. They also went so far in their use of hadith that some of them placed hadith above Qurʾanic texts.

Even so, the school of reasoned judgment found many supporters in regions far from the Hijaz, where Islam had first appeared.

This division eventually spread beyond questions of law. It became a wider intellectual division over many of the new problems created by the development of Arab-Islamic society.

We therefore find many members of the school of reasoned judgment supporting an idea that emerged from the debate over divine decree and human action: the idea that human beings are free to choose their actions. Those who later became associated with this view were known as the **Qadarites**.

Many followers of the hadith school, by contrast, supported the opposite view. They denied human freedom and held that every human action, good or bad, comes from God. Human beings, in other words, act under God’s decree and predestination. Those who later became known for this view were called the **Jabriyya**, or the advocates of compulsion.

So each side in the legal debate—the conservatives on one side and the more forward-looking current on the other—moved naturally toward the side that best matched its outlook in this new intellectual struggle.

### 2

We also saw in this chapter that the development of Arab-Islamic society during the early Islamic period—the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the Umayyads—created the need for a broad cultural movement.

This movement laid the basic foundations for organizing the different kinds of knowledge connected with Islam. These included the language of the Qurʾan and hadith, their literary style, their legal and moral teachings, and questions of belief. They also included the history of Islam itself: its preaching, its conquests, its leading figures, and its relationship with pre-Islamic Arab life in language, literature, history, customs, and traditions.

Islam was the first and immediate starting point of this broad cultural movement.

But once the basic rules for organizing this knowledge had been created in response to the needs of Islam, those same rules became the starting point for a wider cultural revival.

Different branches of knowledge began to grow within it and gradually acquired some independence from one another. Each branch almost began to follow its own path. Their paths sometimes met, sometimes ran alongside one another, sometimes crossed, and sometimes joined together for a time before separating again.

They continued to borrow from one another—material, examples, methods, and teaching practices—but this did not remove the relative independence that each field gradually developed.

This independence did not become fully clear until the end of the second Islamic century.

In this way there emerged what came to be known as the **“Arabic sciences”**: language, grammar, rhetoric, history, biography, Qurʾanic interpretation, hadith, and the study of the transmitters of hadith. Then came the sciences connected with poetry: metre, rhyme, classifications of poets, comparisons between them, the transmission of poetry, commentaries on poetry, and so on.

One important feature in the history of these sciences is the way their relationship with Islam gradually changed.

At first, they were tied to Islam mainly as a religion. Over time, however, they became connected with Islam as a whole system for organizing public life.

This is why we argued in the chapter that the rise of these sciences was an important stage in the wider process of social development. They expressed the need for an organized body of knowledge suited to the new economic, social, administrative, and financial structures that were beginning to emerge under the Umayyad state.

They also served the needs created by the continued expansion of the Arab conquests. The conquered lands had to come to terms with the language of the conquerors, together with its literary, rhetorical, and legal meanings.

The development of society and culture also raised new intellectual questions, especially among people involved in the different fields of knowledge.

Some of these questions took a religious form and concerned matters of faith. Others became more theoretical and began to approach philosophical thought.

At the same time, growing social and cultural contact between the Arabs and other peoples, as well as with older civilizations, brought new ideas and new forms of practical experience into these debates.

The social order under the Umayyads, and especially its political structure, also strengthened the connection between these intellectual questions and the social conditions from which they had emerged.

The translation of older cultures into Arabic gradually expanded and eventually became an essential part of Arab cultural life.

Before this came what historians have called the **movement of writing and compilation**. This marked a major change. Culture moved from an earlier stage based mainly on oral accounts, transmission, and listening into a new stage based on writing, authorship, and reading.

This change helped the growing cultural exchange between the Arabs and other peoples. It also allowed the young Arabic sciences, which had until then been concerned largely with questions of form, to come into contact with new sciences that dealt more directly with subject matter and followed either an abstract rational approach or an experimental scientific one.

The centres of this cultural and scientific activity did not remain fixed. They shifted between cities and capitals as the centres of political conflict themselves shifted.

There were Mecca and Medina in the Hijaz. There were Basra and Kufa in Iraq before the rise of Baghdad. There was Damascus in Syria, and Fusṭāṭ—present-day Cairo—in Egypt.

But Basra and Kufa remained the most important and stable centres for a long time. This continued even when Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad caliphate, and even after Baghdad became the capital of the Abbasid caliphate and the main centre of cultural life.

### 3

In the third part of this chapter, we examined the earliest signs of philosophical thinking about questions of religious belief.

We began by discussing the views of a number of Western and Eastern scholars, both earlier and modern, who tried to identify the sources responsible for the appearance of these first philosophical tendencies in Arab-Islamic thought.

From this extended discussion, we reached the conclusion that the movement of Arab-Islamic thought toward rational and philosophical inquiry cannot be explained only by outside influences—Greek, Persian, Indian, or Christian.
