The great Muʿtazilite theorist Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf (135–227 AH / 751–842 CE) introduced a new formula for the problem of the attributes.

In substance, however, it still remained within the general Muʿtazilite idea that God’s essence and attributes are one.

Al-ʿAllāf said that God:

> “knows through a knowledge that is himself, has power through a power that is himself, and lives through a life that is himself.”[^V2-214]

Al-Shahrastānī sees a difference between this formula and the earlier Muʿtazilite statement that God is “knowing without knowledge,” and so on.

In his view, al-ʿAllāf’s formula affirms an essence that is itself an attribute—or an attribute that is itself the essence.

The earlier formula, by contrast, appears simply to deny the attribute altogether.

Al-Shahrastānī believes that al-ʿAllāf:

> “borrowed this view from the philosophers”—meaning the Islamic philosophers—“who believed that God’s essence is one and contains no multiplicity of any kind. The attributes are not meanings existing beyond the essence and residing in it. Rather, they are the essence itself, and they can be understood either as negations or as necessary implications.”[^V2-215]

By “negations,” al-Shahrastānī means, for example, that describing God as knowing can be understood as denying ignorance of him.

The same applies to the other attributes.

By “necessary implications,” he means that affirming knowledge of God necessarily implies the denial of ignorance.

And so on.

A few lines later, however, al-Shahrastānī argues that once al-ʿAllāf treats these attributes as different aspects of the divine essence, they become effectively the same as the Christian hypostases or Abū Hāshim’s “states.”[^V2-216]

Al-Ashʿarī, meanwhile, believes that al-ʿAllāf took his view of the attributes from Aristotle.[^V2-217]

We will briefly move ahead of our argument here to examine these two claims: al-Shahrastānī’s claim that al-ʿAllāf’s attributes are essentially the same as the Christian hypostases, and al-Ashʿarī’s claim that al-ʿAllāf took his view from Aristotle.

First, the general direction of al-ʿAllāf’s thinking on the attributes remains within the broader Muʿtazilite approach.

That approach does not fit the Christian idea of the hypostases, with its complex structure that is difficult to separate from the ideas of plurality and incarnation.

Both ideas are far removed from Muʿtazilite thought in general and from al-ʿAllāf’s thought in particular.

Second, it is difficult to accept al-Ashʿarī’s claim that al-ʿAllāf took his theory of the attributes from Aristotle.

Aristotle did not discuss the problem of divine attributes in this form.

What he discussed was divine thought and the object of that thought.

Aristotle argued that divine thought cannot have anything other than the divine essence itself as its object.

He based this on another argument: divine thought cannot be directed toward an object less noble than the divine essence.

Since God is the highest of all beings, and his existence is the highest form of existence, Aristotle concluded that there are things the divine intellect cannot reasonably think about.

The divine intellect must therefore think itself.

Because the divine intellect is the highest reality, its thought becomes thought thinking itself—intellect thinking intellect.[^V2-218]

This shows the difference between Aristotle’s starting point and al-ʿAllāf’s.

In fact, we can also find an important difference in where their arguments lead.

As we will see shortly, al-ʿAllāf affirms that God has the attribute of knowledge.

The implications of this position connect God’s knowledge with particular existing things.

That directly contradicts Aristotle’s view.

##### 4 — Al-ʿAllāf on God’s Knowledge

Continuing this discussion, we now return to al-ʿAllāf’s new formula for the divine attributes.

We need to do so because there is an important difference between his position and that of the Muʿtazilites before him, especially when it comes to God’s **knowledge**.

To say that God is knowing “without knowledge,” as earlier Muʿtazilites did, means denying knowledge as a distinct attribute.

From this it is possible to conclude that God knows only his own essence.

As we have just seen, Aristotle reached something close to this position.

On this view, nothing belonging to knowledge exists outside the divine essence. Knowledge and essence are one and the same.

And because the divine essence is absolute, knowledge too becomes absolute.

This can lead to the conclusion that God’s knowledge is not connected with particular things—that is, with individual beings in all their specific details.

Al-ʿAllāf, however, says that God is knowing **through knowledge**.

This affirms knowledge as an attribute.

From this it becomes possible to conclude that God’s knowledge is not only universal, absolute, and abstract, but also includes particular things.

If this conclusion is correct, then we have a major difference.

It places the issue at the heart of the later struggle between theological and philosophical schools over the nature of God’s knowledge.

Is God’s knowledge only universal?

Or does God know every individual thing and every individual event, in all its particular detail, throughout the universe and at every moment?

Some of the consequences of this debate are connected with the problem of freedom and compulsion.

If divine knowledge includes every particular event, this comes close to a doctrine of compulsion in human action.

Human actions would become like every other event and thing: eternally included within God’s knowledge.

Since the attribute and the essence are equal within the unity of God, both must also share the same eternity.

Everything and every human act would therefore have been known by God from eternity.

That means its occurrence was already determined from eternity.

And when it occurs, it occurs with this necessary and compelling inevitability.

There would then seem to be no room left for genuine human choice and freedom.

If, on the other hand, God’s knowledge is universal, absolute, and abstract, particular things in their individual detail fall outside divine knowledge as particular things, even if they are still included within God’s universal knowledge in an undifferentiated way.

In substance, this position could come closer to the Qadarite doctrine, which leaves room for freedom of choice in human action.

If these conclusions are correct, they may show us one form of determinism in al-ʿAllāf’s thought.

That would conflict with his well-known Qadarite position: his belief in freedom of choice.

Al-ʿAllāf also introduced another idea into the discussion of the attributes.

He said that God has eternally been hearing and seeing in the sense that he **will hear** and **will see**.

The same applies to the other attributes.

All of them are eternal, even though their action may concern things that occur later.

This supports the conclusion we reached above about knowledge.

All the active attributes apply to particular events that come into existence. They are not simply abstract and universal qualities.

But al-ʿAllāf rejects any physical meaning in God’s hearing and sight, following the general Muʿtazilite rejection of anything that would make God bodily.

He gave the attribute of **will**, however, a separate explanation.

For al-ʿAllāf, God’s will is one thing, while the thing that his will concerns is another.

> “His will concerning what he creates is his creation of it, while his creating of a thing is, in his view, different from the thing itself. Creation, for him, is a speech that exists in no place.”[^V2-219]

That is, God says to the thing: **Be.**

But this creative command does not exist in any particular place.

This means that the creative will does not exist within the essence of the creator, nor within the essence of the created thing.

It stands between the two.

Can we perhaps see here a faint resemblance to Plato’s Forms?

Could this “middle” be something like the separate realities that Plato places between the highest and most perfect Good and the world of appearances and images—that is, the world perceived by the senses?

The resemblance between al-ʿAllāf and Plato on this question is, in our view, too distant to justify concluding that al-ʿAllāf moved toward the Platonic theory of Forms.

Still, it does not rule out the possibility that he was influenced to some extent by Plato’s general picture of a metaphysical world.

##### 5 — Al-Naẓẓām’s Theory

We now take another step in the Muʿtazilite discussion of God’s attributes.

A new kind of thinking appears in another Muʿtazilite thinker who lived at the same time as al-ʿAllāf and studied under him: Ibrāhīm ibn Sayyār al-Naẓẓām (d. 221 or 231 AH / 845 CE).[^V2-220]

Al-Shahrastānī describes him as someone who:

> “read many of the philosophers’ books and mixed their ideas with the teachings of the Muʿtazilites,”

and who:

> “differed from his fellow Muʿtazilites on a number of questions.”[^V2-221]

But al-Naẓẓām’s importance in the Muʿtazilite intellectual tradition goes far beyond the fact that he “read many of the philosophers’ books.”

He built a fairly systematic body of philosophical ideas around many of the major intellectual controversies of his time.

He also seems to have absorbed the culture of his age in remarkable breadth.

Ibn al-Murtaḍā says that al-Naẓẓām:

> “memorized the Qurʾān, the Gospel, the Torah, the Psalms, and their interpretations, in addition to a great amount of poetry, historical reports, and the different legal opinions held by people.”[^V2-222]

The early historians of Islamic sects place him among the greatest Muʿtazilite thinkers.

Later and modern Eastern and Western scholars have generally treated him with similar respect.

T. J. de Boer,[^V2-223] for example, calls him “a thinker worthy of attention.”

The modern Egyptian Arab scholar Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Hādī Abū Rīda even devoted an entire book to him under the title *Ibrāhīm ibn Sayyār al-Naẓẓām and His Theological and Philosophical Views*.

For the moment, however, we are interested only in al-Naẓẓām’s position on God’s attributes.

Here he follows the general Muʿtazilite line by rejecting attributes that exist in addition to God’s eternal essence.

But he says that every attribute has two sides.

The positive side affirms the divine essence.

The negative side denies the opposite quality of that essence.

For example, calling God **knowing** means, on the positive side, affirming God’s essence.

On the negative side, it means denying ignorance of him.

The same principle applies to the other attributes.[^V2-224]

Al-Naẓẓām adds another explanation to answer an obvious objection.

Someone might say:

If every attribute affirms the divine essence, and the attributes are many, does this not mean that the divine essence itself becomes many?

Would that not contradict divine unity?

Al-Naẓẓām answers that the multiplicity does not come from the positive meaning of the attributes.

It comes from the different negative meanings—the different opposites being denied.

Ignorance, which is the opposite of knowledge, is different from inability, which is the opposite of power, and so on.

But all these opposites are denied of God.

There is therefore no multiplicity in the attributes themselves, and the attributes do not introduce multiplicity into the divine essence.

Al-Naẓẓām did, however, introduce a new position into the Muʿtazilite discussion of one particular attribute: **will**.

He said that God:

> “is not truly described by it”—that is, by will. “When revelation describes him as willing in relation to his own acts, what is meant is that he creates them and brings them into being according to what he knows. When he is described as ‘willing’ the actions of human beings, what is meant is that he commands some of them and forbids others.”[^V2-225]

Al-Naẓẓām turns to this special interpretation because he believes that describing God as possessing will in the ordinary and literal sense would imply that God has a need.

Anyone who **wants** something, in the normal meaning of the word, wants it because he needs what he wants.

God, however, must be free of all need.

Al-Naẓẓām’s view of divine will can therefore be summarized as follows.

When we say that God “willed” something, that thing must be either one of God’s own acts or an act performed by human beings.

If it is one of God’s acts, then God’s “will” toward that act is not really will in the ordinary sense.

It is simply God creating the act directly in accordance with his prior knowledge of it.

There are not two separate things—will and creation.

There is only one: **creation**, preceded by knowledge of what will be created.

In al-Naẓẓām’s view, then, “will” ultimately comes back to knowledge.

Knowledge is what precedes creation.

God knows a thing, then creates it.

If, however, the thing that God supposedly “wills” is a human action, it is not accurate to say that God willed the action.

What we should say instead is that God informed people about it in one of two ways: either by commanding it or by forbidding it.

Again, there is no separate “will.”

There is only command or prohibition.

Al-Ashʿarī summarizes al-Naẓẓām’s position in the following words:

> “To describe God as willing the creation of things means that he creates them. His will to create is the act of creating itself. To describe him as willing the actions of his servants means that he commands them, and the command is different from those actions. We say that he now wills the coming of the Hour, and what this means is that he has decreed that Hour and informed us of it.”[^V2-226]

The final result of al-Naẓẓām’s view is therefore the denial of divine will as a separate attribute, whether we are speaking of God’s own acts or of human actions.

##### 6 — Al-Naẓẓām’s Theory of Creation and Emergence

This denial of divine will may have led al-Naẓẓām to another theory concerning the creation of the universe.

To avoid the complications created by denying will, he argued that creation happened only once.

There were not many separate acts of creation.

The problem of denying divine will toward God’s acts could therefore be reduced to a single act: the one original act of creation.

Al-Naẓẓām says that God:

> “created all existing things at once, exactly as they are now: minerals, plants, animals, and human beings. Adam was not created before his descendants. Rather, God concealed some things within others. Earlier and later apply only to their emergence from what contained them, not to their coming into existence.”[^V2-227]

To make this clearer:

According to al-Naẓẓām, every being in our material world—mineral, plant, animal, or human—already came into existence once and at the same time in a single act of creation.

This applies equally to things that seem to us to have existed in the past, things that seem to exist now, and things that seem to come into existence in the future.

No being was created before another, and no being came into existence after another.

Even Adam did not first come into existence and then have descendants who appeared one generation after another, as things seem to us.

Adam and every generation descended from him, from the beginning of creation to its end, all existed together from the first moment of creation.

What appears to us as a continuous series of new beings coming into existence must therefore have another explanation.

For al-Naẓẓām, these are not new acts of coming into existence.

Rather, all beings were concealed within one another from the beginning.

When we observe what seems to be the “existence” of a new mineral, plant, animal, or human being, it is not really a new existence.

It is an **emergence**.

The thing has simply reached the point when it appears from the place where it had remained hidden since the original creation.

How, then, do material beings “emerge” from where they were hidden?

Al-Naẓẓām seems to explain this through motion.

A being that exists, or lies hidden, within another being of the same kind—a mineral within mineral matter, a plant within a plant, and so on—undergoes a certain movement and then “appears” from where it had been hidden.

But this movement is not a transfer from one place to another.[^V2-228]

It is movement in the sense of **change**: the being enters a new state.[^V2-229]

Al-Naẓẓām therefore places this kind of movement under the category known in Aristotelian logic as **position**.

Al-Shahrastānī explains:

> “Movement, for al-Naẓẓām, is the beginning of some change, just as the philosophers speak of quantity, quality, position, where”—that is, place—“when”—that is, time—“and the other categories.”[^V2-230]

This follows from al-Naẓẓām’s broader view of movement.

He says that all human actions are movements.

There is no real state of rest.

What we call rest is itself a movement of resistance or support.

The same applies to knowledge and acts of will. These too are movements of the soul.[^V2-231]

Al-Naẓẓām therefore denies that true rest exists anywhere in the universe.

For him, the universe is nothing but movement.

In this early vision of the universe within Arab thought, we find a philosophical view closely connected with his earlier idea that material beings remain hidden and then emerge.

That theory too contains an advanced philosophical insight that pushes boldly into the metaphysical framework of Muʿtazilite thought.

And if we place beside it another doctrine introduced by al-Naẓẓām—the denial of the indivisible particle, meaning his belief that matter can be divided without limit—we can see a real connection and coherence in his thinking.

This allows us to identify a materialist tendency in al-Naẓẓām’s thought.

Its historical and intellectual importance is not reduced by the fact that it still appears within a metaphysical and idealist framework.

That framework belonged to the historical conditions of al-Naẓẓām’s age and society.

It would be neither realistic nor scientific to demand that representatives of Arab-Islamic thought living under those historical conditions should have escaped that framework completely.

##### 7 — The Source of Al-Naẓẓām’s Idea of Latency and Emergence

Historians of Islamic sects, as well as later scholars of Arab philosophy, tried to identify the source from which al-Naẓẓām took these theoretical ideas about nature and God.

We have already seen that al-Shahrastānī traces them back to the philosophers.

He gives us two clues about which philosophers he means.

The first is his reference to the categories of quantity, quality, position, place, and time.

These are categories of Aristotelian logic.

This suggests that al-Shahrastānī is thinking of the Greek philosophers generally and Aristotle in particular.

His second clue comes in his discussion of al-Naẓẓām’s claim that all beings were created at once.

Al-Shahrastānī says that al-Naẓẓām:

> “took this doctrine from the philosophers who taught latency and emergence. He always tended more toward the doctrines of the natural philosophers than toward those of the metaphysicians.”
> (*al-Milal*, p. 58)

This points us toward a clear original source among the Greek natural philosophers: the doctrine of Anaxagoras.[^V2-232]

Al-Naẓẓām’s theory that all beings were created at once led him to his theory of **latency and emergence**.

This is not far from Anaxagoras’s principle that **“everything is in everything.”**

Anaxagoras described the elements involved in this process as *homoeomeries*.

If we connect al-Naẓẓām’s theory of latency and emergence with his other theory of endlessly divisible parts—the denial of an indivisible particle—we can compare both ideas with Anaxagoras’s belief that the world contains an infinite number of elements from which all existing things are formed.

Anaxagoras called these elements **seeds**.

Different combinations of these seeds produce different things.

This is why, according to Anaxagoras, everything resembles other things to some degree.

And precisely because of this underlying similarity, one thing can change into another.

Something is described as black rather than white, for example, not because blackness contains absolutely no whiteness, but because blackness predominates in it even though whiteness is also present.

And so on.

The comparison between these two ideas in al-Naẓẓām and Anaxagoras’s theory of “seeds” gives some support to al-Shahrastānī’s suggestion that al-Naẓẓām took the idea of latency and emergence in creation from the Greek natural philosophers.

Al-Shahrastānī does not identify a particular Greek school in the passage just quoted.

But elsewhere, when he discusses “the view of Anaxagoras,”[^V2-233] he becomes more specific.

He writes of Anaxagoras:

> “He was the first to teach latency and emergence.”

He also says:

> “He affirmed the actual existence of an infinite body made up of similar parts.”

It is worth noting in passing that al-Shahrastānī’s account of Anaxagoras on latency and emergence comes surprisingly close to the core of Anaxagoras’s doctrine as it is known from the history of Greek philosophy.

Once we make this comparison between al-Naẓẓām’s theory and that of Anaxagoras—and in our view the comparison rests on solid ground—there is little reason to accept the claims of other historians and scholars who trace al-Naẓẓām’s theory of creation to Stoic influence.

The Stoic idea of the “seminal cause” does not appear in al-Naẓẓām nearly as clearly as Anaxagoras’s theory does.[^V2-234]

On this point, we can therefore disagree with Abū Rīda in one respect while agreeing with him in another.

Abū Rīda denies that al-Naẓẓām was influenced either by Stoicism or by Anaxagoras.

He argues instead that al-Naẓẓām’s theory of creation was an original idea that grew directly out of the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity.[^V2-235]

We disagree with him when he denies the influence of Anaxagoras’s theory of latency and emergence.

The resemblance is too clear for serious research to dismiss or ignore.

At the same time, we can agree with Abū Rīda that al-Naẓẓām’s theory of creation also grows out of his own Muʿtazilite commitment to divine unity.

There is no contradiction between saying that the theory was rooted in Muʿtazilite thought and saying that al-Naẓẓām was influenced by Anaxagoras.

Al-Naẓẓām clearly remained committed to the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity. There is no doubt that this principle remained a foundation of his thought.

But he was also a thinker who had absorbed the culture of his age with unusual breadth and depth.

He could hardly have avoided drawing on the many intellectual traditions with which Arab-Islamic thought had come into contact.

Nor could he have avoided enriching his own doctrine through the new philosophical traditions he encountered and engaged with.

This allowed him to develop his ideas and bring his philosophical thinking into closer contact with the intellectual world of his time.

None of this means that he deliberately set out to borrow particular ideas in a direct or mechanical way.

A thinker who has deeply absorbed several intellectual traditions naturally allows them to enrich the concepts he already holds.

How far this happens depends on his theoretical awareness and on his ability to draw new conclusions that remain consistent with the basic ideas formed by the conditions of his own society and age.

Here we are satisfied with establishing that al-Naẓẓām was influenced by Anaxagoras in those questions that were connected with his Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity.

But we continue to affirm the basic principle on which this entire study rests:

**The first source of every major path taken in the historical development of Arab-Islamic thought was the objective reality of the developing Arab-Islamic society itself.**

For this reason, we also reaffirm that Muʿtazilite thought continued along an intellectual line reaching back to the political struggles of the earliest period of Islam, and that the five principles on which Muʿtazilite doctrine was founded represent a continuation of the ideas of those who came before them along the same line, especially thinkers who lived around the time of Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, the founder of the Muʿtazilite school. These included Maʿbad al-Juhanī, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī and ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ among the Qadarites; Jahm ibn Ṣafwān among the advocates of predestination; al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, who helped lay the foundations for rational interpretation of Islamic texts; Abū Hāshim ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, from whom Ibn al-Murtaḍā says[^V2-236] Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ learned; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Wāṣil’s teacher; and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Wāṣil’s companion at the beginning of the Muʿtazilite movement.

But none of this should make us forget that the relationship between thought and the real world does not always remain direct or mechanical. As thought rises to the level of abstract concepts, its reflection of reality no longer simply reproduces reality in its immediate form. Thought gains a new degree of relative independence. It also gains the ability to act back on the real world. In other words, thought is both influenced by reality and capable of influencing it; it does not remain purely passive.

From this we must draw three conclusions about the influence of outside cultures on Arab-Islamic thought.

First, that influence was real. It genuinely happened, and no scientific approach to history can deny it.

Second, Arab-Islamic thought did not simply absorb these cultures passively. It also acted on them. It added to them, criticized them, rejected what deserved to be rejected, and developed what was capable of further development.

Third, no matter how powerful or rich the influence of other world cultures may have been, it could not cut Arab-Islamic thought off from its own roots. Nor could it erase the original relationship between intellectual activity and the social soil from which it grew, together with the particular conditions of life that shaped it.

##### 8 — The Maʿmariyya and the Idea of “Meanings”

In the Muʿtazilite discussion of God’s attributes, the attribute of “creation” takes on a new form in the thought of one of their thinkers, Maʿmar ibn ʿAbbād al-Sulamī. The Maʿmariyya, a group within the Basran Muʿtazila, were named after him.

Like the other Muʿtazilites, Maʿmar began from their principle of divine unity, which led them to deny that God has attributes separate from His essence. On this basis, he argued that God created nothing except bodies. The temporary properties that arise in bodies—the things theologians called “accidents”—are created by the bodies themselves.

Maʿmar divided these properties into two types.

Some arise naturally and necessarily. Fire produces burning, for example, and the sun produces heat.

Others arise through choice. Movement and rest, coming together and separating, are produced by living beings in the broad sense, including human beings.[^V2-237]

Maʿmar also introduced a new idea into Muʿtazilite thought: the idea of **“meanings.”** His followers were therefore called the “People of Meanings.” The fact that they were known by this name shows how distinctive the idea was in Muʿtazilite history.

But what did the Maʿmariyya mean by “meanings”?

The historians of Islamic sects give us somewhat confused accounts.

Al-Shahrastānī explains Maʿmar’s position as follows:

> “He said that the accidents within each kind are infinite. He also said that whenever an accident exists in something, it exists there because of a meaning that made it exist there.”
>
> He added:
>
> “Movement differs from rest not simply in itself, but because of a meaning that makes the two different. The same applies when one similar thing differs from another or resembles it, and when one opposite stands in opposition to another. In every case, this happens because of a meaning.”[^V2-238]

From this text, we can understand two things.

First, Maʿmar says that the “accidents” themselves are infinite within every category.

Second, whenever a particular property appears in something, there must be a “meaning” that causes that property to appear.

Movement, for example, does not differ from rest simply by occurring. Behind that movement there is a meaning that makes it different from rest. The same applies to rest: it differs from movement because of a meaning.

Likewise, when one thing differs from another similar thing, or when the two resemble one another, there is a meaning that produces either the difference or the resemblance. The same applies to opposites. Two things stand in opposition to one another because a meaning produces that opposition.

When we turn to al-Ashʿarī, we find a fuller explanation.

According to him, Maʿmar argued that when a body moves, it moves because of a meaning, namely movement. Without this meaning, there would be no reason for that body rather than another body to be moving, and no reason for it to move at that particular moment rather than at an earlier one.

The same reasoning then has to be applied to movement itself. There must be another meaning that explains why this movement belongs to this particular moving body rather than to another one. And that meaning, in turn, exists because of another meaning behind it.

There is no complete totality made up of these meanings as if they were parts of one whole. They all arise at the same time. The meanings that have no final total are produced by the thing in which they exist. And we must therefore accept an infinite number of meanings within it. Life, for example, belongs to this particular living thing rather than another because of a meaning. That meaning exists because of another meaning, and so on without end.[^V2-239]

Al-Khayyāṭ, one of the major Muʿtazilite thinkers and historians, gives us a much shorter version of the same idea:

> “Everything moves and comes to rest because of a meaning within it. That meaning has another meaning behind it, and so on without end.”[^V2-240]

There is an obvious difference between al-Shahrastānī’s account and the accounts given by al-Ashʿarī and al-Khayyāṭ.

Al-Shahrastānī seems to say that it is the **accidents** that are infinite in Maʿmar’s theory. The other two texts say that the **meanings themselves** are infinite.

But the difference is not fundamental.

If every accident requires a “meaning” behind it, as Maʿmar argues, then an infinite series of accidents also requires an infinite series of meanings.

What the theory seems to imply, then, is that every event in our material world belongs to an endless chain of “meanings.” These meanings are connected with one another, yet each remains distinct, and the whole chain exists at the same time.

Take the movement of a body. That movement depends on an immediate meaning that acts as its cause. Without it, the movement would not happen and the body would not move.

But this meaning itself depends on another meaning that makes it active and gives it the power to produce movement. The second meaning then depends on a third, which plays the same role in relation to it, and so on without end.

What, then, are these “meanings”?

Are they simple spiritual substances connected with Plato’s world of Forms, or with the separate intellects of Plotinus?

Are they generative causes, each producing the next in a chain like Aristotle’s series of causes or movers?

Or are they simply a chain of secondary causes?

The texts we have about Maʿmar al-Sulamī and the Maʿmariyya do not give us a clear answer.

The modern scholar Dr ʿAlī Sāmī al-Nashshār, whose own outlook is Ashʿarite, draws attention to another statement attributed to Maʿmar himself:

> “God’s attributes are meanings.”

Al-Nashshār then tries to connect this statement about God’s attributes with Maʿmar’s “meanings” in the natural world. From this connection, he develops a metaphysical interpretation of the theory.

He writes, in effect, that these meanings must be the divine attributes. The meanings are simple because God’s attributes are simple. The meanings are infinite in number, and God’s attributes are infinite in number. The series of meanings has no end, and God’s attributes have no end. Finally, these meanings are mental considerations, because an attribute is itself a mental way of considering the divine essence.[^V2-241]

Al-Nashshār concludes that Maʿmar solved the problem of the divine attributes through this extremely subtle and difficult theory. He rejects the other interpretations given by historians of Muʿtazilite thought.

In our view, however, Maʿmar’s theory of “meanings” is a philosophical explanation of the **natural world**.

Despite the confusion in the texts, their internal logic seems much closer to Aristotle’s explanation of movement in nature and to his chain of movers ending in the eternal First Mover.

Al-Nashshār’s attempt to connect the “meanings” that Maʿmar uses to explain movement in nature with the “meanings” mentioned in the statement about God’s attributes requires a long chain of comparisons.

Those comparisons begin mainly from the fact that the same word, “meanings,” appears in both places. Al-Nashshār also assumes that the meanings behind natural movement are simple. He then builds further comparisons on that assumption until he reaches the conclusion that Maʿmar’s “meanings” in the material world are really the divine attributes.

But this assumption needs convincing evidence from the texts themselves.

The Maʿmariyya also held a distinctive view of the description of God as **qadīm**, meaning eternal or without beginning.

Al-Shahrastānī[^V2-242] and al-Baghdādī[^V2-243] both say that Maʿmar denied that God should be called *qadīm*. Al-Baghdādī adds that Maʿmar still described God as “existing eternally.”

Al-Shahrastānī explains Maʿmar’s reasoning through the Arabic word itself. *Qadīm* comes from a verb connected with something having existed earlier or having become old. On this reading, the word carries a suggestion of time.

But God’s existence is not temporal.

Maʿmar’s reasoning here therefore rests on the linguistic logic of the word *qadīm* and on the way it is derived from a verb. If the description comes from an action, and action is tied to time, then describing God as *qadīm* would suggest existence through time. Yet God’s existence is not in time.

Al-Ashʿarī,[^V2-244] however, reports another statement by Maʿmar:

> “I do not say that the Creator is *qadīm* except once He has brought created things into existence.”

This suggests that for Maʿmar the description *qadīm* is relative rather than absolute.

God is called *qadīm* only in relation to created things that come into existence after Him.

In our view, this is the correct way to understand Maʿmar’s position.

This question of God’s eternity, and the attempt to study it through the temporal logic built into the word itself, later became a major subject in the work of Muslim theologians and philosophers.

Here again, we can see the Muʿtazilites laying the foundations for later discussions.

Maʿmar and his followers also held a distinctive view of God’s attribute of **knowledge**.

Al-Shahrastānī tells us:

> “Jaʿfar ibn Ḥarb reported that Maʿmar said: it is impossible for God to know Himself, because that would mean that the knower and the known were not one and the same. And it is impossible for Him to know anything other than Himself, just as it is said that it is impossible for Him to exercise power over something that already exists simply insofar as it exists.”

Al-Shahrastānī then explains Maʿmar’s reasoning:

> “Because this man inclined toward the philosophers, and because their doctrine holds that the Creator does not possess receptive knowledge—that is, knowledge that follows and is affected by the thing known—but rather active knowledge, He knows insofar as He acts. His knowledge is what brings the act about. It therefore relates to a thing when that thing comes into existence, but cannot relate to something that remains nonexistent.”[^V2-245][^V2-246]

According to al-Shahrastānī’s account, then, Maʿmar believed that God cannot know either Himself or something other than Himself.

Why can God not know Himself?

Because if God knows Himself, then within the divine essence there would have to be both a knower and something known. Knowledge normally involves two sides: the one who knows and the thing that is known.

That would introduce multiplicity into God.

For Maʿmar, this would violate the first of the Muʿtazilites’ five main principles: divine unity.

Why, then, can God not know something other than Himself?

Because knowing something normally means being affected by that thing. The thing known acts on the knower in some way.

But the philosophers held that God’s knowledge is not passive or receptive. It does not depend on something outside God and is not affected by it.

God’s knowledge is **active**.

In other words, it does not receive its object; it produces it.

God’s knowledge is itself what brings the act into existence.

For this reason, Maʿmar can still describe God as “knowing” a particular thing once that thing comes into existence. But he cannot say that God knows it before it exists. Before then it is nonexistent, and how could God know something while it remains nonexistent if His knowledge is itself an act—that is, an act of bringing something into existence?

We can see philosophical thinking gradually becoming more visible here and entering every area of Muʿtazilite thought, even while the Muʿtazilites continued to work within the framework of one or another of their five main religious principles.

#### B — The Question of the Created Qurʾān

##### 1 — How the Question Arose

We said earlier that the Muʿtazilite understanding of divine unity led them to adopt a number of rational positions that differed sharply from those of the traditionalists.

One of these concerned God’s attributes, which we have already discussed at length. But that discussion is not yet finished.

The question of the **created Qurʾān** is one of its most important branches.

This question produced some of the fiercest and, at times, bloodiest conflicts in the history of Arab-Islamic thought. Those conflicts reached deeply into social and political life.

Yet despite these dangerous consequences, the issue retained a degree of relative independence at the intellectual level. This allowed it to develop into a much deeper theoretical problem.

In doing so, it helped push Arab-Islamic thought further toward the philosophical and scientific forms it was beginning to seek. These first took shape in *kalām*, or systematic theology, and later reached their fullest form in what we call Arab-Islamic philosophy.

So where did the question come from, and what was it really about?

Its origin lies in the Muʿtazilite debate over God’s attributes.

Once the Muʿtazilites had declared that God’s essence and attributes were one, and had therefore denied the existence of attributes added to the essence, they had to deal with the attributes mentioned in religious texts.

Their method was to interpret these texts rationally in a way that agreed with their understanding of divine unity.

Among the attributes mentioned in the texts, they found **speech**.

The Qurʾān says:

> “And God spoke to Moses directly.”[^V2-247]

The Qurʾān itself is also described as “the speech of God,” as in the verse:

> “If any of the polytheists asks you for protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of God.”[^V2-248]

Here, “the speech of God” means the Qurʾān itself.

God is therefore described as one who speaks, and the Qurʾān is described as His speech.

What were the Muʿtazilites to do with this attribute?

Could they say that speech was one of the attributes identical with the divine essence?

If they did, they would have to say that this attribute was permanent and unchanging, because in their system there was an absolute identity between God’s essence and His attributes.

They all agreed that God’s essence cannot change. The attributes would therefore have to be equally unchanging.

But if God’s speech is fixed and unchanging, a problem immediately appears in the Qurʾān itself.

The Qurʾān contains many different kinds of speech. There are commands and prohibitions, promises and threats, laws, reports and descriptions.

If the attribute of “speaking” is identical with God’s essence, and if the Qurʾān is God’s speech, then the variety and difference within this speech would imply variety and difference within the divine essence itself.

That would mean division.

And division would mean multiplicity.

The final result would be a denial of the unity of the divine essence. This would contradict the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity—and indeed the principle of divine unity accepted by Muslims in general.

The Muʿtazilites therefore argued that God’s speech is not *qadīm*—not eternal and identical with the divine essence.

It is something that came into existence.

The Qurʾān, which all of them accepted as God’s speech, therefore came into existence as well.

In other words, it is **created**, just like everything else in the created universe.

To say that God “speaks,” on this view, simply means that God creates speech.

This is the origin and basic meaning of the question as the Muʿtazilites understood it.

But they did not stop there.

They also tried to support their position with other arguments. Some of these aimed to show that belief in an eternal Qurʾān did not merely conflict with divine unity. It also conflicted with the rational character of Qurʾānic law.

Their argument went like this.

Suppose the Qurʾān were eternal speech—that is, an eternal attribute of the eternal divine essence.

Then the commands contained in the Qurʾān would also have to be eternal.

But that would mean that God’s commands existed before the people to whom they were addressed existed.

Before human beings existed, there would have been no one for the commands to apply to.

Human beings are the subjects of these commands.

How, then, could God issue commands to people who did not yet exist?

The Muʿtazilites argued that this would be meaningless, and meaningless action cannot be attributed to God.

They also said that speech requires both someone who speaks and someone who is addressed.

Before the people subject to God’s commands existed, there would have been a speaker but no listener or addressee.

For this reason, they argued, belief in an eternal Qurʾān would make divine legislation irrational, and the claim must therefore be false.[^V2-249]

They also approached the question from another direction.

They argued that God’s created speech exists in a particular place or medium. It consists of letters and sounds, while the written copies found in Qurʾānic manuscripts reproduce those letters and sounds. Anything that exists in a particular place is an accident, and accidents pass away immediately.[^V2-250]

This argument returns us to the distinction between **substance and accident**.

The Muʿtazilites began from what they accepted as established: God is a simple substance and cannot be one of the accidents.

An accident, in their argument here, is bodily, while divinity is absolutely free from bodily form.

Now consider the Qurʾān.

It exists somewhere because it consists of letters and sounds that are spoken and heard. These therefore exist in the physical organs of speech and hearing.

The Qurʾān is also written on paper. Many copies can be made, each reproducing the same text. In this sense too, it exists in a particular place.

Anything that exists in a place is an accident, and accidents pass away.

The spoken letters and sounds that make up the Qurʾān disappear as soon as they have been spoken or heard.

All of this separates them from a substance that does not exist in a place, does not take bodily form and does not pass away.

The Qurʾān therefore cannot be eternal or identical with the divine essence.

It must have come into existence and been created, like other created things.

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, whom al-Shahrastānī calls the leading master of the Muʿtazila, gives another version of essentially the same argument.

We saw earlier that al-ʿAllāf understood God’s will as an act of creation.

When God wills something, He creates it. His will for a thing is His saying to it, “Be,” and it is.

But al-ʿAllāf distinguished between two kinds of divine will: the will that creates, and the will that imposes duties.

The first, in his view, does not exist in a particular place.

The second does.

The Qurʾān belongs to this second kind because it contains duties and laws addressed to human beings: commands, prohibitions and statements about paradise and hell.

The Qurʾān is therefore legislative speech that exists in a place.

But what is this “place”?

Al-ʿAllāf answers that it obviously cannot be God’s own essence.

God’s essence cannot be the place in which commands, prohibitions and reports exist.

The place must therefore be something other than God.

If the Qurʾān is speech that exists in something other than God, then it is a created accident like other accidents.

God created the Qurʾān in the Preserved Tablet. By this expression, al-ʿAllāf means the mental or immaterial existence of created things before their material existence.

The Qurʾān, he says, exists in three kinds of place: a place where it is preserved, a place where it is written, and a place where it is recited and heard.

It can exist in many places at the same time without literally being transported, moving or passing from one place to another.

But if God were to destroy all the places in which it is preserved, read or heard, the Qurʾān would cease to exist.[^V2-251]

The logical conclusion of al-ʿAllāf’s argument is that the Qurʾān is an accident rather than a substance.

It is therefore created and came into existence in time, rather than being eternal.

Maʿmar ibn ʿAbbād al-Sulamī, whom we discussed earlier, also accepted the Muʿtazilite position that the Qurʾān was created rather than eternal.

But he differed from the other Muʿtazilites in one important respect.

He argued that the Qurʾān was not directly an act of God.

His reasoning followed from his wider theory of bodies and their properties.

The Qurʾān is something produced, and as such it is an accident. But Maʿmar held that accidents cannot literally be produced by God.

The Qurʾān must therefore be produced by the thing from which its sound is heard.

If Qurʾānic speech were heard from a tree, for example, that speech would be an act of the tree itself.

Whenever it is heard, it is the act of the thing in which it occurs.[^V2-252]

Al-Ashʿarī explains this by saying that Maʿmar regarded the Qurʾān as an accident and believed that accidents could not be acts of God.

Al-Shahrastānī gives the same idea in another form. According to him, Maʿmar believed that God created only bodies. The properties or accidents of bodies are produced by those bodies themselves.

Some arise naturally: fire produces burning, the sun produces heat and the moon produces changes of colour.

Others arise through choice: living beings produce movement and rest, coming together and separating.[^V2-253]

Yet Maʿmar does **not** deny that the Qurʾān is created by God, as al-Baghdādī tries to interpret his position.[^V2-254]

For Maʿmar, the Qurʾān is a body, and God creates bodies.

What God does not create are the actions and temporary properties of those bodies.

This is similar to what the Muʿtazilites say about human beings and their actions.

The human being is created by God, but human actions are not. Human beings create their own acts. This is how the Muʿtazilites defend human freedom.

##### 2 — Interpreting the Qurʾānic Texts

Once the Muʿtazilites had developed rational arguments for the created nature of the Qurʾān, they turned to the Qurʾānic text itself.

They interpreted its verses in ways that agreed with the conclusions they had already reached through reason, and they used those interpretations to support their position.

For example, they considered the verse:

> “A Book whose verses were made firm and then set out in detail.”
> (Sūrat Hūd, verse 3)

They argued that this shows the Qurʾān to be made up of parts that appeared in stages: first made firm, then set out in detail.

That can only apply to something that comes into existence, not to something eternal.

They also considered the verse:

> “We sent it down…”
> (Sūrat al-Dukhān, verse 3)

They argued that “sending down” is clearly an event—something that happens.

What is eternal does not “come down.”

Perhaps their strongest textual argument came from the verse:

> “Whenever We abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We bring one better than it.”
> (Sūrat al-Baqara, verse 106)

For the Muʿtazilites, abrogation means change.

And change is one of the clearest marks of something that has come into existence, as opposed to something eternal that cannot undergo any change.[^V2-255]

##### 3 — The Intellectual Basis of Muʿtazilite Theory

Any realistic assessment of the Muʿtazilite position on the created Qurʾān—and indeed on the whole question of God’s attributes—must begin from two points.

First, the Muʿtazilites were determined to defend an idea of divine unity completely free from every form of multiplicity, even purely mental multiplicity.

Second, they were equally determined to understand divine unity rationally.

They judged religious texts in the light of reason. They did not simply ignore apparent contradictions in those texts and surrender them to unquestioning faith. When the literal meaning of a text seemed to conflict with reason, they interpreted it.

A proper study of the intellectual basis of Muʿtazilite theory in this area has to begin from these two principles.

From the same starting point, we can also examine the claim that the Muʿtazilites took these ideas from outside sources.

Some writers say that they borrowed one idea or another from the philosophers, as al-Shahrastānī suggests.

Others say they took their ideas from Jews, Christians or Persian Manichaeans, as some early historians and some Orientalists have claimed.

There is no reason to deny the relationship between later Muʿtazilite thinkers and the philosophers.

It is a historical fact, and we have no doubt about it.

Here we mean the later Muʿtazilites, beginning with al-ʿAllāf and al-Naẓẓām.

But the real question is **how** they learned from the philosophers.

Did they simply take philosophical ideas from outside and copy them mechanically?

Or did philosophy enter into an active process of interaction and internal development within Arab-Islamic thought itself?

That is the real issue.

It seems clear to us that the second is what happened.

The Muʿtazilites began from the intellectual foundation we have just described, built on two principles of their own.

The first was divine unity, which came from religious and metaphysical thought.

The second was the insistence that reason should be the primary judge when divine unity was being understood.

This second principle grew out of the Muʿtazilites’ own position within the intellectual and cultural development of their society during a highly dynamic historical period.

It also grew out of the social and political conditions from which their Qadarite and Jabrite predecessors had emerged.

When Muʿtazilite ideas and knowledge later came into contact with the philosophers and with ancient philosophical sources, the Muʿtazilites did not take their basic starting point from those sources.

What they took, first, was **method**.

Second, they took the new intellectual tools that philosophical learning placed at their disposal.

These tools gave them a new ability to use rational arguments and logical methods in support of principles that had already arisen from their own specifically Islamic position.

They had inherited that position from earlier Muslim thinkers.

Those earlier thinkers had gradually built up a new body of ideas, one step at a time.

The first raw material for this development came mainly from the great political crisis created by the struggle over the caliphate.

That political conflict was deeply and organically connected with religious thought and with practical religious positions as well.

The claim that Muʿtazilite ideas about God’s attributes and the created Qurʾān came from Jewish, Christian or Persian Manichaean thought is another question, and one that deserves some discussion within the limits of the sources now available to us.

It has been said, for example, that belief in the created Qurʾān probably came from the Jewish belief that the Torah was created, while belief in an eternal Qurʾān resembles the Christian doctrine of the eternal Word.[^V2-256]

But where does this claim come from?

We have already seen that Jahm ibn Ṣafwān believed that the Qurʾān was created.

The question therefore did not begin with the Muʿtazilites.

It is also known that al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham held this view before Jahm, and that Jahm was influenced by him.

Ibn Taymiyya,[^V2-257] Ibn Kathīr[^V2-258] and others report this.

These sources say that al-Jaʿd took the idea of the created Qurʾān from Bayān ibn Samʿān, who took it from Ṭālūt, the nephew of Labīd. Labīd, in turn, was the nephew of al-Aʿṣam, who had been an opponent of the Prophet and had lived during the rise of Islam.

The whole point of producing this chain seems to be to reach Ibn Kathīr’s final conclusion: that Labīd himself took the doctrine of the created Qurʾān from a Jew in Yemen.

And so Jahm took it from al-Jaʿd, al-Jaʿd from Bayān, Bayān from Ṭālūt, Ṭālūt was Labīd’s nephew, Labīd was al-Aʿṣam’s nephew, and al-Aʿṣam was an enemy of the Prophet.

We are therefore expected to search for a source that is both non-Islamic and hostile to Islam until, at the end of the chain, we finally discover a Jew in Yemen who supposedly introduced this heresy into Islam!

Scientific historical research cannot accept an artificial chain like this without solid historical evidence.

There is also evidence that directly weakens the supposed connection between the created Qurʾān and Judaism.

The doctrine arose among its supporters from an intense desire to preserve the absolute purity of divine unity and to deny every form of bodily existence to God.

Judaism, by contrast, contains the idea that when God spoke to Moses, He appeared to him in some form and Moses saw Him physically.

That stands in complete opposition to the theory of those who defended the created Qurʾān, from al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham to the most important early and later Muʿtazilite thinkers.

Early historians even report that al-Jaʿd himself was killed by the Umayyad governor of Kūfa, Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī, on the charge that he said:

> “God did not truly speak to Moses.”[^V2-259]

There is another claim found uniquely in Ibn al-Nadīm’s *al-Fihrist*.

He says that al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham was the tutor of Marwān ibn Muḥammad, the last Umayyad caliph in the eastern Islamic world, and that al-Jaʿd “led him into *zandaqa*.”

In that period, the word *zandaqa* most often referred to Manichaeism, which was widespread in Persia.

There is no historical evidence to support this claim.

It is also intellectually implausible.

There is no meaningful similarity between the doctrine that the Qurʾān is created—a doctrine based on divine unity—and Manichaeism, which rests on the idea of two divine principles.

A third claim remains. This is especially common among later researchers, though it ultimately goes back to earlier writers such as Ibn Taymiyya.

According to this view, al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, from whom Jahm ibn Ṣafwān took the doctrine of the created Qurʾān, was influenced by the Sabians or by Christianity.

This influence may have been direct, or it may have come indirectly through Christian churches that had themselves absorbed ideas from the Greek Stoics.

We therefore have not one claim but three:

al-Jaʿd was influenced by the Sabians;

or by Christianity;

or by Stoicism through the Daysanite and Christian churches.

How well do these claims agree with the historical and theoretical evidence?

In theory, some Sabian influence is possible.

By “Sabians” here we mean the Harranians: the scholars—or more accurately, the priests—of the school of Ḥarrān in al-Jazīra, in northern Syria.

They later played a well-known role in transmitting Greek science into Arabic during the great translation movement.

We know that when the Arab conquest took place, the school of Ḥarrān already had links with ancient Greek mathematics and astronomy and had been influenced by Pythagorean and Neoplatonic theories.

For this reason, it was later able to contribute to the Arabic translation movement during the scientific flowering of the early ʿAbbāsid period.

The Harranians also seem to have formed a distinct religious community, and divine unity was one of the basic principles of their doctrine.

Ibn al-Nadīm[^V2-260] tells us that in the age of al-Kindī, the “philosopher of the Arabs,” they possessed a book containing their teachings on divine unity. They attributed this book to Hermes, whom they regarded as one of their prophets.

Ibn al-Nadīm reports that al-Kindī described it as:

> “a work of the highest perfection in its treatment of divine unity, whose teachings a philosopher, however hard he tries, can hardly avoid accepting.”

Al-Bīrūnī[^V2-261] also writes of the Harranians:

> “What we know of these people is only that they affirm the oneness of God and declare Him free from imperfections. They apply the beautiful names to Him metaphorically, because in their view He has no attributes in the literal sense. They assign the ordering of the world to the celestial sphere and its bodies, and they say that these are alive, speaking, hearing and seeing. They also venerate light.”

From these two sources, al-Kindī and al-Bīrūnī, we can see that the Harranians affirmed divine unity.

So in theory, it is possible that someone like al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham could have been influenced by them.

Historically, however, this seems unlikely.

The evidence makes it difficult to believe that al-Jaʿd could have known the details of Harranian doctrine at such an early date.

Al-Jaʿd was killed in the third decade of the second Islamic century, around the middle of the eighth century CE.

Yet Ibn al-Nadīm’s own account tells us that the Harranian book containing their teachings on divine unity appeared in the time of al-Kindī.

And al-Kindī lived from the end of the second Islamic century until after the middle of the third, roughly from the early ninth century until late in that century.[^V2-262]

This suggests that Arab thinkers became familiar with the basic features of Harranian doctrine only **after** the question of the created Qurʾān had already appeared with al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham and then Jahm ibn Ṣafwān.

Christianity is equally difficult to accept as the original source of the problem.

The general Muʿtazilite approach to God’s attributes, and especially to the created Qurʾān, was clearly aimed not only at protecting God from multiplicity but also at denying every possible form of embodiment or indwelling.

Yet the Christian doctrines that could have influenced Arab and Muslim intellectual centres at the time were known to Muslim thinkers above all through the Trinity and through the idea that God dwelt in Christ and appeared through him.

Moreover, to say that the Qurʾān was created is to deny the eternity of the Word of God.

Christian doctrine, by contrast, affirms the eternity of the Word.

The two positions are therefore opposed.

If Christian influence must be admitted—and there is nothing strange about cultural influence of this kind—then the more likely form is **negative influence**.

In other words, the theory of the created Qurʾān may have developed partly as a response to the Christian doctrine of the eternal Word, rather than as an imitation of it.

This seems the more likely possibility.

For the same reason that we ruled out Manichaeism as the source of the doctrine, we also rule out the Daysanites.

Manichaeism and the Daysanite doctrine rest on the same basic principle: dualism.

Mani ibn Fātik al-Ḥakīm, from whom Manichaeism takes its name, held that:

> “The world is made from two eternal principles: one light and the other darkness.”[^V2-263]

The followers of Daysān likewise:

> “affirmed two principles, light and darkness. Light produces good intentionally and by choice, while darkness produces evil naturally and by necessity.”[^V2-264]

The conflict with the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity is obvious.

We should emphasize once again what we are—and are not—arguing here.

When we criticize claims that the questions of God’s attributes and the created Qurʾān came from outside sources, we are not denying outside influence in general.

We are denying it only as the original source for those Muslim thinkers who raised these questions **before** the Muʿtazilites.

That is the first point.

Second, our argument does not mean that we believe cultures develop in isolation from one another.

Quite the opposite.

The idea of completely isolated cultures conflicts with the logic of history and, even more clearly, with the laws of social development.

What we reject is the opposite extreme: the attempt to explain Arab-Islamic thought entirely through outside sources while ignoring its internal sources.

That position conflicts with the logic of history and social development even more strongly.

##### 4 — Currents Opposed to the Muʿtazilites

The historical and intellectual picture of the created Qurʾān would remain incomplete if we looked only at the Muʿtazilite position.

To complete the picture, we must also examine the views that opposed them.

This question formed an important link in the historical development of Arab-Islamic thought and in its movement toward examining Islamic beliefs through theological and philosophical methods.

That movement soon encountered resistance.

In the end, the disagreement developed into a sharp conflict over the role of **reason itself**.

The main currents that opposed the Muʿtazilites can be grouped into three:

**A — the Salafi current**
**B — the Hanbali current**
**C — the Ashʿari current**

**A — The Salafi current:** The followers of this current were also called the **Ṣifātiyya**, the “Affirmers of the Attributes,” because they accepted eternal attributes of God.

This name arose in opposition to the Muʿtazilites, who denied such separate eternal attributes.

The Salafis answered with a name of their own for the Muʿtazilites: **Muʿaṭṭila**, the “Negators.”

They claimed that the Muʿtazilites had stripped God of the qualities of divinity and emptied those qualities of meaning by denying the divine attributes and by teaching that human beings freely create their own actions.

The two names therefore stood as opposites.

The Salafis, also known as the People of the Sunna and the Community, were called Salafis because they claimed to follow the beliefs of the earliest Muslims.

They held that believers must accept God’s attributes exactly as they appear in the Qurʾān, with complete faith, without subjecting them to rational analysis and without trying to reinterpret them according to reason.

These Qurʾānic attributes include power, will, knowledge, hearing, sight and speech.

Their ordinary linguistic meanings should be accepted as they appear.

Their deeper reality should be left to God alone.

Human beings have no right to interpret them through reason, because reason is incapable of grasping God’s intention in these matters.

The earliest Muslims had taken this approach, and therefore their method must remain binding. It must never be crossed.[^V2-265]

This is why the Salafi confrontation with the Muʿtazilites over God’s attributes, including the created Qurʾān, took such a strict and conservative form.

Some Salafis rejected even debate and argument in religious matters.

They insisted that believers accept what appears in the Qurʾān and in the Prophet’s traditions exactly as it appears and stop there.

Questions such as whether God’s attributes are identical with His essence or distinct from it, how created things can come from an eternal being, and how God’s eternal knowledge can relate to things that come into existence later were, in their view, beyond the power of reason.

To investigate such questions was therefore to depart from the way of the early Muslims—and so, in their eyes, from religion itself.

From this general outline, it is clear that the deepest difference between the Salafis and the Muʿtazilites concerned **reason**.

The Salafis denied that reason could grasp divine truths, including the true nature of God’s attributes.

The Muʿtazilites, by contrast, gave reason an almost unlimited ability to understand such truths.

They believed that reason could develop arguments leading reliably to them without falling into error.

The conclusions reached by rational proof could therefore be treated as certain.

These conclusions should then become the standard by which religious doctrines were understood and religious texts interpreted.

The texts had to be brought into agreement with reason.

Seen in this light, the progressive side of Muʿtazilite thought becomes much clearer.

The Salafis, by contrast, went so far in denying the role of reason that some of them accepted the literal meaning of Qurʾānic verses that appear to give God bodily features.

These include references to God’s “face,” “hand” and “throne,” examples we discussed earlier.

According to al-Shahrastānī, the Salafis divided into two groups over such verses.

Some interpreted them, but only in ways that the wording itself could naturally support.

Others refused interpretation altogether.[^V2-266]

This second group simply accepted the verses as Qurʾān revealed by God and saw no need to go any further.

Al-Shahrastānī describes their position in their own words:

> “Reason has shown us that God is unlike anything else. He does not resemble any created thing, and no created thing resembles Him. Of this we are certain.
>
> “But we do not know the meaning of expressions such as ‘The Merciful established Himself on the Throne,’ or ‘I created with My two hands,’ or ‘Your Lord came,’ and similar statements.
>
> “We have not been commanded to interpret these verses. What we have been commanded to believe is that God has no partner and that nothing is like Him. Of that we are certain.”[^V2-267]

One phrase in this passage deserves attention:

> “Reason has shown us…”

Does this mean that the Salafis accepted reason as one of the sources of religious knowledge?

In fact, they did—but only within very narrow limits.

They accepted a kind of basic reasoning that, in their view, establishes the necessity of God’s existence and His absolute unity, without partner or equal.

From this basic knowledge followed belief in prophecy and in the world to come.

One of the best-known supporters of this refusal to go beyond the text was Mālik ibn Anas (96–179 AH / 714–795 CE), founder of the Mālikī school, one of the four major Sunni schools of law.

In Mālik’s case, this position appears even more conservative and more strictly traditionalist.

He was responding to interpreters who refused to take literally Qurʾānic verses that seem to describe God in bodily terms.

One example is:

> “The Merciful established Himself on the Throne.”
> (Sūrat Ṭā Hā, verse 5)

Taken literally, this suggests that God has a throne and sits or establishes Himself upon it. The throne is material, and sitting upon it would be a physical act.

Mālik’s famous response was:

> “The establishing is known. How it happens is unknown. Belief in it is required. Asking about it is an innovation.”[^V2-268]

Mālik therefore forbids even asking **how** God is established on the throne.

He treats the question itself as a religious innovation.

And in Islam, *bidʿa*, religious innovation, was associated with error and deviation.

If even the question was condemned, rational interpretation was more objectionable still.

**B — The Hanbali current:** This current takes its name from Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, founder of another of the four major Sunni schools of law, who died in 241 AH / 855 CE.

This was also a Salafi current, but one that accepted a limited form of interpretation.

It corresponds to the first of the two Salafi groups mentioned by al-Shahrastānī: those who interpreted religious texts only in ways that the wording itself could reasonably bear.

Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal became personally involved in the great conflict over the created Qurʾān.

During the final months of the caliph al-Maʾmūn’s life and throughout the reign of al-Muʿtaṣim, he was subjected to a severe religious examination over his position.

At that time, the ʿAbbāsid state had adopted the Muʿtazilite position.

It began testing judges, jurists, religious leaders and officials to see whether they accepted the doctrine of the created Qurʾān.

Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal stood firmly and courageously by the opposite view despite imprisonment and torture.

Many other opponents of the doctrine gave way under pressure, but he did not.

When he finally left prison, he was even more determined in his position.[^V2-269]

Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal held that the Qurʾān was **not created**.

He explained his position at length in a work entitled *Refutation of the Heretics and Jahmites concerning the Ambiguous Verses of the Qurʾān That They Doubted and Interpreted Incorrectly*.[^V2-270]

There he responds, for example, to the Jahmites and Muʿtazilites when they cite the verse:

> “We made it an Arabic Qurʾān.”
> (Sūrat al-Zukhruf, verse 3)

They argued that the Arabic verb *jaʿala*, “to make,” here means “to create,” and that the verse therefore proves that the Qurʾān was created.

Ibn Ḥanbal replies that the word *jaʿala* is used in the Qurʾān in two different senses.

Sometimes it means **to create**.

For example:

> “Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light.”
> (Sūrat al-Anʿām, verse 1)

Here “made” means “created.”

But elsewhere *jaʿala* means something closer to “to appoint” or “to make into.”

God says to Abraham:

> “I am making you an imam for the people.”
> (Sūrat al-Baqara, verse 124)

Here, Ibn Ḥanbal argues, “making” Abraham an imam obviously does not mean **creating** Abraham as an imam, because Abraham already existed before he became an imam.

The word must therefore mean an act of appointing or making something into something else.

He applies the same meaning to:

> “We made it an Arabic Qurʾān.”

The Qurʾān, he concludes, is therefore an act of God, not something created in the sense intended by the Muʿtazilites.

Ibn Ḥanbal also answers a Jahmite argument based on the verse:

> “The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is only the Messenger of God and His Word.”
> (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, verse 171)

The Jahmites argued that Jesus was created, and if Jesus is called God’s Word, then God’s Word must also be created.

Ibn Ḥanbal replies that the Qurʾān uses many descriptions of Jesus that are never used of the Qurʾān itself.

Jesus is described as born, as a child, as a boy and as a grown man.

Can those same descriptions be applied to the Qurʾān?

He answers:

> “It is not lawful for us to say of the Qurʾān what we say of Jesus.”

When the Qurʾān calls Jesus “His Word,” Ibn Ḥanbal says, it refers to the creative command:

> “Be.”

God said “Be” to Jesus, and Jesus came into existence.

Jesus exists **through** the word “Be.”

He is not himself the word “Be.”

That word is speech, and the speech itself is not created.

Ibn Ḥanbal then continues by responding both to Christians and to Jahmites over expressions such as “the Word of God” and “the Spirit of God.” The discussion appears on page 30 of the work just mentioned.

We have presented these examples from Ibn Ḥanbal’s arguments so that his method becomes clear.

He limits himself to arguing from the religious texts.

He does not engage with the rational proofs used by the Muʿtazilites.

That is both his position and his method.

Some later Hanbalis went further than Ibn Ḥanbal himself.

They extended the eternity of the Qurʾān beyond its content and argued that the Qurʾān was eternal even in its letters and sounds.

Some went so far as to say:

> “Even the leather and the cover are eternal, not only the Qurʾānic codex itself.”[^V2-271]

Al-Shahrastānī reports their reasoning:

> “It is agreed that what lies between the two covers is the speech of God, and that what we read, hear and write is the speech of God.
>
> “The words and letters themselves must therefore be the speech of God.
>
> “And since it is agreed that God’s speech is uncreated, these words and letters must themselves be eternal and uncreated.”[^V2-272]

Al-Shahrastānī then writes:

> “…until the age reached ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd al-Kullābī, Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Qalānisī and al-Ḥārith ibn Asad al-Muḥāsibī.
>
> “These men belonged to the Salaf, but they took up the discipline of *kalām*. They defended the beliefs of the Salaf with theological arguments and systematic proofs. Some wrote books, while others taught.”[^V2-273]

This statement marks the beginning of a new line within the picture we have just described.

With these thinkers, the Salafi current begins to take on a different form.

It moves beyond the absolute traditionalism of Mālik ibn Anas, beyond the simple refusal to interpret found among some Hanbalis, and beyond Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal’s limited interpretation based closely on the wording of scripture.

Yet it still remains within the wider Salafi framework.

Al-Shahrastānī is right to place these three thinkers—al-Kullābī, al-Qalānisī and al-Muḥāsibī—inside that framework.

All three belonged firmly to the People of the Sunna and the Community.

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī[^V2-274] said of the followers of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kullāb al-Qaṭṭān that:

> “They hold most of what we have reported from the People of the Sunna.”

And, as we know, the People of the Sunna rejected the Muʿtazilite teachings on God’s attributes and on the created Qurʾān.

Ibn Kullāb himself, who died in 240 AH / 854 CE, affirmed eternal attributes of God, including speech.

God’s speech was therefore uncreated.

He also accepted the traditional Sunni position on predestination: both good and evil come from God.[^V2-275]

Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Khālid al-Qalānisī, who died around 255 AH / 868 CE, and al-Ḥārith ibn Asad al-Muḥāsibī, who died in 243 AH / 857 CE, also appear to have belonged to Ibn Kullāb’s school.[^V2-276]

Although this school remained Salafi in doctrine, it differed from earlier Salafism in the **method** it used.

It defended its beliefs and attacked the Muʿtazilites using the techniques of theological argument.

Al-Shahrastānī had already pointed this out.

Al-Subkī[^V2-277] described ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kullāb as:

> “one of the leading theologians.”

Al-Baghdādī said of al-Qalānisī that in his time he was a leading defender of Sunni belief:

> “His writings on *kalām* exceeded one hundred and fifty books. Among them were a refutation of al-Naẓẓām, together with other books and treatises.”[^V2-278]

Ibn Taymiyya also noted al-Muḥāsibī’s connection with the teachings of Ibn Kullāb.[^V2-279]

From Ibn Taymiyya’s account of the Kullābite school, it appears that one of its innovations within Salafi doctrine was the claim that the Qurʾān was eternal and inseparable from God’s essence, and that God did **not** speak through an act of His will and power.

Earlier Salafis had usually gone no further than saying that the Qurʾān was uncreated and that God “has always been speaking,” or that “He speaks through His will and power.”[^V2-280]

Ibn Taymiyya explains what the Kullābite school meant by saying that God does not speak through His will and power.

For them:

> “The speaker is the one in whom speech exists, without that speech being produced by his own act, will or power.”[^V2-281]

In other words, God’s speech is an attribute permanently belonging to His essence, not an act that He performs.

Why?

Because if God’s eternal speech were an act of divine will, then before human beings existed that speech would have been directed toward people who did not yet exist.

And if speech depended on divine will and power, it would mean that God had possessed the power to speak from eternity, including at a time when no one existed to hear Him.

The Kullābites rejected this conclusion.

Speech, they argued, requires both a speaker and someone being addressed.

If the second does not exist, speech itself does not occur.

Through this kind of theoretical reasoning, the Kullābite school took Salafi thought beyond its traditional reluctance to use reason in theology.

It began to follow the method of the theologians.

This was really an expression of a larger new intellectual development.

Rational theological thinking had apparently become so deeply rooted in religious thought that its influence now extended even to some of the most conservative thinkers, those who had previously been most resistant to the rational methods of *kalām* associated with the age of philosophy.

**C — The Ashʿari current:** It is very clear that Ashʿarism developed out of the Kullābite school.

After mentioning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd al-Kullābī, Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Qalānisī and al-Ḥārith ibn Asad al-Muḥāsibī and describing their use of *kalām*, al-Shahrastānī continues:

> “…until Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī and his teacher entered into a debate over the question of what is good and what is best. They broke with one another, and al-Ashʿarī joined this group”—meaning the group of al-Kullābī, al-Qalānisī and al-Muḥāsibī.
>
> “He then defended their position with the methods of *kalām*. This became the doctrine of the People of the Sunna and the Community, and the Ṣifātiyya developed into the Ashʿariyya.”[^V2-282]

The appearance of al-Ashʿarī, who died in 330 AH / 941 CE, and of his theological school opposing the Muʿtazilites brought the traditionalist opposition into a more complete and systematic form.

From then on, the struggle against the Muʿtazilites increasingly used the same weapon the Muʿtazilites themselves had used: rational theological argument.

The two sides now formed parallel currents within the same wider intellectual movement—the theoretical inquiry that became the discipline of *kalām*.

But to say that Ashʿarism continued the Kullābite school means continuity mainly in **method**.

The details of their doctrines were not identical.

Al-Ashʿarī developed the theory of **inner speech**, an idea that Ibn Kullāb had already placed, more implicitly, at the foundation of his theory of God’s speech.

Ibn Kullāb argued that God’s speech is eternal.

For this reason, he said, it cannot literally be command, prohibition or report, because these are things that arise in time.

How can something eternal possess qualities that come into existence?

He therefore distinguished between two kinds of speech.

The first is eternal speech, one of God’s permanent eternal attributes.

The second is speech that arises when there are people to address, such as commands, prohibitions and reports.

The first belongs to God’s essence.

The second belongs to His acts.

Ibn Kullāb used a similar distinction when speaking of God as Creator.

The attribute of creation also has two forms: an eternal attribute inseparable from God’s essence, and the act of creation that occurs when something is actually created.
