At this point, the two kinds of rational knowledge begin: necessary knowledge and acquired, theoretical knowledge.

From Abū al-Hudhayl’s statements as a whole, we can conclude that theoretical rational knowledge belongs to the third and final stage in the development of reason.

At this stage, a person reaches a new understanding of divine unity and justice, as the Muʿtazilites understood them. This understanding is now based on argument, evidence, and demonstration rather than simply on the first self-evident judgments of reason.

#### 3 — The Idea of the “Two Inner Promptings” in Rational Knowledge

The Muʿtazilite view of rational knowledge also rests on an idea that explains how rational choice takes place. They called this the idea of the **“two inner promptings.”**

They say:

> “Before revelation is heard, a thinking person finds within himself two promptings. One urges him to know the Creator, to thank the Benefactor, and to follow the paths of goodness and virtue. The other urges him toward the opposite. He then chooses what leads to salvation and avoids what leads to destruction. These two newly arising promptings that call him in opposite directions are expressions of the speech and inner conversation of the self.”[^V2-450]

This shows that even the kind of necessary rational knowledge which Abū al-Hudhayl described as something **“grasped by reason through reflection alone”** still involves a process of human choice.

The Muʿtazilites were determined to preserve this principle of **choice**, not only in human actions but in the acquisition of knowledge as well.

This may explain al-Aswārī’s statement that a human being has a power that is equally capable of either of two opposites.[^V2-451]

The principle of choice itself requires a person to stand in relation to both possibilities before choosing one of them.

At first there is hesitation between two inner promptings: one calls the person toward one course, while the other calls him toward its opposite. The person then ends this hesitation by choosing one of them.

The Muʿtazilites call the human ability to do either a thing or its opposite, before the final choice is made, **capacity** (*istiṭāʿa*).

Al-Naẓẓām explains the idea of the two promptings on this basis when he says:

> “There must be two promptings: one commanding a person to act, and the other telling him to hold back, so that choice can genuinely take place.”[^V2-452]

Again and again, whenever the Muʿtazilites discuss one of their basic principles or a question that follows from it, they make a point of defending human choice through the different theoretical principles on which their system rests.

This shows how strongly Muʿtazilite thought is marked by internal unity and coherence.

In our view, this is one of the features of a way of thinking deeply shaped by philosophical reflection and philosophical system-building.

#### 4 — The Idea of Inner Speech

In the passage from al-Shahrastānī quoted above about the **“two promptings,”** there was a brief reference to what the Muʿtazilites called **“the speech of the self and its inner conversation.”**

We cannot simply pass over this without asking what they meant by it.

Al-Shahrastānī himself explains the Muʿtazilite view of this inner speech:

> “As a person moves through the stages of reflection and reasoning, he proposes one statement and rejects another. He divides a general proposition into alternatives, rejects one of them, and thereby identifies the other. The act of dividing is itself the inner conversation of the self, while identifying one of the alternatives is itself the judgment of reason. A person may even take up a pen and write an entire volume from the conversation of his thought, filling a book with the conversation of his self, while his tongue remains silent and says nothing.”[^V2-453]

What can we learn from this account of the Muʿtazilite position?

We agree with Dr Albert Nasri Nader that in this discussion the Muʿtazilites **“reached into the essence of the process of thought and regarded it as arising directly from the power of reason and being guided by its natural light.”**[^V2-454]

The reason is that this passage gives an analytical description of the thinking process that comes close to a scientific account.

For the Muʿtazilites, the speech or inner conversation of the self is not some mysterious act of intuition outside reason or rational thought.

It is the first of two stages in the activity of theoretical consciousness. Together, these two stages make up the complete process of thinking and carry it forward toward reflection and reasoning.

As we understand al-Shahrastānī’s account, the **speech of the self** or its **inner conversation** is the internal process of reasoning by which the mind distinguishes one meaning from another.

It considers one general idea or another. It then looks at what that general idea contains, and at the different ways it can be divided. Finally, it selects one of these alternatives rather than the other.

So there are two movements within the overall process of thought.

The first is a movement of distinguishing, dividing, and comparing.

The second is a movement of deciding.

The first prepares the ground for the second.

The first is the **“inner conversation of the self.”**

The second is the **“judgment of reason.”**

This, then, is how the Muʿtazilites describe the process of rational reflection that produces rational knowledge, or science.

#### 5 — Reason as the Most Distinctive Feature of Human Beings

The Muʿtazilites held that this inner speech forms the basis of rational thought.

They also held that it is completely internal and does not depend on spoken language. As al-Shahrastānī said in the passage above, a person may **“take up a pen and write an entire volume from the conversation of his thought, filling a book with the conversation of his self, while his tongue remains silent and says nothing.”**

On this basis, the Muʿtazilites concluded that inner speech is the feature that most clearly distinguishes human beings from animals.

In other words, it is the basic quality that makes a human being human.

Here they differ from the logicians, who defined the human being as a **speaking animal**.[^V2-455]

The Muʿtazilite definition would instead amount to something like this: the human being is a **rational animal**, a **thinking animal**, or an animal that speaks through thought—that is, through the silent inner speech of the mind rather than through words spoken by the tongue.

Their argument is that

> “the way spoken expressions point to meaning differs from one nation and age to another, while the way judgments [that is, judgments of reason] point to knowledge is the way of reason itself, and this does not differ between nations and ages.”[^V2-456]

Different words can therefore point to the same meaning.

The meaning understood when you say **“God”** is the same meaning understood from words such as **Khudā, Tamkri, Sarnā, Nad**, and so on.

The speech within the human self is therefore genuine speech and real expression. For the Muʿtazilites, it is the most distinctive quality of the human self and the feature that separates human beings from other animals.[^V2-457]

They also say:

> “The inner conversations of the self are representations of the expressions spoken by the tongue. Do you not see that a person who does not know a word of Arabic does not have Arabic speech occur in his mind, and a person who does not know a foreign language does not have the speech of that language occur in his mind? But someone who knows both languages will sometimes speak inwardly to himself in Arabic and sometimes in the other language. Know, then, that in truth these are representations that follow the expressions a person learned while growing up. Yet the expressions themselves have those representations as their source: from them the expressions emerge, and back to them they return.”[^V2-458]

As we see it, this argument in all its detail rests on the Muʿtazilite belief that the **intellectual meaning or content remains one**, even when the words used to express it differ from one people to another and from one language to another.

This is why they said that

> “speech is not a kind of attribute with an independent rational reality like other attributes. Rather, the term is applied to speech by the tongue because people have agreed among themselves to use it in this way.”

A human being can be in a state in which neither speech nor its opposite is present, while still remaining fully human. A person is therefore distinguished from animals by his **form and structure**, not by spoken speech.[^V2-459]

Spoken language, then, is not something that has an independent rational reality of its own. It consists of terms and expressions that people agree among themselves to use.

And a human being can at times be silent—neither speaking nor doing the opposite of speaking—without ceasing to be human.

So spoken language cannot be what fundamentally distinguishes human beings from animals.

What distinguishes them instead is their **form and structure**.

Here, “form” is meant in the Aristotelian sense. The point is that matter itself is not what distinguishes the human being. What does so is the particular form that makes a human being human and separates the human kind from the other kinds of beings in the external world.

In short, for the Muʿtazilites, **rational reality is the basic feature that distinguishes human beings from animals.**

If we look more closely at the Muʿtazilite explanation of language and of the relationship between language and thought, we can see a limitation in their view.

Given the period in which they lived, they were unable to recognize that language and thought cannot truly be separated, even in the silent **inner speech** that is never spoken aloud.

But their account also contains something else that was highly progressive in relation to the ideas about language common in their own society and age.

As we have seen, they argued that language comes into existence through **agreement among people**. Human beings themselves create it.

Today this may seem completely obvious. So what was important about the Muʿtazilites saying something that now appears so self-evident?

The answer is that it was not self-evident in their own time or in the intellectual world in which they lived.

The idea that language came from divine revelation was widespread.

Against this, the Muʿtazilites argued that language comes from people themselves, who agree on words in order to express meanings. In its own time, this was an advanced position.

They also gave this view another theoretical basis beyond the arguments we have just examined.

Their second argument was that language is **something that came into being in time and is material**. The proof, they said, is that languages differ from one people to another.

If language were eternal, it would be fixed and there would be a single language shared by all peoples.

This theoretical principle became one of the foundations of the Muʿtazilite doctrine of the **created Qurʾān**.[^V2-460]

#### 6 — The Question of Rational Good and Evil

This question also grew out of the Muʿtazilite principle of **divine justice**, and especially from their belief that human freedom of choice is essential to any meaningful idea of justice.

The Muʿtazilites agreed that reason alone can recognize that the world has a Creator, and that reason can distinguish good from evil.[^V2-461]

They also held that because God is just, He requires of human beings only what they are genuinely free to choose to do. That freedom rests on the reason God has given them, because reason is the faculty through which choice becomes possible.

From this it followed that they had to accept a position such as Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf’s:

> A morally responsible human being must know that what is good is good and what is evil is evil. He must therefore do what is good, such as truthfulness and justice, and turn away from what is evil, such as lying and injustice.[^V2-462]

The same idea appears in al-Naẓẓām and others, who held that reason itself judges all human actions to be good or bad.[^V2-463]

It also appears in al-Jubbāʾī and his son Abū Hāshim ʿAbd al-Salām, who argued that knowing what is good and what is evil is itself a rational obligation.[^V2-464]

Statements like these, found across the writings of different Muʿtazilite thinkers, all belong to the issue that became known during this rich period in the development of Arab-Islamic thought as **“the question of rational good and evil.”**

We saw earlier, when discussing Jahm ibn Ṣafwān, that he was the first to think seriously about this issue and to give its theoretical basis an early form.

The Muʿtazilites then developed it further until it took on the philosophical form associated with the theologians of *kalām*.

Its basic meaning, however, remained what Jahm had first proposed: **reason by itself can discover whether things and actions are good or bad, beneficial or harmful.**

On this basis, Jahm and, after him, the Muʿtazilites argued that **“reason makes knowledge obligatory before revelation is heard.”**

That is, reason obliges a morally responsible person to know God and to know the basic principles of religious law even before hearing what is taught by prophets, messengers, or books of divine revelation.

When discussing this question in relation to Jahm, we said that at first sight it might appear to have only one side: a metaphysical purpose and content, since the knowledge said to be required by reason includes knowledge of God and of the basic principles of divine law.

But we should not overlook another side of the issue, which is implied rather than stated directly.

This second side has two rationalist aspects.

First, it recognizes that reason can reach knowledge on its own, without the mediation of revealed law. In this sense, reason has an independent role in acquiring knowledge.

Second, it recognizes that good and evil exist objectively in things and actions themselves.

And this, in turn, implies that the things themselves also exist objectively.

There is, however, a major difference between the way this question appears in Jahm and the way it appears among the Muʿtazilites.

The difference lies in their way of thinking.

Jahm contradicted his own deterministic method when he accepted the idea of rational good and evil.

The Muʿtazilites, by contrast, remained completely consistent with their own coherent system. They based this question on their doctrine of human freedom of choice, which in turn rested on the human faculty of reason.

Abū al-Hudhayl comes close to saying this openly in the passage quoted above:

> “He must therefore do what is good, such as truthfulness and justice, and turn away from what is evil, such as lying and injustice.”

For Abū al-Hudhayl, **doing** and **turning away** are human actions performed because reason itself requires them.

Here, “requirement” means an inner and voluntary motive guided by reason.

The same applies to al-Naẓẓām’s statement that reason judges actions good or bad in everything a person does.

His judgment of good and evil is directly connected to human conduct, and the motive comes from the person’s own reason.

This is why the question remained somewhat isolated and abstract in Jahm’s thought, while among the Muʿtazilites it became closely connected with the other parts of their theory of divine justice.

Above all, it was connected with the central part of that theory: **human freedom of choice**.

This idea makes the theory as a whole into a bridge between the concept of divine justice and the practical responsibility of human beings—not only in the moral sphere, but in the social sphere as well.

There is another side to the Muʿtazilite development of this question: they placed it on a rational and argumentative foundation.

By doing so, they gave the issue a new theoretical form and prepared the way for it to become part of the first Arab-Islamic philosophical system to take on the character of an organized science: **the science of *kalām*.**

The Muʿtazilites offered several arguments for their belief that reason can judge good and evil. We will mention three of them here.[^V2-465]

The first is based on historical observation and an inductive method.

They argue that before revealed laws appeared, people already used reason to settle disputes. They argued with one another rationally, and each side tried to bind its opponent by what reason itself required.

This was possible only because people appealed to what reason could recognize as good or evil in things themselves, independently of any revealed law—since no revealed law yet existed.

For example, rational people before the coming of religious laws regarded saving a drowning person or rescuing someone from destruction as good. They regarded oppression and aggression as bad.

Their second argument works through logical necessity.

The prophets, they say, ask people to use their reason and reflect on the things in the universe.

But suppose things were not good or bad in themselves, and suppose reason could not recognize their qualities without first depending on revelation.

People could then say to the prophets:

We are not required to examine your miracles or your claims to prophethood unless revelation first tells us to do so. But revelation itself cannot be established unless we first examine your prophethood and your miracles.

The prophets would then have no answer, and their whole mission would collapse.

But that conclusion is false, the Muʿtazilites argue.

So the logical problem is resolved only if things really can be good or bad in themselves, and if reason can recognize this before revealed law arrives.

Their third argument is that if actions were not good or bad in themselves, and received these qualities only from revealed law, then legal scholars would be unable to use reason in cases where no scriptural ruling exists.

It would also become impossible to explain **why** a particular rule exists.

The question “Why?” and the answer “Because…” would lose their meaning, because every explanation depends on the assumption that things and actions possess real qualities of their own.

Aḥmad Amīn sums up what the Muʿtazilite position truly means:

> “The Muʿtazilites affirmed the authority of reason in knowing good and evil. Good is not good merely because God imposed it on things, nor is evil evil for that reason. To put it differently, God’s command does not make a thing good, and His prohibition does not make it evil. Rather, God commands a thing because it is good in itself, and prohibits it because it is evil in itself. Things possess qualities in their own nature that make them good or evil, and reason is capable of recognizing these qualities and thereby knowing good and evil. There is no doubt that this principle frees reason from rigidity and from stopping at the literal text…”[^V2-466]

To understand the historical and intellectual place of the Muʿtazilite position more clearly, we need to compare it with the Ashʿarite view.

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, the founder of the Ashʿarite school, says:

> “Reason makes nothing obligatory, nor does it judge anything to be good or evil. Knowledge of God is reached through reason, but it becomes obligatory through revelation.”[^V2-467]

The Ashʿarite theory can be summarized like this:

Nothing is good in itself, and nothing is evil in itself.

Something is good because revealed law declares it good by praising the person who does it. Something is evil because revealed law declares it evil by condemning the person who does it.

At the same time, revelation does not praise, blame, command, or prohibit something because the thing itself already possesses an inherent quality of good or evil.

For this reason, reason has no independent authority to judge that one thing or action is good and another is bad.

One of the Ashʿarite arguments for this view is that if goodness and badness belonged objectively to a thing itself, then whatever was good would always be good, and whatever was bad would always be bad. Neither quality would depend on any conditions.

But in reality, they say, good and bad are not absolute. They are relative.

The same thing may be good in one situation and bad in another.

Killing, for example, is bad when the person killed has committed no crime deserving death. But it may be good when it is carried out as just punishment for a crime.

If good and evil existed objectively in the thing itself, their character could not change with circumstances.

Likewise, the same thing may be good at one time and not good at another.

Revealed laws themselves prescribe one thing for one people and something different for another. If good and evil existed objectively within things themselves, religious laws would not change with time, place, and people.[^V2-468]

This Ashʿarite argument is right in one respect and weak in another.

It is right in saying that good and evil are relative rather than absolute.

But how can we judge, before revealed law appears, that killing in one case is good and in another bad? And how do we decide that a truth which helps someone is good, while a truth which harms someone is bad? What standard are we using?

In making this argument, the Ashʿarites themselves were admitting that good and bad have an objective, though relative, basis in things. Yet they did not show that reason is incapable of recognizing this relative good and bad. So they could not overturn the Muʿtazilite position at its foundation, because reason is the very basis of that position.

Besides, the Muʿtazilites themselves never said that things were good or bad in some absolute sense. Their position can instead be understood like this: killing as just retribution is good in itself, while unjust killing is bad in itself; telling a truth that helps is good in itself, while telling a truth that causes harm is bad in itself, and so on. In other words, what they judged good or bad was not simply “killing,” “truth,” or “lying” in the abstract. It was **just killing** or **unjust killing**, **helpful truth-telling** or **harmful truth-telling**, and the same applies to lying.

There are also things such as injustice, where we can identify a relatively fixed basis for judging them bad. The same is true of justice when we judge it good. Injustice remains injustice regardless of changes in people, circumstances, or periods of history. Justice likewise remains justice. The Ashʿarite argument does not cover acts of this kind, whose goodness or badness reason can recognize in themselves whether or not religious law has spoken about them.

Some Ashʿarites added another argument. They said that our judgments about what is good or bad come either from earlier religious laws or from human customs and conventions:

> “Suppose a person were created with a sound nature and a complete mind, but had never acquired the morals of any people, learned the manners of his parents, received a religious upbringing, or been taught by a teacher. Then suppose two propositions were put before him. The first: two is greater than one. The second: lying is bad. He would have no hesitation about the first, but he would hesitate about the second.
>
> “What remains, then, is simply the custom by which people call whatever harms them bad and whatever benefits them good. We do not deny the use of such names. But they differ from one people to another, from one period to another, from one place to another, and according to different relationships and circumstances. Anything that varies with such relationships and circumstances cannot have an intrinsic reality of its own. One people may consider the slaughter of an animal good while another considers it bad. The same act may be good for one people, in one time and place, and bad in another.”
>
> And: “Reasonable people approve of saving those who are drowning and condemn aggression because they seek praise and fear blame.”[^V2-469]

What we said about the Ashʿarites’ first argument also applies here. But two further points can be added.

First, the Muʿtazilite position assumes that there was a time before divine laws had been revealed.

Second, human customs themselves must rest on some rational judgment that one thing is good and another bad. Customs do not simply appear at random, with no basis in human understanding.

It seems that later Ashʿarites became aware of this weakness in their argument against the Muʿtazila. The author of *al-Mawāqif* reports them as saying that there is actually no disagreement between the Ashʿarites and the Muʿtazila when the words “good” and “bad” refer to perfection and deficiency in a thing. We can say, for example, that knowledge is good and ignorance is bad, and both sides agree that reason can recognize this.

The same words can also refer to what serves a purpose and what does not, or to what brings benefit and what causes harm. In this sense, whatever serves the purpose or brings benefit is good, while whatever frustrates the purpose or causes harm is bad. Here too, there is no disagreement that reason can recognize the difference, even though the judgment is relative. Something may be good for one group and bad for another in this sense.

The real disagreement, they say, concerns whether an action deserves praise and reward, or blame and punishment. The Muʿtazila say that reason can judge this too, and that we can therefore judge some actions deserving of blame and punishment. Their opponents say that this can only be known through revealed law.[^V2-470]

What can we conclude from this?

The strength of Muʿtazilite reasoning, together with the steady development of intellectual debate toward greater reliance on reason, gradually narrowed the disagreement between the Muʿtazila and the Ashʿarites on this issue. The same happened in other areas as well. Despite their deep differences in principles, assumptions, and starting points, rational argument increasingly became the dominant method in both schools.

## Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

### 1 — A Process of “Fusion and Transformation”

We have discussed many of the questions in these two chapters at great length, sometimes in considerable detail. This was not accidental, nor did we simply allow ourselves to drift into one digression after another. It was part of the plan from the beginning.

Our aim was to reach an important conclusion.

The emergence of philosophical thought among the Arabs, and its later development from the historical period in which it first appeared, did not take place apart from the internal development of Arab-Islamic society in its economic, social, political, and cultural life.

This brings us back to a point we made when we began our discussion of atomism. During the period in which the Muʿtazila emerged, Arab thought—and Arab culture more broadly—was certainly influenced by philosophical ideas, theories, and schools that came from outside. But this influence worked **from within**. Foreign ideas entered an internal process that was closely and objectively connected with the laws governing the social, intellectual, and religious development of Arab-Islamic life.

After examining many of the disputes between the Muʿtazila and the Ashʿarites, and also the disagreements among the leading Muʿtazilite thinkers themselves, we can now return to the idea we introduced at the start of our study of atomism: the process of **“fusion and transformation.”**

By this we meant that philosophical ideas, theories, and schools from many different foreign sources were drawn into the internal current of Arab-Islamic intellectual life, a current that often moved with great force. Within it, those ideas were fused and transformed until they became an integral and original part of Arab-Islamic thought itself.

This is how that thought acquired its own distinctive character and became noticeably independent of the foreign sources from which many of these ideas, theories, and concepts had originally come.

In every disputed question we examined, whether it concerned purely divine matters or the natural world and human society, the basic starting points were Islamic. But they did not come from Islamic metaphysics considered in the abstract. They came from the real relationship between Islam and the lives of the people among whom its concepts took concrete form—in economic, social, and political systems, and in forms of culture and thought.

There is no doubt that cultural and social interaction between these people and the cultures and inherited civilizations of other peoples was one of the powerful forces driving change. During the historical period in which the Muʿtazila appeared, this interaction helped give development a new pace and a new character.

But **interaction** is not the same thing as mere passive influence.

Interaction takes place between two sides and produces a qualitative change in both.

That is exactly what happened when Arab thought in this period came into contact with the intellectual heritage of the Greeks, Indians, Persians, and Christians, as well as the wider cultural and civilizational traditions of the peoples whom the Arabs encountered in many different ways after the rise of Islam.

This interaction produced a qualitative change not only in Arab thought. It also had a major effect on the direction of philosophical and scientific thought in other parts of the world, especially once its mature results began to appear from the twelfth century onward.

At the same time, it changed the cultures of the peoples who formed the other side of this interaction. Here we mean the non-Arab peoples across wide areas of Asia and Africa who adopted Islam, whether as a religious faith or simply as a social and political system.

One sign of this qualitative change is that many of the Muʿtazilite thinkers and their opponents during the period when philosophical thinking began to emerge were themselves not of Arab origin. The same is true of many later philosophers who came to represent the distinctive character of Arab philosophical thought. They came from peoples living across the eastern lands stretching from India and Persia to the regions south and north of the Caucasus, Asia Minor, Central Asia, North Africa, and the rest of the Maghreb.

All of this is very different from saying that Arab-Islamic thought merely **received** foreign intellectual and philosophical influences.

To describe the relationship as mere passive influence is to make Arab-Islamic thought a follower: something that copies and transmits rather than creates.

Yet in the previous chapter we saw ideas, theories, and concepts among both the Muʿtazila and their opponents that had indeed been influenced by similar ideas among Greek, Indian, and other philosophers. At the same time, however, we saw that Muʿtazilite thinkers approached these foreign ideas from within their own social and ideological setting. That setting, within Arab-Islamic society, formed the root and foundation even of the internal workings of Muʿtazilite thought itself.

The Muʿtazilite relationship with the cultures around it was therefore one of internal and objective **fusion and transformation**. It did not depend on a deliberate mechanical process of accepting some ideas and rejecting others, nor on an artificial act of picking and choosing.

On this basis, we can say that the Muʿtazila absorbed from these cultures whatever enabled them to deepen their own ideas about the two principles of **divine unity** and **divine justice**, as they understood them within their own Islamic and Muʿtazilite framework.

“Absorption” here means something much broader than acceptance or rejection. In fact, it makes that distinction almost meaningless. It means taking in the whole body of intellectual material available in these cultures, whether it agreed with Islamic ideology or contradicted it.

This is why, throughout our discussion of Muʿtazilite questions in the previous two chapters, we repeatedly found that even the ideas, theories, and concepts they drew from outside were changed in the process. Sometimes they were developed further. In every case, they were made to serve the Muʿtazila’s own basic direction and starting points, both in doctrine and in method.

That, in itself, is an act of intellectual creation.

One example is Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf’s discussion of the divine attributes, one of the questions connected with the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity.

As we saw, when discussing the unity of God’s essence and arguing that the attributes and the essence are one rather than many, he said that God is knowing through a knowledge that is His essence, powerful through a power that is His essence, and living through a life that is His essence.

What he means is that God’s essence **is** knowledge, power, and life. These qualities are not something separate from the divine essence. They are the essence itself.

Al-Shahrastānī says that this view was borrowed from philosophers “who held that His essence is one and contains no multiplicity of any kind, and that the attributes are not meanings existing beyond the essence and residing in it; rather, they are the essence itself.”[^V2-471]

Al-Shahrastānī then says: “If Abū al-Hudhayl establishes these attributes as aspects of the essence, then they are exactly the hypostases of the Christians.”[^V2-472]

Dr. Jamīl Ṣalībā, meanwhile, says that Abū al-Hudhayl’s view “resembles Plato’s claim that the highest good is intellect, life, and soul, because knowledge comes through intellect and power through soul. It also resembles what the philosophers of Alexandria said about the three principles: the One, Intellect, and Soul.”[^V2-473]

If it is true that Abū al-Hudhayl borrowed his view from philosophers—meaning here the Islamic philosophers—or from the Christian doctrine of the hypostases, or especially from Plato, or from the philosophers of Alexandria, he still gave the question a form of his own.

He began from the specifically Muʿtazilite understanding of divine unity. He did not simply adopt those earlier theories as they stood, nor did he accept their philosophical direction apart from his own Islamic and Muʿtazilite starting point.

### 2 — The Question of Reason

Our study of Muʿtazilite thought has shown that the Muʿtazila were so committed to reason that this commitment sometimes came close to outweighing their adherence to certain established principles of Islam.

They made reason the judge that could move Qurʾānic texts away from their apparent meaning whenever that meaning conflicted with what reason required.

We even saw them make human freedom of choice take priority over the freedom of God’s will and, in this sense, place a limit on divine power.

Why?

Because their principle of human freedom necessarily depended on the existence of reason. And reason itself would have no meaning unless human beings also possessed the power to choose. Without reason and choice, people could not be held responsible for their actions, and divine justice would no longer be truly just.

Reason, then, stands at the center of this entire system.

The same is true of their theory of knowledge.

For the Muʿtazila, there were almost no limits to the reach of reason, either in the natural world or beyond it. Even knowledge of God was not merely within reason’s reach. It was reason’s first necessary duty and, indeed, one of its most basic forms of knowledge.

There was therefore no question in existence that the human mind was completely incapable of understanding in some way.

Even sensory knowledge fell within the work of reason in two ways.

First, things perceived by the senses were themselves objects of rational knowledge.

Second, reason was what transformed sensory perceptions into rational understanding.

Many earlier and modern scholars have thought that the Muʿtazila went too far in extending the authority of reason.

One modern scholar, however, found the reason for this apparent excess in what he described as something like “a reaction to the state of certain doctrines in their time.”

He explained that the Muʿtazila “affirmed the authority of reason, and exaggerated it, in the face of people who recognized no authority for reason at all. These people said: we stop at the text. Where the text is clear and decisive, we follow it. Where it is ambiguous or obscure, we leave its meaning to God.”

He explained their insistence on freedom of choice in the same way. They “went to an extreme in defending it because they faced people who stripped human beings of all will, making a person like a feather blown by the wind or a piece of wood tossed in the sea.”

In this scholar’s view, “error in affirming the authority of reason and freedom of will, even when taken too far, is better than going too far in denying them.”

He continues:

> “If the Muʿtazilite teachings on these two matters—the authority of reason and freedom of will—had prevailed among Muslims from the age of the Muʿtazila until today, Muslims would have occupied a very different place in history from the one they occupy now. Submission has left them powerless, determinism has paralyzed them, and passive dependence has held them back.”[^V2-474]

In our view, this is a sound and realistic explanation of the Muʿtazilite position on reason and human freedom of will, despite the author’s description of that position as excessive or extreme. That description itself comes from a cautious, even conservative, view of the issue.

But his explanation deals only with the immediate intellectual side of the question. It does not address the social dimension that we uncovered earlier in our discussion of the Qadarites.

His final comment, however, leads us to a conclusion that we consider extremely important: the historical value of the Muʿtazila’s insistence on reason in that period.

Their firm and courageous defence of reason helped, in our view, to drive intellectual life rapidly and far into new areas of rational and philosophical inquiry.

In doing so, it helped prepare the ground not only for the coming philosophical period but also for the later rise of scientific activity, both in breadth and in depth.

By opening so many fields of knowledge to rational inquiry, the Muʿtazila helped create the strong intellectual foundation needed for the later development of philosophy and science on the wide scale that would characterize the Arab-Islamic world for at least four centuries.

Ahmed Amin’s explanation also helps us understand a second point.

It shows how deeply Muʿtazilite thought was connected with the wider intellectual life of its own society and period, and with the many competing positions people were taking on the major questions of that society.

This is what Ahmed Amin means when he says that the Muʿtazilite position on reason “was unavoidable, because it was something like a reaction to the state of certain doctrines in their time.”

And this is another example of the point we stressed in the previous section: the process of **fusion and transformation**.

There was an Arab-Islamic intellectual world already dealing with its own questions and its own intense internal conflicts, even as it was also engaging with intellectual sources from outside.

There is a third issue that matters here when we try to assess the historical importance of the Muʿtazila’s belief in the almost unlimited role of reason in questions of religion, existence, and nature.

Again, we can begin with Ahmed Amin himself.

He saw one of the Muʿtazila’s weaknesses in the fact that:

> “They went too far in reasoning from the unseen by analogy with the seen—that is, in comparing God with human beings and subjecting God Almighty to the laws of this world. They required God, for example, to be just according to the human conception of justice and according to justice as a worldly system.”[^V2-475]

### 3 — The Meaning of Reasoning from the Seen to the Unseen

This is certainly a clear feature of Muʿtazilite thought, especially in the method they used when discussing divine justice.

But we see another side to it that Ahmed Amin does not.

Although metaphysical questions occupied most of the Muʿtazila’s intellectual activity, their thought never completely lost its roots in material reality—in the **seen world**.

This is why, in many Muʿtazilite ideas, theories, and concepts, we have found an underlying recognition of the objective existence of the material world, sometimes implicit and sometimes openly stated.

None of this, however, took their thinking outside its broadly metaphysical framework.

When a Muʿtazilite approached questions of divine unity through reason, he still began, above all, from a position of religious faith.

Of course, we should not expect anything very different in that period or in that society.

The Muʿtazila were innovative thinkers, but they were taking only the first steps toward philosophical thought. In an age and society such as theirs, we cannot expect them to have broken beyond the intellectual limits of their world much further than they actually did. And they had already crossed those limits with unusual courage from the moment they entered the struggle over the basic questions of religious belief.

But is this philosophical direction alone what determines the Muʿtazila’s place in the history of Arab-Islamic thought?

We believe something else is even more decisive. It can be measured historically on the one hand and rationally on the other.

What is it?

First, they gave reason a central place in the theory of knowledge.

They did not separate knowledge from religious faith. Their thought remained within the close connection between knowledge and faith established by Islam. Yet even within that framework, they made reason the primary source of religious knowledge.

Second, through this philosophical direction, they brought Arab thought into the realm of **concepts**—that is, into the realm of rational abstraction, which represents a higher form of conscious thought.

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī had already taken the first step in this direction, as we saw in our discussion of the Qadarites. But he did not move beyond the simplest stage of abstraction. He did not use philosophical analysis and synthesis in the way the Muʿtazila later did.

The Muʿtazila developed this method significantly beyond anything that had existed before them.

They began working with logical categories and philosophical terms such as **substance** and **accident**, along with the many rational questions that followed from them. Much of this represented real progress at the theoretical level.

At the same time, we also find materialist elements appearing within these discussions—sometimes openly, sometimes hidden behind idealist veils that could be thin in one case and much thicker in another.

The forms of materialism we can discover within Muʿtazilite thought must, of course, be understood in their own historical setting. They had a specifically Islamic religious character. They belonged to a society far removed from our own, one in which religious thought dominated the different forms of intellectual life.

In this sense, it is right to say that the Muʿtazila were the starting point of Arab-Islamic philosophy.

### 4 — The Question of Causality

The previous chapter also showed how firmly the Muʿtazila held to the principle of causality in explaining events and actions.

They even connected God’s creation of the world with this principle.

We also saw that they linked causation in nature with the idea of responsibility at the human and social level, without reducing human action to rigid determinism.

They distinguished between causation in nature and causation in human action.

Natural causes, they said, operate according to fixed and necessary laws.

Human action includes another element: **will**.

This was consistent with their doctrine of human freedom of choice and with the principle on which that doctrine rested: reason.

The progressive importance of the Muʿtazila’s defence of causality, and of the theoretical arguments they developed around it, becomes clearer when we compare their position with the opposing view that was widespread in their time.

The Ashʿarites in particular represented this opposing position, and they rejected the principle of causality completely.

Once causality was denied, reason was also pushed out of the field of knowledge, and knowledge became tied entirely to a divine source.

A comparison between the Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite positions on causality—and between the theories of knowledge that followed from accepting or rejecting causality—therefore shows the importance of what the Muʿtazila did.

They confronted an intellectual current that denied the existence of objective laws governing the relationships between things and events throughout the universe. In doing so, that current also denied the possibility that reason could achieve any real independence in knowledge, whatever kind of knowledge was involved.

The Muʿtazila stood against a current supported at the time by a large body of influential religious thinkers. These included the Ashʿarites, and later sections of the theologians and members of both Sunni and Shiʿi schools.

Despite all their own disagreements, the Muʿtazila were united in confronting this current.

Their weapon was an advanced body of theoretical thought through which they defended both reason and the principle of causality: causality as a universal law, and also as a rational principle underlying the other objective laws of the universe, nature, and the human world.

This part of Muʿtazilite thought gives us another element in a scientific historical understanding of their progressive role in intellectual history.

That role belongs not only to Arab-Islamic history. It can also be placed on the wider level of human intellectual history, because the region in which Muʿtazilite thought flourished later became one of the great centers of scientific thought for a long period during the Middle Ages.

There is little doubt that the Muʿtazila played an important part in preparing the intellectual conditions that made it possible for this region to become such a major historical center.

### 5 — Rational Inquiry into Nature

As we saw in the previous chapter, the Muʿtazila made a number of attempts to study the natural world, or the material world more generally.

But these attempts had a basic weakness.

They relied almost completely on pure rational thought when studying material phenomena. They did not rely on sensory observation and experiment to discover the general laws governing those phenomena.

In other words, they did not begin with particular observable cases and things in the material world, study the relationships between them, and then use those relationships to understand natural phenomena and derive general laws.

Instead, they tried to reach such laws through pure reasoning, apart from observing phenomena in their actual movement.

To put it another way, they relied on abstract logic rather than on the inner, dialectical logic of natural phenomena themselves—the way those phenomena actually move, change, and develop.

This abstract method led some of them to static conclusions in which nature appeared fixed and motionless, without real change or development.

Their use of abstract logic in studying the natural world therefore created a contradiction between their theory and their practice.

At the theoretical level, especially in their theory of knowledge, we saw them recognize the relationship between sensory knowledge and rational knowledge.

They understood that what we perceive through the senses becomes material for rational knowledge.

We also saw that they reached an essentially sound understanding of how theoretical reason transforms sensory perceptions into rational concepts.

For thinkers living in their historical circumstances, this was a remarkable achievement.

But they were unable to apply this theory of knowledge to their own attempts to study nature and the human world.

We saw this, for example, in their different views on the question of the indivisible substance, or “the part that cannot be divided”—what later became known as the problem of atomism.

We also saw it in their discussions of substance and accident, motion, and similar questions.

As for the human world, considered as part of this observable material world, the Muʿtazila discussed many questions involving human action and the physical powers connected with it.

They did this especially when discussing a person’s capacity to act and trying to define that capacity in physical, spatial, and temporal terms. These questions grew out of their wider discussion of the relationship between God’s power and will and human power and will.

Yet they approached these questions through abstract reasoning in order to build further rational judgments about the relationship between divine power and human power.

In other words, they were discussing physical and objective questions that really required scientific and experimental investigation.

We should also keep one important fact in mind.

What we know of Muʿtazilite thought on these questions comes mostly from sources that were not written by the Muʿtazila themselves. We therefore do not have direct access to the exact methods by which they investigated these issues or argued for their conclusions.

In later sources—such as al-Ashʿarī, al-Shahrastānī, and others—their views appear broken into pieces and scattered across different discussions, with the connections between them often lost.

We will explain this and its historical causes below.

The gap between theory and practice in Muʿtazilite thought had real historical causes.

The first is something we have already mentioned here and at several points in the previous chapter.

When the Muʿtazila studied questions concerning nature and the human world, they were usually not studying them for their own sake. They used them mainly as tools for dealing with questions belonging to the world of metaphysics.

Second, the historical conditions of their time did not yet provide them with the experimental means needed to investigate such problems.

The experimental sciences of nature and humanity had not yet developed far enough in practice to place these tools in the hands of thinkers carrying out theoretical investigations of this kind.

One exception must be made here: al-Jāḥiẓ.

He was a Muʿtazilite whom historians regard as the founder of a distinctive tendency within Muʿtazilism and as one of al-Naẓẓām’s most important students.

He stands apart from the rest of the group because of his experimental tendency and his use of something approaching a scientific method in this field.

Even so, this tendency did not appear as clearly or fully in his Muʿtazilite theological views as it did in his scientific and literary works.

### 6 — The Erasure of the Muʿtazilite Heritage

There is a well-known historical fact that is both disturbing and difficult to explain.

Was it merely a coincidence that, not long after the Muʿtazila disappeared from the center of intellectual life during the caliphate of al-Mutawakkil in 847 CE, the original sources of Muʿtazilite thought almost completely disappeared from Arab libraries as well?

These were the works and documents in which Muʿtazilite thinkers themselves had set out their ideas and theoretical principles in their own words and in complete form.

It is difficult for a researcher to believe that some historical accident alone caused such extraordinary damage to thought, knowledge, and history.

Arab-Islamic intellectual history has certainly seen many tragedies of this kind. But the disappearance of the Muʿtazilite heritage happened under conditions very different from those in which the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage as a whole later began to scatter and disappear.

Why, then, did Muʿtazilite thought alone suffer this fate at a much earlier stage, long before the later conditions that brought destruction to the heritage more generally?

Perhaps the answer lies in the progressive features of Muʿtazilite thought that we have described throughout the previous two chapters.

These may have been precisely what led to the sudden disappearance of its heritage from Arab libraries so early in the history of Arab intellectual life.

A number of conservative intellectual and political currents joined together against the Muʿtazila.

Their hostility appeared in many forms. The most severe was the almost complete erasure of original Muʿtazilite writings and documents.

As a result, only one original source survived into later times: *al-Intiṣār* by Abū al-Ḥasan al-Khayyāṭ, even though historians of Islamic sects and schools mention many other Muʿtazilite works that remain unknown to us today.[^V2-476]

The destruction of this large and fertile intellectual heritage has prevented us from studying it as a complete and connected body of thought.

Instead, we have had to reconstruct it from fragments scattered through non-Muʿtazilite sources, especially Ashʿarite sources written by some of the Muʿtazila’s fiercest opponents.

The heritage therefore reaches us in torn pieces, without the unity that originally held it together.

Its internal structure has been lost.

As researchers, we have also lost the ability to watch the system develop in the complex and logical form in which it originally arose, grew, and changed.

This makes it extremely difficult to reconstruct a new overall picture that truly matches the logic of the original system.

If, in the previous two chapters, we have managed to identify a degree of consistency and coherence in the thought of some leading Muʿtazilites, we have done so only by feeling our way along a number of major lines that can still be followed through a record broken and interrupted at many points.

In our view, the tragedy of the Muʿtazila’s intellectual heritage—the effort of their enemies to erase it—was even more severe than the physical persecution they suffered beginning under the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil.

Indeed, it is more accurate to say that this first tragedy was not theirs alone.

It was also a tragedy for thought, knowledge, and history.

We can now ask: why was there such bitter hostility toward the Muʿtazila? And why did they suffer this double tragedy?

The answer is clear.

The rational and liberating character that dominated both the content and method of Muʿtazilite thought was highly progressive when measured against the conditions of their time and society.

It was this character that brought together a wide range of conservative religious schools, intellectual tendencies, and social groups against them, especially groups whose social position was closely tied to the institutions of the caliphate’s theocratic state.

Among these were, above all, the traditionalists devoted to hadith and many of the jurists.

Despite all the differences between these groups, their opposition to Muʿtazilite rationalism united them on common ground.

It is true, as we have said before, that Muʿtazilite thought as a whole never left the framework of Islamic ideology. That broad framework was shared by the Muʿtazila and their Ashʿarite opponents.

But we must still pay attention to what distinguished the Muʿtazila.

That difference split people who shared the same broad religious ideology into two separate schools: Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite.

And these were not simply different schools. They became rival and, in important ways, opposing ones.

The Muʿtazila’s insistence on reason and on human freedom to act or refrain from acting pushed their thought down a distinctive path.

As we saw in Chapters Four and Five, this led them to conclusions that objectively turned Muʿtazilite thought into something like a fuse capable of setting off contradictions within the very ideology to which it belonged.

Hostility toward the Muʿtazila was therefore hostility toward these conclusions, because of the cracks they opened within that ideological structure.

This helps explain why the same wave of hostility eventually spread to science and philosophy as well.

Both the practical sciences and philosophy rely on principles of rational knowledge, even though each uses them in a different way.

Yet history shows that this wave of hostility, violent as it was—and even when it became physically bloody—could not extinguish the spark that Muʿtazilite thought had helped ignite.

### 7 — How Did the Rationalist Movement Survive Repression?

We can ask the same question in another way.

How was the movement of rational inquiry, especially in its philosophical form, able to continue developing despite the continuing wave of opposition?

One modern scholar explains this by saying that rational inquiry into Islamic doctrine found an organized tool in logic. Logic gave the movement clear theoretical forms and made it difficult to suppress.[^V2-477]

But this explanation does not tell the whole story.

It is true that the introduction of logic gave the movement greater organization and helped its thinkers express their theories in a more systematic way.

But logic did not do much more than this formal work. It did not add a new dimension to the movement’s intellectual content, its direction, or the subjects it addressed.

For that reason, it is hard to believe that formal logic alone gave rational and philosophical thought the strength to survive and continue developing despite the repeated waves of repression directed against it from the persecution of the Muʿtazila down to the age of al-Ghazālī.

In our view, the source of this resilience—the force that prevented rational inquiry from being swept away by intellectual and physical repression and thrown outside history—was the same force that had brought it into existence in the first place.

That force was **life itself**.

More precisely, it was the continuing development of Arab-Islamic society.

The development of society had first created the need for rational inquiry among the early Qadarites and later among those who followed them.

That same social development also created the conditions that allowed the movement to survive and continue.

Indeed, the continued existence and further development of rational inquiry had now become closely connected with the development and progress of society itself.

This was especially true of cultural development.

The foundations of cultural life were becoming steadily stronger as social life developed and as the movement of translation and Arabization brought a growing range of foreign cultures into Arabic.

The social relations created under the caliphate produced increasing interaction between peoples with very different historical backgrounds.

By this stage, that process had become too powerful for conservative or repressive forces simply to block it.

We should also remember the political problems created by religious division.

These divisions demanded arguments about doctrine. And because of the cultural development we have described, those arguments increasingly took a rational form that was historically linked with philosophical thought.

This reality itself made logical and philosophical thought the leading and most developed form through which people could express the rapidly changing conditions of Abbasid society.

For all these reasons, the campaign against the Muʿtazila and against the rational and philosophical direction whose earliest foundations they had laid could not destroy that direction or stop its development.

In fact, the opposite happened.

The hostility directed against it, together with persecution and physical violence, gave new momentum to philosophical thought and won it new supporters across different intellectual and cultural circles, including within the Islamic schools themselves.

This was especially true among groups whose ideologies stood against the ideology of the caliphate’s theocratic ruling system.

Ibn Khaldūn makes a statement that is openly sectarian in tone but also contains an implicit historical insight. From it, we can draw a picture that supports what we have said about why rational and philosophical inquiry survived and continued despite growing repression.

Ibn Khaldūn tries to explain the conditions from which the Muʿtazilite “heresy”—his term for Muʿtazilite thought—emerged. In doing so, he also explains the source of the strength that allowed Muʿtazilite ideas to survive and spread.

His account suggests that the development of the sciences in their period helped philosophy become widely known and drew people’s attention toward it.

This created the conditions in which the Muʿtazila could introduce their “heresy” by using philosophy in their arguments.

Their opponents found it difficult to answer them until al-Ashʿarī appeared and began using rational arguments in the same way they did. This allowed him to refute them.

Once the leading Ashʿarites themselves adopted philosophy as a weapon against the Muʿtazila, theologians were able to bring philosophical studies into *kalām*.

As Ibn Khaldūn puts it, “From the time of the later theologians onward, philosophy became part of *kalām*.”[^V2-478]

Ibn Khaldūn’s account, presented in this way, contains an important historical truth.

Philosophical thought in the age of the Muʿtazila had become a response to real conditions created by the development of culture and by the scientific revival in its many forms.

Philosophy had become an organic part of the inner life of society as a whole.

Formal logic was therefore only one part of the story.

Rational and philosophical inquiry had become powerful enough to impose itself even on some of its most conservative opponents.

This does not mean, however, that the tragedy of Muʿtazilite thought—which at the same time became a tragedy for philosophy itself—did not obstruct the development of rational thought in the Arab-Islamic world.

The unfortunate reality is that this tragedy dealt the wider rational movement a serious setback.

Its effects remained visible until the end of that movement’s historical period, when the civilizational role of the Arabs declined in both East and West from the fifteenth century onward.

Without this setback, the scientific advances already visible in the ninth century suggest that rational and philosophical thought might have moved in a more realistic direction and become more closely connected with the advances being made in the practical sciences of the period.

Instead, beginning with the reign of al-Mutawakkil, a conservative traditionalist wave became dominant.

The historian al-Masʿūdī describes the change in these words:

> “When the caliphate passed to al-Mutawakkil, he ordered people to abandon speculative debate and to leave behind the practices that had prevailed under al-Muʿtaṣim and al-Wāthiq. He ordered people to submit and follow established authority, and he instructed the leading hadith scholars to teach hadith and openly promote the Sunna and the community.”[^V2-479]

And:

> “Although he [al-Mutawakkil] was one of the most unjust of the caliphs, the people of the Sunna praised him and overlooked his wrongdoing because he ended the *miḥna*”—that is, the period of Muʿtazilite dominance. “Many hadith scholars even reported dreams in which they were told that God had forgiven him.”[^V2-480]

Al-Suyūṭī, discussing the same subject, says that al-Mutawakkil:

> “…brought the hadith scholars to Samarra”—his capital—“gave them generous gifts, honored them, and ordered them to teach the traditions concerning the divine attributes and the vision of God.”

These were two questions that the Muʿtazila rejected.

Al-Suyūṭī continues:

> “Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba sat in the mosque of al-Ruṣāfa, and around thirty thousand people gathered around him. His brother sat in the mosque of al-Manṣūr, and around thirty thousand gathered around him. The people prayed abundantly for al-Mutawakkil and went to great lengths in praising and honoring him.”

Then al-Mutawakkil ordered his governor in Egypt to shave the beard of Egypt’s chief judge, Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Abī al-Layth, who was a Muʿtazilite, have him beaten, and parade him through the streets on a donkey.

The order was carried out.

He then replaced him as judge with al-Ḥārith ibn Miskīn, a follower of Mālik.[^V2-481]

The Mālikī school to which al-Ḥārith ibn Miskīn belonged was, as is well known, among the legal schools most firmly attached to the traditionalist approach. It relied very heavily on hadith and was among those most strongly opposed to rational inquiry in matters of religious doctrine and law.

This helps us understand the meaning of the return, under al-Mutawakkil, to the dominance of this earlier traditionalist tendency after the Muʿtazila suffered their political defeat at his hands.

It was therefore a reactionary response to the Muʿtazilite movement, which had firmly established the role of reason not only in questions of religious belief, but also in Islamic law.

Historically, the Muʿtazila had made a clear distinction between these two fields: belief and law. From the third Islamic century onward, they separated the subjects of *kalām*—the study of religious beliefs—from those of *fiqh*, the study of Islamic law. Before that, “all the major books of *kalām* recognized by most Muslims had dealt with some questions of jurisprudence as well.”[^V2-482]

The Muʿtazila thus became “the first Islamic school to free itself from all the tendencies of the jurists, and the only purely theological school”[^V2-483] among the five major groups into which Muslims were then divided: the Sunnis, Muʿtazila, Murjiʾa, Shiʿa, and Kharijites.[^V2-484] They held that every qualified scholar who exercised independent judgment could arrive at a valid answer in questions of law.[^V2-485] Muʿtazilites could therefore be found in every school of jurisprudence, “even among the scholars of Hadith, who are usually regarded as the fiercest enemies of the theologians.”[^V2-486]

This fact about the Muʿtazila gives us further evidence of the deep influence their thinking had on the intellectual life of their age. They helped direct it toward rational inquiry and, later, toward philosophy in particular. Their influence was so strong and so deeply rooted that successive waves of hostility toward reason and rational knowledge could not wipe it out.

# Chapter Six

## Kalām

### 1 — From Quantity to Quality

Scientific method points us toward an important fact in the history of human societies and civilizations: when gradual quantitative changes build up over time, their eventual transformation into something qualitatively new can take many different forms.

The result may be political, social, or intellectual. It may take the form of a new theoretical outlook, or it may erupt as revolutionary violence.

Engels studied the different forms taken by revolutionary opposition to medieval feudalism. He found that, depending on the historical conditions, this opposition appeared at one time as mysticism, at another as open heresy, and at another as armed revolt.[^V2-487]

The particular form taken by a qualitative transformation in any society and at any time is determined by the concrete conditions of real life. Sometimes those conditions may be ripe for several kinds of transformation at once. Political, social, and intellectual changes may all occur together. They may be accompanied by armed uprisings, they may prepare the way for them, or development may proceed without revolutionary violence at all.

This idea helps us understand the long process of accumulation in Arab-Islamic society during the seventh and eighth centuries, a process whose most representative intellectual transformation was *kalām*.

The accumulation began with a succession of events immediately after the Prophet’s death. At first, conflict centered on who would hold the caliphate. Under ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, it became a struggle over the material advantages that the caliphate had made available to the Umayyads. After ʿUthmān’s death, conflict between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya led to two wars: the Battle of the Camel and the Battle of Ṣiffīn.

All of this was followed by the rise of the first medieval Arab state in which the idea of the state appeared in a form that, by the standards of its own age, can be called a developed civilization state:[^V2-488] the Umayyad state.

The Umayyad state was the first major qualitative transformation produced by the accumulation of conflicts that came before it. This transformation was political above all, but it rested on an economic and social form and later produced an intellectual one as well.

The Umayyad ruling power became an active part of the feudal system of production. It protected that system and worked to develop and renew its productive forces, especially in Syria. This determined the economic form of the transformation. At the same time, it also determined its social form, because the Umayyad state’s economic position within feudal relations of production necessarily shaped social relations and the wider social order.

The intellectual form appeared in the first three major competing theories that emerged from the earlier conflicts and from the Battles of the Camel and Ṣiffīn: the Umayyad position, the ʿAlid position—that is, the position of ʿAlī’s supporters—and the Kharijite position.

But once quantity and quality come together in a transformation of this kind, the process does not stop. The dialectical relationship between them cannot simply freeze in place. Constant change is the essential revolutionary feature of this relationship.

Every new quality contains within itself continuing quantitative changes, and these eventually produce further qualitative transformations. The process then begins again.

In Volume I, we saw how new contradictions with new characteristics began to develop within feudal relations of production and under the political rule of the Umayyad state. By the time we reached the reign of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, these contradictions had become increasingly intense. Their gradual accumulation then produced new qualitative changes in several forms at once: political, social, intellectual, and theoretical, accompanied by armed uprisings.

In Volume I, we identified the most important features of each of these forms. But the intellectual and theoretical form, which concerns us here, now needs to be examined again and placed within the actual historical development of Arab-Islamic society under the Umayyads.

*Kalām*[^V2-489] began simply as *talk* about the question of divine decree. At that stage it was not yet a separate field of knowledge. It was one intellectual form taken by the growing social anger of various groups: the *mawālī*, agricultural workers, small landowners, slaves working either on the land or in public services, and the large numbers of poor and destitute people living in the cities, including small tradesmen and workers in craft shops.

At the same time that armed revolts[^V2-490] were breaking out against Umayyad rule in widely separated parts of the vast empire, the school of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī—and the intellectuals, thinkers, and leading scholars of Arabic and Islamic law who developed from it—adopted another form of opposition. They challenged both the absolute political power of the Umayyads and the ideology of absolute predestination used to support it.

The voices of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, Maʿbad al-Juhanī, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, and others like them were the first voices in Arab-Islamic thought to rise openly against official doctrine and against the determinism of the economically and politically dominant group. Their message was clear: there is no divine decree that completely and irresistibly controls the human will.

As this intellectual opposition developed, rooted above all in social and political opposition, the changing society continually placed new questions before the thinkers of the time. On one side, the causes driving opposition continued to accumulate. On the other, social development itself created conditions that pushed thinkers to examine these questions more and more deeply.

The question of divine decree became closely tied to the question of whether human beings are free to choose their own actions, and this in turn was tied to their position toward the political authority then in power. From this starting point, the wider conflicts of society and politics began to appear in new intellectual forms based on abstract rational reflection.

Among the most important questions were the status of a Muslim who commits a major sin, the relationship between reason and faith, the meaning of justice in Islam, the proper attitude toward an unjust ruler,[^V2-491] the duty to command what is right and forbid what is wrong, and the meaning of God’s transcendence and unity.

For decades after the question of divine decree first appeared, discussions of these issues remained scattered across several different fields. They appeared in works of jurisprudence and legal theory,[^V2-492] and sometimes in philosophy, Sufism, and natural science. They had no clearly defined identity as a separate discipline and no systematic connection with one another.

Eventually, Arab thought reached a stage at which it was able to define and distinguish them more clearly.

At that point, these scattered discussions passed from a state of gradual quantitative accumulation into a distinct new form. They were classified as an independent field called *kalām*.

This meant that they had entered the broader stage of scientific classification that Arab thought as a whole was then beginning to reach. This was a genuinely advanced stage. Before it, the basic boundaries between different fields of knowledge were often unclear. The lines between jurisprudence, legal theory, and the foundations of religion could easily blur, as could those between grammar, rhetoric, and literature, or between Hadith, Qurʾanic commentary, history, and biography.

The reason was simple: each field had not yet developed its own clear boundaries, concepts, and categories.

This explains why the term *ʿilm al-kalām* appeared relatively late. It did not become common in books, debates, and intellectual struggles until the age of al-Maʾmūn,[^V2-493][^V2-494] around the end of the second and beginning of the third Islamic centuries—that is, the ninth century CE.

We think the name *ʿilm al-kalām* became a formal term for this newly independent field because it gave a fixed name to an ordinary expression people had already been using informally.

When they discussed one of the questions that would later belong to this field, they often described what they were doing simply as *kalām*—“talk” or “discussion.”

We can see an example in a passage quoted by Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr (d. 463 AH/1070 CE):

> Muṣʿab ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Zubayrī reported that Mālik ibn Anas used to say: “I dislike discussion about religion.[^V2-495] The people of our city have always disliked it and warned against it—discussion of Jahm’s views, divine decree, and similar matters. I approve only of discussion concerning matters on which lawful action depends.”
>
> Abū ʿUmar said: “Mālik, may God have mercy on him, has made clear that discussion of matters connected with action was permitted in his view and in the view of the scholars of his city. He also tells us that by ‘discussion about religion’ he meant such matters as the views of Jahm, divine decree, and so on.”[^V2-496]

In this passage, the word *kalām* is used repeatedly for discussion of questions of religious belief—the same questions that later came to make up the field of *kalām*.

Before it became a technical term, however, the word was still being used in its ordinary linguistic sense of “speech” or “discussion.” Because it appeared so often when people spoke about what would later be called theological questions, the formal term *ʿilm al-kalām* eventually emerged during the period of classification as a fixed name for this already familiar usage.[^V2-497]

### 2 — Writing on Questions of Kalām

Historical evidence shows that Arabs began systematically recording knowledge and writing books during the first Islamic century, the seventh century CE.

This means that writing about questions later associated with *kalām* must also have begun during that period. After all, the most important intellectual questions debated from the second half of that century onward—and the questions around which sectarian and ideological battles became most intense—were precisely those concerning human freedom of action, followed by questions of justice, God’s attributes, the meaning of faith and its relationship to reason, the status of a Muslim who commits a major sin, and so on.

All of these later became questions belonging to the field called *kalām*.

The logic of the situation therefore strongly suggests—if it does not make it almost certain—that more was written about these questions, which occupied nearly the whole intellectual life of first-century Islamic society, than about many other subjects.[^V2-498]

Unfortunately, almost none of the works on *kalām* written during that period, and especially none of the Muʿtazilite works, survived even into the age immediately following it: the Abbasid period. If they had survived that long, we would surely have received at least some Umayyad writings on *kalām* and logic through Abbasid sources.

This historical fact raises an obvious question: why were these works lost?

We think the reason may be that Muʿtazilite thought at the time was especially productive, widespread, and attractive to the people of its society,[^V2-499] precisely because, as we have already said, it challenged official Umayyad ideology more strongly than other currents did.

It is therefore quite possible that the political authorities of the time, together with the intellectual groups that supported them, worked to suppress this body of thought and perhaps even destroy it. As a result, most of what we know about it comes from the writings of its opponents.

After the middle of the second Islamic century, the eighth century CE—and especially from the reign of al-Maʾmūn onward—the writing of works on *kalām* expanded enormously. It would hardly be an exaggeration to say that books on *kalām*, together with the intellectual battles they provoked, became the most visible feature of intellectual life at the time.

This continued until philosophy emerged as a field separate from *kalām*, and indeed as something standing opposite it: a new and more advanced kind of ideological weapon.

The main source of this remarkable growth in writing on *kalām* was the increasingly intense struggle between the two camps that came to dominate almost the entire field: the Muʿtazila and the Ashʿarites. We will return to this later.

### 3 — Definitions of Kalām

What exactly is *kalām*?

What are its main features and methods? What concepts distinguish it? What are its basic principles?

And who were the Muslim *mutakallimūn*, the practitioners of *kalām*? Were they only the Muʿtazila? Only the Ashʿarites? The Muʿtazila and Ashʿarites together, but no one else? Or should we also include the Shiʿa, Kharijites, Murjiʾa, and others?

How can we answer these questions scientifically, on the basis of historical documents and sources?
