The first thing a researcher naturally does when trying to find an answer is to turn to definitions of the field given by scholars who belonged to it, historians who wrote about it, and later researchers.

In principle, the definition of any field should help us identify exactly what that field is, because a definition is supposed to state its essential features in the most precise and concentrated form.

Unfortunately, the surviving definitions of *kalām* do not do this.

The earliest definition that has reached us[^V2-500] comes from Abū Naṣr al-Fārābī.[^V2-501] His definition of the “art of *kalām*” says only that it is:

> “a faculty by which a person can defend the particular beliefs and actions proclaimed by the founder of a religion, and refute through argument anything that opposes them.”[^V2-502]

This does almost nothing to answer the questions before us.

It tells us only the purpose of *kalām*: to defend the beliefs and practices laid down by the religious lawgiver. It tells us nothing at all about the field’s basic structure, foundations, or general principles.

Immediately after this definition, however, al-Fārābī discusses two further points. First, he distinguishes jurisprudence from *kalām*. Second, he describes the different “methods and opinions by which religions are to be defended.”[^V2-503]

For al-Fārābī, the essential difference between jurisprudence and *kalām* is this: the jurist takes the beliefs and actions laid down by the religious lawgiver as accepted foundations and then uses them to derive further rulings. The theologian’s task is simply to defend the very principles that the jurist takes for granted.

Al-Fārābī then explains how such a defense might be carried out.

But he does not present one specific method of *kalām*. Instead, he describes four different “methods” used by four groups of theologians, without telling us which one he himself accepts.

The first is the method of those who reject reason as a means of defending religious beliefs.

The second is the method of those who compare these beliefs with what is known through the senses, what is commonly accepted, and what reason establishes. If the beliefs agree with these, they use that agreement to defend them.

If there is a contradiction, they try to interpret the wording of the religious beliefs in a way that removes the conflict.

If interpretation cannot solve the problem, they try instead to challenge the sensory evidence, commonly accepted opinions, or rational conclusions and reinterpret them so that they agree with the religious beliefs.

If these forms of evidence themselves conflict with one another, they accept whichever ones agree with the religious beliefs and reject the others.

Finally, if none of these methods works and the contradiction remains between the religious beliefs on one side and sensory evidence, accepted opinion, or rational judgment on the other, then the religious beliefs must simply be accepted as the truth and defended on that basis.

The third method is to search other religions for every objectionable or scandalous feature that can be used to attack and discredit them. In this way, its followers defend their own religion.

The fourth is the method of those who defend their religion by making it appear attractive to others by whatever means happen to work—even if this requires “lying, sophistry, slander,[^V2-504] and sheer stubbornness.”[^V2-505]

So al-Fārābī gives us little more than a vague general description that defines almost nothing.

There is another problem as well. His treatment of theological method does not give the Muʿtazila their proper place among the theologians.

Where exactly are the Muʿtazila in al-Fārābī’s picture?

Perhaps they belong among the followers of the second method. But if so, the picture is unstable and incomplete. It does not clearly show the full character of their rationalist position.

In al-Fārābī’s account—if the Muʿtazila are indeed the group he means—they ultimately reject the judgment of reason whenever they cannot reconcile it with the meaning of the religious text.

But is this really an accurate description of the Muʿtazila?

It does not seem so.

One of the first things we know about them is that they developed a concept of faith radically different from that held by most Muslims. For them, knowledge and understanding were essential parts of faith itself.[^V2-506]

This means that a faith not based on knowledge and understanding—on rational conviction—could not count as genuine faith.

The Muʿtazila also held that good and evil can be known by reason. In other words, whether something is good or evil exists objectively in the thing itself and does not depend on whether the religious lawgiver commands or forbids it.

A command to do one thing and a prohibition against another simply confirm the goodness or evil already present objectively in them.

Reason can recognize this objective reality on its own, even without knowing whether the religious lawgiver has commanded or forbidden the act.

This is why the Muʿtazila described good and evil as rational. They also described them as intrinsic, meaning that their goodness or evil exists objectively in the thing itself and does not come from outside it—that is, it does not come from the commands and prohibitions of religious law.

Taken together, these positions on faith and on rationally knowable good and evil show that reason occupies a much higher and firmer place in Muʿtazilite thought than it does among the followers of al-Fārābī’s second theological method.

If reason had held no greater place among the Muʿtazila than al-Fārābī’s account suggests, Sunni opposition to them would have been far less intense than the history of intellectual conflict shows it to have been from the birth of the movement down to the present day.

“Down to the present day”?

Yes, because even contemporary researchers sometimes write about the Muʿtazila with a hostility no less severe than that of their ancient enemies.[^V2-507]

Al-Fārābī’s picture of the second theological method ultimately makes the religious text the final judge.

But both the historical record of Muʿtazilite thought and the surviving documents of that thought show something different. For the Muʿtazila, reason is the judge when dealing with ambiguous Qurʾanic verses. It is also the judge when evaluating prophetic Hadith: if a report conflicts with reason and cannot be interpreted in a rationally acceptable way, they reject it as inauthentic.[^V2-508]

Even so, despite our criticism of al-Fārābī’s definition of *kalām* and despite the unclear place of the Muʿtazila in his account of its methods, his discussion does give us something important that we do not find in the other definitions available to us.

His account includes several different theological schools and methods.

From this, we learn that *kalām* did not belong to one Muslim school alone. It was an intellectual and ideological field shared by several schools and groups.

Other definitions take the opposite approach. They restrict *kalām* either to the Ashʿarites or to the Muʿtazila.

Very few original Muʿtazilite texts have reached us directly. They are, in fact, extremely rare. On this particular question, we have found only one passage, by al-Khayyāṭ, who says:

> “You should know that *kalām* belongs to them”—meaning the Muʿtazila—“and to no one else.”[^V2-509]

The remaining definitions are Ashʿarite. In all of them, *kalām* appears as a purely Ashʿarite discipline, as if the Muʿtazila had never had anything to do with it, and as if no group outside the Sunnis had ever taken part in it.

Consider, for example, Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī’s explanation of the “purpose of *kalām*”:

> “Its purpose is to preserve the creed of the Sunnis and protect it from the confusion introduced by the people of innovation. (...) Then Satan planted in the minds of the innovators ideas that contradicted the Sunna. They became absorbed in them and came close to disturbing the true belief of its followers. So God raised up a group of theologians and moved them to defend the Sunna through ordered argument, exposing the deceptions of the new innovators who opposed the inherited teaching of the Sunnis. From this arose *kalām* and its practitioners, and so on.”[^V2-510]

If we take al-Ghazālī’s words at face value, then the history of *kalām* begins only when Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī founded his school in opposition to the Muʿtazila.

Everything the Muʿtazila had written and debated in the field before that point would then have to be erased from the history of *kalām*.

Ibn Khaldūn follows the same path in his definition. He begins:

> “*Kalām* is a field of knowledge that argues for the beliefs of faith through rational proofs and refutes innovators who depart in their beliefs from the doctrines of the early Muslims and the Sunnis.”[^V2-511]

As he explains this definition, it becomes clear that by “innovators who depart in their beliefs from the doctrines of the early Muslims and the Sunnis,” he means the Shiʿa, Murjiʾa, anthropomorphists, Muʿtazila, and Imamis.

He then says that the innovations of these groups and schools created the need “to defend these beliefs with rational proofs against the attacks of these innovations,” and that “Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, the imam of the theologians, undertook this task,” and so on.[^V2-512]

Ibn Khaldūn then reviews the questions al-Ashʿarī addressed in his response to these “innovators and deviants,” and concludes that after the question of the imamate had been added, the whole collection of these questions came to be called *kalām*.[^V2-513]

There can therefore be little doubt that among the Ashʿarites, the term *kalām* had a particular meaning and a particular content that applied only to Ashʿarite theology.

The same was true of the term *mutakallimūn*, “theologians,” which was likewise restricted to Ashʿarite theologians.

This removes from the history of *kalām* all the rational thought based on philosophical reflection that appeared before Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī.

It also excludes all the creative rationalist theologians of that earlier period who helped prepare the way for Arab-Islamic philosophy. At an early stage in its intellectual awakening, they trained Arab-Islamic thought to work with abstraction, concepts, and categories.

We have no objection to the Ashʿarites choosing whatever names and terms they wish for their own school and their own thought.

But we do object when they cut away part of the history of *kalām* so completely that the field appears to begin and end with them.

### 4 — Two Opposing Stages

We should therefore set aside the claims of both the Muʿtazila and the Ashʿarites that *kalām* belongs exclusively within the boundaries of their own particular school.

Instead, we must look at history and historical reality as they actually developed, in all their dimensions.

If we do this, and follow the long history of *kalām* from Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ (d. 131 AH/748 CE), the founder of the Muʿtazilite school, to Ibn Taymiyya (661–728 AH/thirteenth–fourteenth centuries CE), one of the best-known later traditionalist theologians, two basic conclusions emerge.

First, *kalām* includes the whole range of questions framed in religious and doctrinal terms that arose from different forms of social and political conflict in Arab-Islamic society from the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs onward.

Over time, these questions were transformed into complex ideas about the world beyond nature. Their original social dimensions became almost hidden behind a fog of abstractions. Alongside these appeared views with a philosophical direction concerning the natural world, though still approached from a theological point of view.

Many different schools and tendencies of *kalām* appeared during this long history. Yet the basic questions they discussed and disputed remained largely the same.

And if we look beyond the outward form of the ideas, the deepest reasons for disagreement over each of these questions—whether individually or as a whole—were always rooted in social reality. At their deepest level, they arose from the position occupied by the supporters of these ideas within the wider social structure of their society.

Second, *kalām* passed through two main stages during this history of roughly six centuries: a Muʿtazilite stage and an Ashʿarite stage.

This division does not mean that we have forgotten the many theological ideas and debates that belonged to neither school.

The Imami Shiʿa, for example, developed their own theological positions, especially on the question of the imamate. The Kharijites, Murjiʾa, Jahmite determinists, those who likened God to created beings, those who described God in bodily terms, the incarnationists, and later traditionalists such as Ibn Taymiyya all developed views of their own.

Our division into two stages is based instead on the main direction taken by *kalām* across its history as a whole.

If we study *kalām* according to its broad intellectual and ideological direction, we are led to this conclusion: its history was dominated by two major tendencies, forming two stages that were opposed to one another just as Muʿtazilite thought was opposed to Ashʿarite thought.

#### A — The Muʿtazilite Stage of Kalām

##### 1 — The Muʿtazilite Method

We can say that the Ashʿarite stage was, in a sense, a reaction against the Muʿtazilite stage.

From its beginnings and throughout its development, the Muʿtazilite movement had two striking features.

The first was its opposition to traditionalist thought and ideology.

The second was the method it used in carrying out that opposition.

That method was itself the revolutionary side of the movement. It was a rationalist method whose most distinctive aim was to examine every question of Islamic metaphysics through reason and to give the human mind the leading role in the search for knowledge.

But this rationalist approach itself grew out of another question that, under the historical conditions of the time, was perhaps even more closely connected with social reality: the freedom of the human mind to think without being bound by a predetermined fate,[^V2-514] and, through this, the freedom of the human will to act without being constrained by a will that had already decided everything in advance.[^V2-515]

Looking at the Muʿtazilite movement through these closely connected questions allows us to see its historically revolutionary character.

It is true that the Muʿtazila usually dealt with theological questions through abstract rational reflection.

This tendency became stronger as they came into closer contact with Greek philosophy and as the questions before them became more numerous, varied, and complex.

It is also true that Muʿtazilite thought remained deeply marked by theology, even when it dealt with the natural world—for example, in discussions of the indivisible particle, or atomism.

All of this is true.

But first, this reflected the historical conditions themselves: religious knowledge dominated intellectual life, and Islam exerted a powerful influence throughout society.

Second, under those conditions, no new intellectual movement could have expressed its revolutionary character in any other form or by any other method.

And third, none of this could hide another essential feature of Muʿtazilite thought: its opposition to absolute faith in the unseen, to the idea that faith should come before reason, and to the belief that absolute predestination governs the movement of individuals and society and determines all human choices.

We should also note an important fact about the Muʿtazila’s social position.

The Muʿtazila did not form an independent social class or group simply by being Muʿtazilites, either under the Umayyads or under the Abbasids.

They belonged instead to a much larger learned group that emerged as Arab-Islamic society developed socially and culturally: the scholars of jurisprudence, Hadith, Qurʾanic commentary, and related fields such as Arabic language studies and logic.

Like Shiʿi, Kharijite, Murjiʾite, and Sunni theologians, every Muʿtazilite scholar of *kalām* was also counted among the jurists, Hadith scholars, Qurʾanic commentators, grammarians, or often several of these at once.

This large learned group was not separate from the political movements alongside which it existed. In many cases, it formed their religious component. Yet it still had a distinct position within them and exercised a special influence on public opinion.

That position gave it the ability to respond to, and interact with, social and political movements of many different kinds within the wider public.

This is one reason ideological struggle could become just as intense as direct political struggle.

It also helps us understand why the positions taken by the Muʿtazila in the ideological battles of their age were historically necessary and played a real part in the development of society at that stage.

This historical role represents the positive and revolutionary phase of Muʿtazilite *kalām*.

Its importance did not lie simply in the ideas themselves, but in the historical effect they produced.

That effect was possible, first, because society at the time was receptive to ideas that challenged the ideology of the existing political order, and second, because Muʿtazilite *kalām* had a particular power of attraction.

Its appeal came from the fact that it confronted the basic principles and questions on which the ideology of the caliphate itself rested.

Its effect in shaking those foundations was stronger than the wars of the Kharijites, despite the violence of those wars—or perhaps, we might say, partly because of that violence.

##### 2 — The Muʿtazila and al-Maʾmūn

At this point we face an important question that deserves serious study: the relationship between the Muʿtazila and the power of the caliphate under the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn.

The ruler who occupied the throne at the time embraced Muʿtazilite doctrine so fully that it became the official doctrine of the caliphate for the reigns of three Abbasid caliphs.[^V2-516]

This seems to cast doubt on what we have said about Muʿtazilite *kalām* carrying the banner of intellectual and ideological opposition to state power.

The doubt may seem even stronger because, for more than sixteen years, it was the opponents of the Muʿtazila who carried the banner of opposition, while the Muʿtazila encouraged the state to persecute their opponents, even physically.

Does this mean that the ideology of the state had changed?

Or had the ideology of the Muʿtazila changed?

Our scientific method warns us against making judgments in absolute terms.

An absolute judgment is, by its nature, static and metaphysical. It contradicts both dialectical method and the dynamic movement of life itself.

So we cannot say that every opposition to political authority is necessarily progressive or revolutionary in every respect.

Nor can we say that every existing state power is necessarily reactionary in every respect.

That is the general principle.

But the particular historical relationship that developed between the Muʿtazila and the Abbasid state under al-Maʾmūn—and continued under al-Muʿtaṣim and al-Wāthiq—has until now usually been studied from an idealist and subjective point of view.

Researchers have not seriously tried to uncover the economic and social factors lying behind it in the early Abbasid period.

Modern studies often say, for example, that al-Maʾmūn was highly educated, deeply interested in scientific and literary study, philosophically minded, and intellectually open. Because the Muʿtazila were the school most committed to intellectual freedom and reason, their doctrine naturally appealed to him. He therefore brought Muʿtazilites close to him, and they gained influence at court.[^V2-517]

If this explains the matter during al-Maʾmūn’s reign, how do we explain the fact that this policy continued for about sixteen years after his death, through the caliphates of al-Muʿtaṣim and al-Wāthiq, even though neither of them had al-Maʾmūn’s intellectual gifts, learning, or freedom of thought?

This question deserves a full study using the method of historical materialism. Here, however, we can do no more than lay some groundwork for such a study. We will draw on a number of economic and social indicators from the age of al-Maʾmūn, as well as on the general laws that govern the dialectical movement of society.

We cannot simply dismiss the role of al-Maʾmūn himself. He was an educated and intellectually open-minded ruler, and under him the state adopted the Muʿtazilite position on the famous theological question of whether the Qurʾān was created.

What we should reject is the idea that al-Maʾmūn’s personal role was either the main cause or the only cause, rather than one contributing factor, behind this bold move. He officially declared that the caliphal state accepted the Muʿtazilite position on the created Qurʾān despite the opposition of conservative public opinion, especially Sunni jurists, hadith scholars, and Qurʾān commentators. He also made the Muʿtazilite school as a whole the doctrine of the state and punished those who opposed it, sometimes even physically.

The main explanation for this development must be sought in the wider historical conditions in which al-Maʾmūn secured his position on the Abbasid throne at the end of the second and beginning of the third Islamic centuries—that is, in the ninth century CE.

The first thing that stands out is the way he came to power. Al-Maʾmūn reached the caliphate after a bloody struggle between two sets of forces. On one side were the leaders and princes of the feudal forces who supported his brother al-Amīn. On the other were forces rooted in the urban economy and in the commercial, moneylending, and craft-based life of the cities, together with the educated circles that carried freer ideas. These urban forces supported al-Maʾmūn in his struggle for the throne and absolute power.

Trade had flourished during the first period of Abbasid rule. Once Iraq became the center of the caliphate, it also became a meeting point for major international trade routes. Commerce expanded, and many city-dwellers entered trade because of the large profits it offered and the rising social position of merchants.[^V2-518]

The Abbasids generally encouraged overseas trade, and this became one of the most important forms of economic activity during the early Abbasid period.[^V2-519]

This naturally strengthened certain social groups in the cities, especially in the capital. In feudal societies, these groups grow and begin to play a greater political role whenever conditions favor commercial expansion. Their rise comes partly at the expense of major landowners and the wealthy rural classes. This happens especially when transport is regular, communications are reliable, and foreign markets are active.

Those conditions existed at the time.

The growing urban groups in the Iraqi cities were diverse both socially and ethnically. They were not limited to wealthy merchants and owners of commercial capital. They also included people involved in money capital, lending, and banking; owners of craft workshops and their skilled workers; small traders; shopkeepers; and people engaged in simple forms of buying and selling.

Every one of these groups contained a mixture of Arabs and members of the many other peoples who lived within the Abbasid Empire.

This was especially clear among the *ʿāmma*—the broad mass of workers and poor people. They included Arabs, Persians, Turks, Zanj, Daylamites, Byzantines, Nabataeans, Armenians, Georgians, Slavs, Kurds, and Berbers. What united them was the dominant common language: Arabic.[^V2-520]

This was generally true across the cities of Iraq.[^V2-521] Ethnic distinctions seem to have become almost dissolved within this human mixture.[^V2-522]

From this we can conclude that a person’s class position in third-century Islamic society could, to some extent, shape their political position as well.

We can see this in the support that many urban social groups gave to al-Maʾmūn’s bid for the Abbasid throne. They did so partly because princes and major landholders had rallied around his brother al-Amīn.

Those princes and leaders hoped to benefit from al-Amīn’s weak personality, his attraction to a life of entertainment, and his lack of interest in the wider affairs of the state. They hoped this would allow them to expand their own power and perhaps even achieve a degree of independence in one region or another of the empire.

Al-Maʾmūn therefore came to supreme power with the backing of social groups whose class interests conflicted with those of the groups tied to rural feudal estates.

Under his rule, the conflict between these forces had to take on a new form. This included a new attitude toward the people who had supported al-Amīn and toward their representatives in intellectual life: the conservative jurists, hadith scholars, and Qurʾān commentators.[^V2-523]

This, as we see it, helps explain why the banner of free thought rose so high under al-Maʾmūn in the form of Muʿtazilite *kalām*. Because the same underlying forces remained strong, that banner continued to fly under his brother al-Muʿtaṣim and then under al-Wāthiq, the son of al-Muʿtaṣim.

Al-Maʾmūn himself was determined that this policy should not collapse after his death. In his final instructions to al-Muʿtaṣim he wrote: “Follow your brother’s course regarding the Qurʾān.”[^V2-524] He meant, of course, the Muʿtazilite doctrine that the Qurʾān was created.

The Muʿtazilite school was able to remain the official doctrine of the state under both al-Muʿtaṣim and al-Wāthiq because the conditions we have just described were still in place. In other words, the social forces that had supported al-Maʾmūn remained close to the center of power until the end of al-Wāthiq’s reign.

Under al-Mutawakkil, however, these forces were pushed aside and replaced by others that supported conservative thought, as we will soon see.

##### 3 — The Other Side of Muʿtazilite *Kalām*

We have already seen a revolutionary side to Muʿtazilite *kalām*. It appeared in the method itself, especially in its rationalist character.

But this should not make us overlook its other side.

Muʿtazilite *kalām* still remained within the wider framework of official theological ideology. It did not break free of that framework.

Muʿtazilite thought was based on the principle of the absolute transcendence of the divine essence. This was the “official” understanding of divine unity. It also implied that truth itself was one. That truth was religious truth: the divine law, the *sharia*, which came from a single divine source.

This was the ideological foundation of the ruling class in the Islamic caliphate.

Because the caliphal state presented itself as the state of Islam, it also presented itself as the sole legitimate representative of the social order defined by divine law.

From this comes a line of reasoning that provides an Islamic “theoretical” basis for the idea of a divine right to absolute rule.

It can be set out as follows.

First, the social order approved by the *sharia* is the same order embodied by the caliphal state.

Second, the *sharia* that approves this order is divine, and therefore sacred.

The “logical” conclusion is that the political order of the caliphate is itself sacred.

Once the rule of the caliphal state is given a religiously sacred character, the ruling class gains a claim to absolute authority.

Opposition to that authority, disobedience to it, and especially rebellion against it can then be treated, within the law of the ruling system, as nothing more than religious heresy.

To oppose the state becomes opposition to God’s rule. To disobey it becomes disobedience to the “holder of authority,” whose obedience God is said to have commanded.

And if this is true even of ordinary opposition, what then of open revolt?

Whether the Muʿtazilites wanted this conclusion or not, and whether they consciously thought it through or not, is beside the point.

The issue does not depend on their wishes or intentions. Nor does it depend on whether this interpretation of Muʿtazilite thought is correct in some final or absolute sense. That is not the question we are trying to settle here.

Our concern is with the ideological meaning of Muʿtazilite *kalām* and with the relationship between that meaning and the ideology of the existing caliphal state.

If we look at Muʿtazilite *kalām* through its rationalist method, it was progressive in relation to its historical setting.

If we look at its ideological content, however, it supported that ruling ideology and gave it a “theoretical” foundation.

Even so, the rationalist method remained the dominant and genuinely new feature of Muʿtazilite *kalām*. Its progressive side was still the stronger one, because it dealt a damaging blow to the traditionalist ideology of its time.

#### B — The Ashʿarite Stage of *Kalām*

##### 1 — A Traditionalist Turn

A traditionalist turn came after the death of al-Wāthiq.

Al-Wāthiq had refused to pass the Abbasid caliphate to his son Muḥammad. This gave his brother al-Mutawakkil the opportunity to become caliph in 232 AH/847 CE, with the support of forces hostile to the positive gains that had been made since the time of al-Maʾmūn.

One of the greatest of those gains, in terms of its importance for civilization and for social and scientific development, was the movement that translated the sciences into Arabic and brought them into Arab-Islamic intellectual life and society.

But that movement had grown out of the objective development and objective needs of society. It was not simply the product of the will of one ruler or one ruling group.

For that reason, no individual and no opposing movement could simply destroy it and take away what society had gained from it.

As one modern scholar puts it, al-Mutawakkil happened to be “the first of the Abbasid caliphs to surpass his predecessors in his love of luxury.”[^V2-525]

The feudal landholders, the inner court circle, and their conservative intellectual representatives took advantage of this weakness in al-Mutawakkil’s character. They became a source of pressure on him and pushed his policies toward their own interests and outlook.

Muʿtazilite *kalām*, and especially the doctrine of the created Qurʾān, had been tied to the official doctrine of the state since 218 AH, when al-Maʾmūn formally declared this connection.

The dominant forces under al-Mutawakkil made this one of their main targets. They wanted to undo what al-Maʾmūn had established.

Al-Mutawakkil finally abolished it in 234 AH, only two years after becoming caliph.

The conservative forces celebrated this so strongly that they placed al-Mutawakkil alongside the first Rightly Guided Caliph, Abū Bakr, and the Umayyad caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

They said:

“Three caliphs stand above the rest: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq on the day of the apostasy wars, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz when he restored people’s rights, and al-Mutawakkil when he revived the Sunna.”[^V2-526]

We should also say here that the persecution directed against the opponents of the Muʿtazilites and of the doctrine of the created Qurʾān under al-Maʾmūn, al-Muʿtaṣim, and al-Wāthiq ultimately helped those opponents more than it helped the Muʿtazilites themselves.

The conservatives made full use of this persecution in shaping public opinion. They then used it as both an argument and a justification for the persecution that was later turned against the Muʿtazilites and their school for a long period afterward.

For this reason, we see the original campaign of persecution as a historical mistake.

It helped the conservative forces of the period launch a powerful reaction that brought the Muʿtazilite stage of *kalām* to an end before it had exhausted its possibilities and before it had completed its historical role in the development of Arab thought toward philosophy and the natural sciences.

The direction taken by the rationalist tendency within Muʿtazilite *kalām* now changed.

*Kalām* began to move into its second major stage.

About half a century after the end of the Muʿtazilite period, this new stage would be led by a major Sunni thinker who created the first new theoretical formulation of the ideology of the conservative forces. This ideology would later become the official ideology of state power for several generations.

We mean Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī (260–330 AH/873–941 CE).[^V2-527]

This is why the period came to bear al-Ashʿarī’s name, even though it had begun quite some time before him.

Before al-Ashʿarī, it had already been led by al-Ḥārith ibn Asad al-Muḥāsibī, who died in 243 AH/857 CE, and by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd ibn Kullāb. They were the first founders, after the defeat of the Muʿtazilites, of a school that based itself on the texts of the Qurʾān and Sunna alone and openly declared a doctrinal war against Muʿtazilite thought.[^V2-528]

How, then, should we understand the strength of the Ashʿarite school and the dominance it achieved from the end of the third Islamic century—the ninth century CE—not only over *kalām*, but over Sunni Islamic thought more generally?

We cannot understand the answer without looking at the method al-Ashʿarī used when he returned to the doctrine of the early hadith scholars.

There was nothing new about relying in theory on Sunni teaching in questions of religion, society, and nature.

What was new, and what gave Ashʿarism its special importance, was the method al-Ashʿarī used.

That method gave his school enough strength to justify its continued existence after Muʿtazilism had disappeared from the main arena of *kalām*.

What was this method?

If we look at the substance of the matter rather than its surface appearance, and if we do not concern ourselves with personal intentions or wishes, it becomes easy to see a kind of continuation of the Muʿtazilite method within the Ashʿarite method itself.

The rationalist direction that the Muʿtazilites had established in Arab thought, and had made the foundation of *kalām* from the moment they first shaped it as a discipline, could not simply be extinguished by the conservative wave that removed them from direct influence over intellectual development.

Nor could that conservative wave build a strong enough barrier to prevent Muʿtazilite rationalism from continuing to influence intellectual development indirectly, despite the severe repression directed against free thought and independent thinkers.

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī could not return to the doctrine of the Sunnis without carrying with him the results of the historical process that had given Arab thought as a whole—including *kalām*—a rationalist direction.

The Muʿtazilites had led that process from the late seventh century, throughout the eighth century, and into the first third of the ninth century CE.

It was therefore natural that when al-Ashʿarī entered the intellectual battlefield to fight Muʿtazilite thought, he appeared armed with the Muʿtazilites’ own weapon:[^V2-529] the weapon of rational method.[^V2-530]

But, as we will soon see, he changed that method in a fundamental way. The change stripped it of its original meaning and emptied it of its essential rationalism.

It might be argued that al-Ashʿarī’s commitment to rational method, even if only at the level of form, came from his own intellectual background.[^V2-531]

After all, he had been trained in *kalām* by the Muʿtazilites. He studied under one of their leading teachers in Basra, Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī, who died in 303 AH/915 CE.

Al-Ashʿarī remained a Muʿtazilite until around 300 AH, when he broke with them. From the pulpit of a mosque in Basra, he publicly announced that he had repented and abandoned the positions in which he had followed the Muʿtazilites. He declared that he would now refute them and expose their “scandals.”[^V2-532]

Even so, we do not think his Muʿtazilite upbringing is enough to explain why a rationalist method, in some form, appeared in Ashʿarite *kalām* and continued among later Ashʿarite thinkers, from Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī to al-Ghazālī and beyond.

There are two reasons for this.

First, al-Ashʿarī was a major thinker who was highly conscious of what he was doing. He made a serious effort to watch for the continued influence of his Muʿtazilite period on his later thinking.[^V2-533]

He did this so that the “holy” war he had declared against Muʿtazilism could be carried through without compromise.

Second, if his Muʿtazilite upbringing were really the main reason for the appearance of rational method in Ashʿarism, we would expect that feature to disappear among his followers.

In fact, the opposite happened.

Some of the greatest Ashʿarite theologians after Abū al-Ḥasan developed the method further. They introduced new questions into their theology that had more in common with this rational method than with the methods of the Sunnis before the rise of the Muʿtazilites.

One example is the judge Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī, who died in 403 AH/1012 CE. He “developed the method and laid down the rational premises on which proof and inquiry depend, including such matters as establishing the indivisible atom, the void, the principle that one accident cannot inhere in another accident, and the principle that an accident does not remain for two moments.”[^V2-534]

For all these reasons, we argue that when al-Ashʿarī used the outward forms of rational method in his theological school against Muʿtazilite *kalām*, he understood that his age no longer allowed Muʿtazilite thought to be fought with an entirely different kind of thought.

A purely traditionalist method had already been left behind by the historical process.

The same is entirely true of al-Ghazālī when he later declared his own ideological “holy war” against philosophical thought that had moved beyond traditional theology.

This is why we find Ashʿarite *kalām* using logical argument, speaking in the language of the authority of reason, refusing to openly accept absolute determinism in the question of human action, and discussing substance and accident, atomism, and even causation.

This is the general structure of the Ashʿarite method.

It gives the appearance of being “rationalist” because it needed a justification for its own existence in an age when Muʿtazilite rationalism had already established both direct and indirect influence.

But what was the real value of this Ashʿarite “rationalism”?

1 — It is true that al-Ashʿarī did not abandon logical argument.

But rationalism does not consist simply in the formal use of logic. It also depends on the rational starting points from which the premises of an argument are drawn.

For the Ashʿarites, all those starting points were confined to the content of religious texts, and nothing else.

2 — It is also true that they refer to reason when discussing the existence of God, the creation or beginning of the world, or the eternity of the divine attributes.

But according to the basic principles of their school, reason is not the true source of knowledge.

Reason cannot by itself decide what is good or bad in things, actions, values, or meanings.

They hold that knowledge of God can be reached through reason, but that revelation is what makes belief in God binding.[^V2-535]

In other words, knowledge reached by reason is not enough to create religious obligation or responsibility.

Reason therefore plays only a secondary and guiding role.

The final authority is divine revelation.

3 — It is also true that the Ashʿarites rejected the strict determinist position that God creates human actions in an absolute sense.

But what did their own position really amount to?

They said that they occupied a middle position between the determinists and the Muʿtazilites.

Human actions, they argued, are created by God. Human beings cannot create any of those actions themselves.

But even if people cannot create their actions, they can still “acquire” them.[^V2-536]

The Andalusian Ẓāhirī thinker Ibn Ḥazm, who died in 456 AH, rightly argued that this position does not differ in any essential way from determinism because it never clearly establishes genuine human choice.[^V2-537]

The Ashʿarites say that God creates both the act and the ability to perform it in the human being.

The person then directs that act as they wish, toward good or evil, and in this way earns either reward or punishment.

This would seem to make people responsible for what they do because they have freedom of choice.

But Ashʿarite atomism creates a serious problem for this position.

According to their atomist doctrine, substances and their accidents are constantly changing and continually coming into existence, while God directly and continuously creates both the substances and their accidents.

This undermines the very freedom of choice the Ashʿarites claim to preserve.

If God is continuously and directly involved in every human act and every human movement, then human freedom becomes impossible to maintain in any real sense.[^V2-538]

4 — The advocates of Ashʿarite atomism also tried to follow what they presented as a “rational” path.

Through this method, they tried to prove that substances and their qualities ultimately come from nothing—that is, from non-being—and are therefore created in time.

The world, which is made up of atoms, or these individual substances that cannot be divided any further, must therefore also have been created in time.

But although this method looked “rational” in form, they departed from the substance of rationalism in two ways.

First, they rejected reason’s conception of the qualities of individual substances. They denied those qualities when they were known through reason.

Second, they rejected the objective existence of the qualities and accidents carried by those individual substances, while at the same time treating the mind itself as the source of their existence.

5 — When the Ashʿarites spoke about causation, they said that God is the direct cause of every change that occurs in substances and accidents.

There is no other cause in the universe apart from this direct cause, which is God.

They based this on one of the supposedly “rational” principles of their school: an accident does not remain for two moments.

At every moment, therefore, a new accident appears and requires a new act of creation by the same direct cause: God.

This Ashʿarite position leads directly to an irrational conclusion.

It denies the laws of nature and society altogether and removes any basis on which a scientific system can be built in any field of knowledge.

The final result is to destroy one of the necessary foundations for the development of society itself.[^V2-539]

Here the signs of the ideological struggle become clearer and clearer.

This was the struggle that reached one stage under the leadership of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī at the end of the third Islamic century, and another under al-Ghazālī at the end of the fifth.

One revealing example of this ideological struggle is the well-known fact that al-Ghazālī wrote his famous book *The Scandals of the Bāṭinites* at the request of the Abbasid caliph al-Mustaẓhir, who came to power in 487 AH/1094 CE.

Al-Ghazālī even gave the work the alternative title *al-Mustaẓhirī*.[^V2-540]

This was one form of the alliance between Ashʿarite *kalām* and official state thought.

Facing them in the ideological struggle was a broad opposing camp made up of a mixture of social and intellectual forces that were hostile to—or at least opposed to—the direction taken by the ruling power.

---

##### 2 — The Place of the Shia in *Kalām*

The Shia played an important role both in the rise of *kalām* and in the later development of its debates.

But in our present discussion, we cannot include every group that has been called “Shia” in Islamic history.

If we tried to cover the full historical meaning of the term in all its different uses, we would enter a maze with no clear way out.

We will therefore limit ourselves to its best-known meaning: the Twelver Imami Shia.

There are two sides to the Imami Shia’s role in *kalām*.

The first is the specifically doctrinal side of Shiism itself.

The second concerns the contributions of theologians who belonged to the Imami school and who played an important part in developing the questions discussed in *kalām* at different stages in its history.

**A — The doctrinal side:** If we look only at the doctrine itself, we can say that many of the principles on which Imami Shiism is built are also major subjects of *kalām*.

Some are directly connected to the great political questions that drove the earliest political conflicts from the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs onward.

These include the question of the caliphate; the question of the person who commits a major sin, which arose partly from the killing of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān; the question of how to deal with an unjust ruler; and the duty to command what is right and forbid what is wrong.

Other theological questions appeared later as the earlier political conflict continued and intensified, while ideological positions were reformulated in new and more developed intellectual forms.

These included divine decree and predestination, human freedom, the concepts of divine unity and justice, faith, the theory of knowledge, and the status of reason.

On all these disputed questions, the Imamis developed views and positions that formed both the structure of Shiite doctrine and the structure of Shiite *kalām*.

If we look at Shiite *kalām* in broad terms, we find that the Twelver Imamis took some positions that were unique to them.

The clearest example is the caliphate.

Unlike either the Ashʿarites or the Muʿtazilites, they regarded the caliphate as a divine right belonging to the person whom God chooses for it.

They believed this divine right belonged to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and then to his descendants through his wife Fāṭima, the daughter of the Prophet, in a direct line down to the twelfth Imam, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan.

They also believed that the Imam who possesses this right is protected from error.

On some other questions, the Imamis agreed with the Ashʿarites rather than the Muʿtazilites.

One example is the status of a Muslim who commits a major sin.

Like the Ashʿarites, the Imamis say that such a person remains a believer but is sinful and deserves punishment in proportion to the sin.

The Muʿtazilites, by contrast, say that this person is neither a believer nor an unbeliever, but occupies a position between belief and unbelief.

The Kharijites say that such a person is an unbeliever.

The Imamis also agree with the Ashʿarites on the interpretation of religious texts—the Qurʾān and Sunna—when their apparent meaning conflicts with reason.

Like the Ashʿarites, they allow interpretation when the plain meaning of a text conflicts with the most basic judgments of reason.

Outside such cases, they do not favor this approach.

They hold that religious knowledge remains the basic authority, rather than the judgment of reason.

On still other questions, the Imamis agree with the Muʿtazilites rather than the Ashʿarites.

One example is the question of whether reason itself can recognize good and evil.

Like the Muʿtazilites, the Imamis believe that some actions and things are good or bad in themselves and that reason can recognize this.

In other words, goodness and badness exist objectively in such actions and things.

They are not good or bad only because religious law declares them so.

The question of human freedom remains.

What is the Shiite position on whether people freely choose their actions?

On this important question, their position is based on a saying attributed to the sixth of the Twelve Imams, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq:

“Neither compulsion nor delegation, but something between the two.”

The Shia explain this by saying that human actions must be looked at from two directions: their immediate causes and their more distant causes.

If we look at the immediate causes, the human being is the direct cause of the action.

The action comes from the person by choice.

From this point of view, the person is responsible for whether the act is good or evil.

But if we look at the more distant causes, we find that these lie outside the person’s own will and choice.

They are necessary conditions, and from this point of view the action cannot simply be attributed to the person alone.

In the Shiite explanation, a person’s ability to perform an action belongs to these more distant causes.

That ability is something God created in the person.

Human actions are therefore created by God in the sense that God created the power that makes them possible.

But they are also created by the human being in the sense that the person directly performs them by an act of will.[^V2-541]

The position is therefore presented as a middle ground between the Ashʿarites, who say that people do not truly possess their actions or determine their fate, and the Muʿtazilites, who say that people determine their own fate without the Creator exercising any influence over their actions.[^V2-542]

More generally, we often find the Shia occupying a middle position between the Ashʿarites and the Muʿtazilites in *kalām*.

The deeper explanation for this “middle position” may lie in the extremely difficult historical situation the Shia faced over several centuries.

They were repeatedly forced into painful forms of conflict.

At times they confronted their opponents openly and firmly.

At other times they relied on *taqiyya*—protective concealment—combined with withdrawal.

At still other times they used concealment while continuing their opposition in secret.

Throughout all this, they suffered terrible disasters, including at times physical destruction on a large scale.

If we try to identify the ideology of Shiism as a whole simply from the theory of Shiism itself, we quickly find ourselves inside a closed circle of contradictions.

One of the clearest contradictions can be seen by comparing two sets of Shiite positions.

On one side is the theory of the Imamate: the belief that the caliphate is purely a divine right, the denial of the people’s right to choose the caliph, the belief that the Imam is protected from error, and the restriction of the source of religious knowledge after the Prophet to the Imam.

On the other side are the Shiite positions on human freedom and on reason’s ability to recognize good and evil.

We can draw the following conclusion.

The first set of positions belongs to the original foundation of Shiite doctrine.

The second developed later under the influence of the historical situation we have just described.

From the time the Umayyads established themselves at the head of the Islamic state, the practical position of the Shia became tied to opposition against the ruling power, both under the Umayyads and under the Abbasids.

By this I mean that their opposition, together with the persecution they suffered, produced ideological changes in some of the principles on which Shiite theory rested.

This helps explain why the questions on which the Shia agreed with the Muʿtazilites were precisely those important ideological questions that most clearly separated the Muʿtazilites from the Ashʿarites.

This allows us to draw another conclusion.

If we want to identify the ideological character of Shiism, we should not look for it only in the original theory of Shiism itself.

We should also look at the theological positions where the Shia agree with the Muʿtazilites or come close to them.

These positions do not simply reflect Shiite theory as it first arose under the earliest historical conditions of Islam.

They also reflect the practical historical situation the Shia faced after the killing of the first Imam, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and then after the tragic death of the third Imam, al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, at Karbala.

##### 3 — Shiite Theologians

The role of individual Shiite thinkers in *kalām* cannot, as I see it, simply be treated as part of the role of specifically Shiite theology.

Some theologians belonged doctrinally to the Imami school but held views that either conflicted with the school or were not accepted by its followers.

The same can be said of philosophers who originally belonged to the Imami tradition.

They too developed philosophical positions that had nothing specifically Imami about them.

Al-Fārābī and Ibn Sīnā are examples.

One sign of this is the extent to which the views of such thinkers differ from one another, sometimes even directly contradicting one another.

In *kalām*, for example, we find Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam, who lived approximately from 113 to 200 AH, arguing that God does not know a thing before creating it, and that the knowledge by which God knows things is neither eternal nor created in time.[^V2-543]

In his atomism, he also held that physical bodies can actually be divided into an infinite number of parts.[^V2-544]

All these positions are foreign to the basic principles of Shiite theory.

Indeed, one of the major theorists of Imami doctrine says, in discussing the indivisible atom, that all believers in divine unity accept it and that no one disagrees “except a few isolated Muʿtazilites, while the atheists reject it.”[^V2-545]

We also find another Imami theologian, who had been a student of Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam, disagreeing with his teacher on many points.[^V2-546]

There are several other examples of Shiite theologians disagreeing with one another, sometimes to the point of direct contradiction.[^V2-547]

For this reason, it is not correct to place all these different or conflicting views under the heading of “Shiite *kalām*” simply because their authors were Shia.

Nor is it correct to attribute the wider role these theologians played in the development of *kalām* to Shiism itself as a doctrine.

##### 4 — The Relationship Between *Kalām* and Philosophy

Is there a relationship between *kalām* and philosophy?

If there is, how far does it go?

The questions discussed by the theologians themselves already give us part of the answer.

Let us begin with the founders of *kalām*, the Muʿtazilites, and look at the way they treated theological questions.

The philosophical character of their approach is clear.

Their way of thinking is philosophical in its reliance on reason, its use of philosophical concepts and categories, and its use of the same tools of logical argument that philosophy itself used.

One example comes from the Muʿtazilite school of Basra.

Abū Hāshim al-Jubbāʾī of Basra[^V2-548] held that universals, or general concepts, have an existence outside the mind.[^V2-549]

He also held that doubt is the starting point of knowledge.

His reasoning was that rational inquiry without prior doubt would amount to trying to acquire knowledge that had already been acquired,[^V2-550] which is impossible.

The Muʿtazilite school of Baghdad gives us another example.

One of its thinkers, Maʿmar ibn ʿAbbād al-Sulamī,[^V2-551] discussed the problem of “meanings,” or conceptualism.[^V2-552]

He held that an accident exists in a subject only because of a particular “meaning,” and that things differ from one another or resemble one another because of such meanings.

Motion, for example, differs from rest because of a meaning that produces that difference.[^V2-553]

We also know that the theologians discussed the nature of the human being.

Maʿmar held that the human being is a substance and is therefore not identical with the body—that is, the human being in this sense is not material.

The relationship between the human being and the body, he argued, is one of direction and control.[^V2-554]

The body is the instrument of the human being as substance. The human being moves and directs it without physically touching it.[^V2-555]

These questions, and many others like them, are philosophical both in origin and in nature.

Yet they also became questions of *kalām* and were discussed by theologians throughout the different stages of the discipline.

Historians of Arab-Islamic thought in that period have written a great deal about the early theologians’ knowledge of Greek philosophy and of the other philosophical traditions available to them.

We can recall here al-Shahrastānī’s statement that some of the earliest theologians, such as Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, who died in 131 AH/748 CE, had read the works of the philosophers.[^V2-556]

Modern scholars have tried to go further and identify both the period when philosophy first entered *kalām* and the individual who first brought about this contact.

Some have said that the credit for introducing philosophical principles into Muʿtazilite thought belongs[^V2-557] to Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf.[^V2-558]

Others have said that al-ʿAllāf was the true founder of *kalām* among the Muslims, or that he was “the first Islamic theologian to be influenced by philosophy.”[^V2-559]

This kind of precise dating may be too rigid.

Intellectual movements, like the many other phenomena that arise in society, cannot normally be assigned to one exact dividing point in time or said to have appeared for the first time in one single individual.

Even so, these claims by both older historians and modern scholars point to the same basic fact.

The relationship between *kalām* and philosophy appeared very early in history, and the Muʿtazilites played the creative mediating role in bringing that relationship into being.

It is also striking that later theologians developed the relationship between *kalām* and philosophy even at the level of how they organized and classified their works.

Among them were the author of *al-Mawāqif*,[^V2-560] the author of *al-Maqāṣid*,[^V2-561] and the author of *Ṭawāliʿ al-Anwār*.[^V2-562]

They began to use Aristotle’s arrangement of philosophical subjects as a model for organizing their own theological discussions.[^V2-563]

This development was only formal, but it was still historically significant.

These later theologians were working at a time when attacks on philosophy had become more intense and when people who studied philosophy were being persecuted.

Yet all those attacks still failed to break the connection between *kalām* and philosophy, or between Arab-Islamic thought more generally and philosophy.

In fact, the opposite seems to have happened.

The relationship continued to reassert itself in new forms, adapted to the particular intellectual movements and historical conditions of each period.

A brief digression is useful here. The point is not really about philosophy for its own sake. It is about development in general, and about the intellectual freedom that development requires. It is also about the need for seeds of liberation to survive for as long as development still needs them, however powerful or cunning the forces of repression may be. The very existence of philosophy, in any form at all, was itself an encouraging sign. It showed that those seeds were still alive and still capable of challenging the rule of backward theological thought.

It is true that by the time of the later theologians, in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, much philosophical thought had begun to harden into conventional forms. It often lost its vitality and its ability to absorb the realities of its own age. Yet the attacks and persecution, which were still growing more intense at the time, were aimed at the rational content of philosophy—the philosophy that was then carrying the torch of a challenge to a theological ideology already in crisis.

To sum up what we have said so far: from its beginnings with the Muʿtazila, kalām gradually found its way toward philosophy, both in subject matter and in method. Even before kalām became an organized discipline, its questions and debates gave Arab-Islamic thought its first route toward philosophical thinking. They provided the necessary preparation for this kind of thought to develop, under its particular historical conditions, into a higher stage than kalām itself: the stage of philosophy.

This brings us to our second question:

**What were the limits of the relationship between kalām and philosophy?**

We have said that each was a relatively independent stage in the development of Arab-Islamic thought. That fact already gives us a first indication of the boundary between them.

A more precise answer comes from looking at the role each one played. Kalām used philosophical thinking as a way of examining questions that had arisen directly within Arab society after Islam, but it dealt with them in the form of religious debate about doctrine.

Philosophy, by contrast, emerged in Arab-Islamic society after kalām had reached maturity. It dealt with existence, nature, society, and thought as concepts in their own right. In those concepts, the material world was reflected indirectly, as a particular society with its own historical conditions, characteristics, and forms of social relations.

Philosophy therefore differed from kalām in two basic ways.

First, it began from concepts rather than from questions arising directly within society.

Second, it did not take the doctrines of Islam as the starting point of its inquiry. It did try to hide the contradictions between the conclusions reached through philosophical investigation and the doctrines of Islamic faith. These attempts later came to be described as a “reconciliation” between philosophy and religion, though that description is inaccurate.

##### 5 — The Contradiction Between Kalām and Philosophy

The dialectic of the relationship between kalām and philosophy inevitably contained serious contradictions. These became clear once each began to need a degree of independence from the other, around the middle of the third century AH, or after the middle of the ninth century CE.

Perhaps the most important source of these contradictions was this: when kalām reached maturity in its Muʿtazilite stage, it had already come close to philosophical thinking by giving reason a broad role in thought and in the search for knowledge, even in questions beyond nature.

According to the general laws of development, kalām should therefore have given way to philosophy in the further development of Arab-Islamic thought. Kalām had fulfilled the need that had brought it into existence and had exhausted its historical tasks. The time had come for it to develop into philosophy proper.

But events took a different course.

A conservative reaction against Muʿtazilite thought arose during the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil. Then came the Ashʿarite school of kalām, which expressed this reaction in a new form.

The result was not what might otherwise have been expected. Muʿtazilite kalām was replaced, on one side, by Ashʿarite kalām and, on the other, by a philosophical movement that had separated itself from kalām as a whole.

The transformation was therefore contradictory from the very beginning. In practice, it produced two opposing poles: philosophy and Ashʿarite kalām.

This explains the historical pattern we have already seen: open hostility and sometimes violent conflict between post-Muʿtazilite kalām and the different philosophical movements, from the Brethren of Purity to the philosophy of Ibn Rushd.

The antagonism between them had an ideological basis from the outset.

As we have seen, Ashʿarite kalām marked a return toward Sunni traditionalism. Its purpose was to tear down the rational structure that Muʿtazilite thought had built. The Ashʿarites tried to present themselves as “rational,” but, as we noted earlier, this rationalism remained largely formal.

From that point onward, it became increasingly clear that the conflict between kalām and philosophy was, above all, an ideological conflict.

Kalām came to express the “official” ideology. Philosophy, together with Sufism, increasingly expressed the outlook of different social groups opposed to the central ruling authority.

The evidence is the persecution that philosophy suffered in different forms over many centuries. It often began as intellectual persecution in the writings of theologians and then became material and physical persecution at the hands of the ruling authorities.

Why, for example, were the copyists of Baghdad required in 277 AH to swear that they would not copy books on philosophy, to the point that some copyists abandoned their profession altogether?[^V2-564] In our own age, forcing copyists to abandon their trade would be equivalent to shutting down the printing presses.

And why did hostility to philosophy eventually spread to almost everything that could be included under the broad heading of science?

The *Kitāb al-Aghānī* tells us[^V2-565] that Abū Zayd al-Balkhī[^V2-566] was accused of unbelief simply because he was “engaged in gathering the ancient and modern sciences, and in his writings followed the method of the philosophers.”[^V2-567]

Aristotle’s metaphysics in particular became a target of anger among the Sunnis:

> Aristotle’s metaphysics was, first and foremost, an object of anger among the Sunnis. They regarded both its premises and its conclusions as completely opposed to the requirements of Islamic belief. Their anger went further and came to include the mathematical sciences as well, because these prepared the way for philosophical study. Geometry, for example, became a cause for suspicion among the Sunnis. Geometrical figures made them uneasy and could cause their owner to be accused of heresy. (...) Abū al-Ḥasan ibn Fāris, in his book *al-Ṣāḥibī fī Fiqh al-Lugha wa-Sunan al-ʿArab fī Kalāmihā*, spoke of the danger that geometry posed to religion and of its limited usefulness. He concluded that engaging in mathematics led a person to abandon religion.[^V2-568]

From this picture, we can also see why it was no accident that theological reaction in medieval Europe made use of al-Ghazālī’s Ashʿarite and anti-philosophical arguments as a weapon against forms of philosophy that opposed theological philosophy.

R. Martin, a contemporary of Thomas Aquinas, did this, for example, in his book *The Defence of Faith*. He wrote it at the request of Raymond Puniaforte, head of the Dominican order, and incorporated many of al-Ghazālī’s ideas into it.[^V2-569]

This was not a coincidence. It was one sign of the way the ideological struggle moved, by the end of the fourteenth century, from its old arena in the East to a new arena in Europe. Arab-Islamic society had begun to decline economically, socially, politically, and culturally, while the seeds of the European Renaissance were beginning to grow in an atmosphere of technical progress whose first signs appeared near the end of the Middle Ages.

This shift also helps explain Ibn Khaldūn’s statement, at the end of the fourteenth century, that “kalām is no longer necessary for the student in this age, since the unbelievers and innovators have disappeared.”[^V2-570]

By “unbelievers and innovators,” Ibn Khaldūn of course meant the philosophers and all those whose ideas and tendencies led them to give philosophical explanations of the truths of the universe outside the unseen world. In other words, he meant the whole intellectual and ideological camp that Ashʿarite kalām opposed and fought against.

But had these people really disappeared by Ibn Khaldūn’s time, leaving only the Ashʿarite theologians in the field?

It seems to us that this was not really a matter of one side disappearing and the other remaining alone. Rather, the very subject of the ideological struggle in the East was beginning to lose its foundation, because the society that had formed the basic ground of that struggle was itself collapsing.

At the same time, a new society was emerging in the West—in Europe. It was preparing to become the new subject of the struggle and the more active arena of a class conflict that would be intense and would eventually give birth to a new world, bringing humanity new kinds of social relations.

---

At the end of this chapter, we can give a short and concentrated conclusion that also serves as a complete summary of the second part of our study:

During its first stage, from the end of the first century AH to the end of the first third of the third century AH, kalām consisted of philosophical practices and ideological reflections that took religious doctrine as the form through which they appeared and developed. This continued until kalām had completed its preparatory role and the conditions were ready for the emergence of an Arab philosophy independent of it.

## Conclusions from Chapter Six

### 1 —

A scientific study of history shows us that gradual, quantitative changes in the development of society can take different forms when they produce a qualitative change. They may produce a political, social, or intellectual and theoretical change, for example, or they may take the form of revolutionary violence.

Seen in this light, we can follow the process of accumulation in Arab-Islamic society during the seventh and eighth centuries. Among the different qualitative changes that grew out of this process, kalām became the most advanced intellectual form.

We saw that this accumulation began after the death of the Prophet. First came the struggle over the caliphate, followed by conflict over the material advantages attached to that powerful office.

We also saw that the establishment of the Umayyad state was the first major political transformation produced by this accumulation of events. It was supported by economic and social changes, and it also produced a new intellectual form.

The economic side of this transformation lay in the fact that Umayyad political power became an active participant in the system of feudal relations of production. It protected that system and helped develop it and renew its productive forces, especially in Syria.

This economic structure also shaped the social side of the transformation. Once the Umayyad state became involved in economic activity within feudal relations of production, the character of social relations and of the wider social system was necessarily affected.

The intellectual side first appeared through three competing theories: the Umayyad theory, the ʿAlid or Shiʿi theory, and the Khārijite theory.

But the relationship between quantitative accumulation and qualitative change could not stop there. Permanent change is the basic revolutionary feature of the dialectic between quantity and quality. Every new qualitative form is itself subjected to further gradual changes, which eventually lead to new qualitative transformations, and so the process continues.

In the first volume of this study, we showed how new contradictions began to develop within feudal relations of production during the Umayyad period. These contradictions accumulated and then produced new qualitative forms: political, social, intellectual, and theoretical. They were also accompanied by violent forms of struggle, including armed uprisings.

The first new intellectual form was the question of divine decree and predestination.

The rejection of predestination expressed, at the ideological level, the anger of working and educated groups. It was the first voice in Arab thought to rise against the official doctrine built on the idea of predestination.

Cultural interaction then introduced new ways of thinking about these problems. Thinkers began to develop principles for dealing with them in more advanced ways.

The Muʿtazila were the pioneers of this development. They relied above all on reason, both in gaining knowledge and in dealing with questions of society and religious belief.

At first, however, their investigations were still a collection of discussions without a systematic structure. Arab-Islamic thought had not yet reached the stage at which each kind of intellectual and theoretical inquiry could be given its own distinct scholarly identity.

Once it reached that stage, fields of knowledge were classified. Islamic jurisprudence became an independent discipline, and kalām became another independent discipline. The first dealt with the legal rulings of Islamic law, while the second dealt with the foundations of Islamic belief.

Most historical sources agree that this classification took shape during the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn. Al-Shahrastānī, for example, says this in *al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal*, vol. 1, p. 32.

The name **kalām**, in our view, probably became established because the word had already been used in earlier theological debates, before kalām became a formal discipline. People would say, for example, that a certain person “had something to say”—*kalām*—about predestination, or that someone else did not like to “speak”—*kalām*—about the attributes of God. We quoted a historical text earlier as an example of this usage.

### 2 —

The writing of works on kalām began before it had become a formal discipline with its own concepts and categories. It began with the wider movement to record knowledge in writing during the first century AH, or the seventh century CE.

Some sources tell us this, but none of the works from that period dealing with questions of kalām have survived, even though works on other subjects have reached us.

It seems that the writings of the early theologians, especially the Muʿtazila, were deliberately suppressed because they challenged the official thought and ideology of the state.

After the first century, writing on kalām became much more active, especially from the reign of al-Maʾmūn onward. Works of kalām became the main intellectual arena in which theoretical and ideological struggles appeared.

They remained so until philosophy emerged and took over the leading role in theoretical and ideological thought.

### 3 —

The surviving definitions of kalām do not include any definition written by the Muʿtazila themselves.

What we have is a definition from al-Fārābī, followed by definitions from Ashʿarite theologians.

For this reason, these definitions do not fully reflect the real nature of kalām or its basic features. We gave examples of them from their original sources earlier in the chapter.

Even al-Fārābī’s definition does not fully reflect how far the Muʿtazila relied on reason. We showed this by comparing his definition with the well-known role that reason played in Muʿtazilite thought. Al-Fārābī’s text comes from his *Enumeration of the Sciences*, pp. 107–108.

If we relied only on Ashʿarite definitions, we would get a distorted picture of kalām.

For that reason, we approached the problem through the Muʿtazilite movement itself and through the way the Muʿtazila thought.

### 4 —

From this discussion, we reached two conclusions.

First, kalām is the name given to a set of questions expressed in religious terms. Debate over these questions was first driven by different forms of social and political conflict beginning in the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Other questions were then added as the multiethnic Arab-Islamic society continued to develop.

Intellectual development later moved these debates into increasingly abstract forms, to the point that their social dimensions could almost disappear from view.

Even so, a scientific approach can still see that the basic starting points behind the differing opinions and positions on these questions lay in concrete social realities.

Second, kalām passed through two main stages in its history: the stage of Muʿtazilite kalām and the stage of Ashʿarite kalām.

This does not mean we should forget the other theologians among the Shiʿa, Khārijites, Murjiʾa, Jabriyya, and Sufis.

Our division of the history of kalām into these two stages is based on our conclusion that two main tendencies ran through its entire history.

The first was the rationalist tendency. It treated reason as the main basis for gaining knowledge about religious belief, nature, and society. This was the tendency of the Muʿtazila.

The second was the opposing tendency, which relied on knowledge of the unseen rather than on reason. This was the tendency of those known as the People of the Sunna. The Ashʿarites became its main representatives and used it to fight the first tendency throughout the later centuries.

We have argued that the Ashʿarite stage was essentially a reaction against the Muʿtazilite stage.

We also concluded that this reaction was fundamentally ideological, while religion provided its historical form.

From its beginnings, Ashʿarite kalām became the doctrine of the caliphal state and remained so until that state collapsed. This supports our view of its ideological character.

The most important feature of the Muʿtazilite rationalist method was its attempt to “rationalize” the whole metaphysics of Islam. Its aim was to give reason the freedom to think without being bound in advance by predestination.

At a deeper level, this grew out of an attempt to affirm human freedom of will against the idea that human action was already determined by a prior will.

This was the fundamental revolutionary drive of the Muʿtazilite movement from the beginning.

It is true that the Muʿtazila dealt with these questions through abstract and speculative reasoning. But that method was imposed on them by the conditions of their time: first, by the dominance of religious forms of knowledge, and second, by a period of transition from simple, direct thinking to more complex and indirect forms of thought.

None of this, however, could hide the basic character of Muʿtazilite thought. It stood in opposition to a faith-based view centered on the unseen, to the idea that faith should come before reason, and to the belief that absolute predestination controlled human action.

The leading Muʿtazilite thinkers belonged to the wider educated group that included jurists, scholars of hadith, and Qurʾanic commentators. At the same time, they were connected to the political camps and parties of their age.

Because of this, they had living ties with public opinion across the different classes of society, and their ideas and views found a response among the wider public.

### 5 —

What, then, should we say about the relationship between the Muʿtazila and the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn, under whom Muʿtazilism became the doctrine of the state and remained so under his brother al-Muʿtaṣim and then under al-Wāthiq ibn al-Muʿtaṣim?

We answered this question by arguing that, during his struggle with his brother al-Amīn for the caliphate, al-Maʾmūn supported urban social groups connected to the city economy: trade, money-changing and banking, handicraft production, and moneylending.

His brother al-Amīn, by contrast, was connected to the owners of agricultural estates among the princes, nobles, and major landholders.

Their struggle was therefore connected to the conflict between the rural economy and the urban economy.

Muʿtazilite ideas expressed the ambitions of the city’s different social groups to gain social and political positions that had previously been monopolized by landowning nobles.

Those nobles, in turn, adopted conservative thought as their ideology.

This interpretation of al-Maʾmūn’s position does not completely exclude his personal role. He was also a highly educated man with relatively open intellectual tendencies.

We based this conclusion on a historical theory about the economic conditions of that period, supported by sources and references that we regard as reliable.

The Ashʿarite stage of kalām began during the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil in 232 AH/847 CE.
