This was the period in which conservative forces hostile to the positive gains of al-Maʾmūn’s reign came to the fore. These forces gained control over the weak personality of al-Mutawakkil, whose main concern was luxury.

From this point began a campaign of persecution and repression against Muʿtazilite thought and against all the positive tendencies it contained.

What is striking, however, is that the Ashʿarite school could not completely eliminate the question of reason and its role. The historical process had already moved too far for that.

The Ashʿarites therefore raised the slogan of returning to the defence of the doctrine of the People of the Sunna **through rational proofs**. Ibn Khaldūn mentions this in the *Muqaddima*, p. 838.

But this slogan was little more than a formal accommodation to the results of historical development. The school still relied fundamentally on transmitted authority, not on reason.[^V2-571]

In this chapter, we discussed several questions in which the Ashʿarites adopted the outward form of a rational method, and we showed in some detail why this rationalism remained formal.

### 6 —

It would have been wrong to study kalām without considering the place of the Imami Shiʿa within it.

In practice, they took part alongside the Muʿtazila and the Khārijites in discussing almost all the major questions of kalām.

Indeed, a large part of the principles and foundations of Shiʿi doctrine belongs directly to the field of kalām.

But Shiʿi doctrine also contains positions that differ sharply from one another and are sometimes even ideologically contradictory.

On one side, the doctrine is based on the Imamate. In Shiʿi theory, the Imamate is a divine right belonging to their Imams. This means denying the people the right to choose the caliph and, after the Prophet, making the Imam the central source of knowledge.

On the other side, the Shiʿa agree with the Muʿtazila on several basic questions connected to the rationalist method. These include resistance to an unjust ruler and the idea that reason itself can judge what is good and what is bad. They also come close to the Muʿtazilite position on human freedom of choice in one’s actions.

We therefore have two different positions. How are we to identify their real ideological place?

In our view, the more likely explanation is that their practical history forced them toward the positions they shared with the Muʿtazila.

They had repeatedly opposed both Umayyad and Abbasid rulers, and they had themselves suffered continuous and often tragic persecution.

These conditions pushed them toward those ideological positions even when they conflicted with the principle of the Imamate, which, in our view, represents the most extreme restriction on the role of reason.

At the same time, there were major thinkers among the Imami Shiʿa who made important contributions to kalām and philosophy, including Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam, al-Balkhī, al-Fārābī, and Ibn Sīnā.

But the ideas they developed in these fields did not arise from the principles of the Shiʿi doctrine itself. They were independent intellectual efforts shaped by social and intellectual conditions that had no necessary connection to that doctrine.

For this reason, we do not think it is correct to attribute their ideas and positions simply to their identity as Shiʿis.

### 7 —

We then examined the relationship between kalām and philosophy.

This relationship existed from the very beginnings of Muʿtazilite thought.

Historical sources tell us that Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, the founder of the Muʿtazilite school, read books of philosophy. The same was true of other major thinkers in the movement.

That is one kind of evidence.

Another comes from the nature of the questions they examined. These questions were philosophical by their very nature.

We can also see the connection in the way they thought about those questions and the methods they used. Their approach was the approach of philosophers and their method was philosophical, whether through their reliance on reason and the language of concepts or through their use of logical argument.

This clear relationship between kalām and philosophy made kalām a preparatory stage in the emergence of Arab-Islamic philosophy.

It was the stage in which Arab thought trained itself to think through concepts and categories. In other words, it learned the method of intellectual abstraction without which philosophical inquiry cannot take place.

But what were the limits of this relationship?

We tried to answer that question in two ways.

First, kalām and philosophy were each relatively independent stages in the development of Arab thought.

Second, we can define the boundary between them more clearly by looking at the function each one performed in its own historical period.

Kalām used philosophical thinking as a way of examining questions raised within Arab society after Islam, but it did so through religious inquiry into Islamic doctrine.

Philosophy, by contrast, appeared in Arab-Islamic society after kalām had reached maturity. It examined existence, nature, society, and thought as concepts in their own right. Through these concepts, the material world was reflected indirectly as a particular society with its own historical conditions, characteristics, and forms of social relations.

Philosophy therefore differed from kalām, first, because it began from concepts rather than from social questions raised directly in society.

Second, it did not take Islamic doctrine as the foundation of its inquiry.

It did try to hide the contradiction between the conclusions reached through philosophical investigation and the doctrines of Islam. Those attempts later led scholars of Arab philosophy to describe it incorrectly as a philosophy of “reconciliation.”

### 8 —

The dialectic of the relationship between kalām and philosophy naturally had to contain a contradiction.

That contradiction arose from the conservative reaction that later gave rise to Ashʿarite kalām.

As we have said, the Muʿtazilite stage of kalām prepared the way for the birth of Arab philosophy.

When this stage was nearing its end, kalām was close to giving up its place in the development of Arab thought and leaving that role to philosophy.

But then the conservative reaction appeared and tried to take philosophy’s place.

This could not succeed.

The conditions for the birth of philosophy had already matured, and philosophy therefore had to emerge.

As a result, the place once occupied by Muʿtazilite kalām was taken by two opposing forces.

On one side stood conservative Ashʿarite kalām, which tried to interrupt the development of Arab thought and return it to the method of the People of the Sunna.

On the other stood philosophy, which represented the natural qualitative transformation produced by the accumulated process of development.

The most visible expression of this contradiction was the repeated campaigns of intellectual, and sometimes physical, repression directed against philosophy and philosophers—and even against the natural and mathematical sciences.

Al-Ghazālī played the most important and influential role in this process of repression. His influence became so great that medieval theological philosophy in Europe later used his ideas as weapons against its own opponents.

# Chapter Seven

## Logic

### 1 — The Historical Setting

How and when did Arab-Islamic thought first come into real contact with Aristotle’s logic, or with Greek logic more generally?

Establishing the historical setting of this question is not an end in itself.

Our aim is to discover, in light of the particular historical conditions, how and when Arab-Islamic thought came to need Aristotle’s logic in order to advance according to its own internal development, in connection with the development of Arab-Islamic society itself, especially during the seventh and eighth centuries.

Historians of Arab-Islamic thought are almost unanimous that logic was the first part of the Greek philosophical heritage to become known to Arab-Islamic thinkers.

But when did this happen, and how?

There are several historical signs from which we can conclude that the process began during the first century AH, or the seventh century CE—that is, during the Umayyad period, from 40 to 132 AH/661 to 750 CE.

Among these signs are the following:

1 — It is historically well established that, during the Umayyad period, representatives of the different trends within Arab-Islamic thought entered into extensive debates with representatives of non-Islamic religious schools that already existed in several centres in Syria and Mesopotamia at the time of the Arab conquests, as well as with Persian religious movements.

These exchanges covered many questions of thought and religious doctrine, together with philosophical questions connected to them and to the ideological conflicts taking shape in the new society under Umayyad rule.

The religious schools we have mentioned were strongly influenced by Greek philosophy and especially by Aristotelian logic.

Some researchers even state specifically that these schools taught Aristotle’s logic as far as the end of chapter seven of the *Prior Analytics*.[^V2-572]

Can we really imagine, then, that contact between Arab-Islamic thinkers and these schools could have become so extensive during the Umayyad period without including logic—or at least some questions of logic?

This is especially difficult to believe when we know that the debates conducted by representatives of these schools with Arab-Islamic thinkers were often based on Greek philosophy and on the method of Aristotelian logic.

2 — Historians of Arab-Islamic thought such as al-Shahrastānī tell us that the earliest theologians, including Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, who died in 131 AH/748 CE, “read the books of the philosophers.”[^V2-573]

Other historians tell us that the “sciences of the ancients” entered Muslim lands during the first century AH, when the Muslims conquered non-Arab peoples, although these sciences did not become widespread because the early religious authorities discouraged people from engaging with them.[^V2-574]

Among these historians, the expression “sciences of the ancients” referred specifically to the sciences of Greek philosophy. Logic was either included among them or treated as their introduction and foundation.

So here too we must ask: how can we imagine that theologians of the first century AH were reading the books of philosophers, as al-Shahrastānī says, and that the sciences of the ancients were entering Muslim lands during that same century, as Ibn Kathīr says, while those theologians somehow remained untouched by logic?

After all, as we have already seen, historians of Arab-Islamic thought agree that logic was the first part of the Greek philosophical heritage to become known to Arab-Islamic thinkers.

---

If we accept what these historical signs suggest and say that Arab-Islamic thought began to encounter logic during the first century AH, in the Umayyad period, we immediately face another historical claim widely accepted by historians.

According to this claim, logic was not translated into Arabic until the Abbasid period.

Historians disagree only about when this translation began: during the reign of the second Abbasid caliph, Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr, from 754 to 775 CE, or during the reign of the seventh Abbasid caliph, Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Maʾmūn, from 813 to 833 CE.

This view would move the beginning of Arab knowledge of Aristotelian logic to around the middle of the second century AH, or the middle of the eighth century CE, or even to the period between the second and third centuries AH, in the ninth century CE.

The Andalusian judge Ṣāʿid, who died in 462 AH/1070 CE, reports that ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, who died in 142 AH/760 CE, translated three of Aristotle’s works on logic from Pahlavi into Arabic while serving as a secretary under al-Manṣūr.

These were the *Categories* (*Kategorias*), *On Interpretation* (*Pari Hermenias*), and the *Analytics* (*Analytica*). He also translated Porphyry of Tyre’s *Isagoge*, or *Introduction to the Categories*.[^V2-575]

Al-Qifṭī[^V2-576] and Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa[^V2-577] repeat the same report from Ṣāʿid.

We have not found the substance of this report in the works of Muslim historians who wrote before Ṣāʿid.[^V2-578]

The Orientalist Paul Kraus, however, rejects the claim that these translations were made by ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muqaffaʿ.

He attributes them instead to Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, who lived under the Abbasid caliphs al-Mahdī and al-Hādī after al-Manṣūr. Kraus bases this conclusion on manuscript no. 338 in the Saint Joseph Library in Beirut.

He also argues that these works were not translations of Aristotle’s books themselves, but summaries of commentaries on them.[^V2-579]

The German Orientalist Karl Brockelmann writes:

> “The translations of the *Categories*, the *Analytics*, and the *Isagoge* held in the Āṣafiyya Library under no. 668 are the work of Aḥmad ibn al-Muqaffaʿ.”[^V2-580]

From all of this, we can conclude that translations or explanations of Aristotle’s works on logic existed before the age of al-Maʾmūn.

The existence of two manuscripts containing such material supports this conclusion. In other words, Arab-Islamic thought was already in contact with these works before al-Maʾmūn’s reign.

As for the age of al-Maʾmūn itself, Muslim historians agree that this was a period in which the translation of philosophical sciences flourished, with logic at the forefront.

Ṣāʿid even wrote that “the first of the philosophical sciences to receive attention were logic and astronomy.”[^V2-581]

Some of the leading figures involved in the translation movement became known specifically for translating Aristotle’s logic.

Among them were Abū Nūḥ and Sallam,[^V2-582] who lived during the reign of al-Maʾmūn.

Sallam was the first to translate Aristotle’s entire *Organon* into Arabic.

Later, in the same period, Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq, who lived from 877 to 909 CE, also translated the *Organon*.

From the age of al-Maʾmūn onward, the translation of works on logic into Arabic continued, together with the writing of explanations and commentaries.

At the same time, a struggle developed between supporters and opponents of logic among theologians and philosophers in the Arab-Islamic world.

This struggle was one of the historical forms taken by the wider ideological conflict of the period.

The philosopher and scientist al-Kindī was the first to write original works on logic in Arabic that were not translations or commentaries.

He wrote a treatise introducing logic and then another shorter version of it, a treatise on the ten categories, a treatise on guarding against the deceptions of the Sophists, and both a long and a short treatise on logical demonstration.[^V2-583]

### 2 — The Historical Reality

From this review of the historical evidence, we can conclude that it is difficult to identify precisely when Arab-Islamic thought first came into contact with Aristotelian logic, or with Greek logic more generally.

The matter is not simple enough to be settled merely by reading historical sources and references, comparing their texts, and deciding that one account is more convincing than another.

The problem is more complicated than this kind of secondary comparison can resolve.

As we have seen, the historical sources themselves are clearly inconsistent, both about the date of this first contact and about what exactly is meant by “contact” in the first place.

Where does this confusion come from?

Could it be because “much of what was translated in the eighth century—the second century AH—was lost, to the point that the earliest surviving translation dates from the ninth century, or the third century AH”?[^V2-584]

We do not deny that this may help explain the confusion among historians.

But for our purposes, it is not enough.

Another question immediately presents itself: if so much translated material from the eighth century disappeared, why did **all** the translations of logic disappear, while at the same time most of the material translated from other fields survived—including Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ’s translations of Persian and Indian literature from the same century?

One possible answer would be this: perhaps this is reasonable evidence that logic was not actually translated until the ninth century. If anything had been translated earlier, at least some of it would probably have survived rather than all of it disappearing.

In our view, however, this answer is wrong because it does not fit the historical reality.

The actual development of Arab-Islamic society during the seventh and eighth centuries gives us evidence on this question that is difficult to dismiss.

That evidence comes close to showing directly that Arab-Islamic thinkers knew some of the main questions and basic rules of logic before the eighth century.

We have already pointed to some of the historical signs that support this conclusion. They form only part of the wider evidence.

If we now look at some of the most important cultural developments in that same society and period, we immediately encounter a well-known phenomenon.

The sciences usually described as the **Arab sciences**—language, literature, history, Islamic law, Qurʾanic commentary, hadith, and kalām—developed at an astonishing speed.

They moved visibly from simpler to more advanced forms, and from relative simplicity toward greater structure and complexity.

This was, in reality, the result of the historical interaction between the Arab conquerors and the other peoples of the young Arab empire.

Most of these peoples belonged to old and varied civilizations and cultures. At the time of the Arab conquests, some of them still preserved the heritage of those civilizations and cultures through forms of living practice.

One result of this vast interaction was that the method of Aristotelian logic entered into the heart of the Arab sciences themselves.

It is well known that the influence of logic on these sciences became so strong that logic eventually served as a reference point even for the rules of Arabic grammar.[^V2-585]

This is particularly striking because grammar, as a purely linguistic discipline, might naturally be expected to resist the control of logical rules and structures.

At the time, this difference appeared clearly in one of the main divisions between two grammatical methods: the method of the Basra school and that of the Kufa school.

The Basra school became known for using logical analogy in deriving the rules of grammar.

The Kufa school, by contrast, became known for deriving grammatical rules from the actual speech of Arabic speakers in the desert. In other words, it returned to Arabic in its earlier forms, extending back to the pre-Islamic period.

For this reason, the grammarians of Basra became known as the “people of logic.”

That name has strong historical significance. It confirms that logic had already entered into a working relationship with the sciences of Arabic and Islam.

This influence also had conservative opponents.

Their hostility found expression in a famous saying from the second century AH:

> “Logic has corrupted reason.”[^V2-586]

This saying points us toward the same historical conclusion. It confirms that this relationship existed at an early stage.

The influence of logic could not have reached so deeply into Arabic linguistics and the Islamic sciences—which themselves were only emerging during the first century AH—unless at least a full generation had passed since the beginning of their contact with logic.

The appearance of the effects of logic within these sciences represents a qualitative change.

And a qualitative change cannot happen without enough gradual accumulation to prepare the way for it.

Such preparation also requires enough time for the transformation to take place.

As we have said, the relationship of influence between one science and another, one form of thought and another, or one culture and another is extremely complex.

It does not happen mechanically.

For that reason, it can never be assigned a completely precise starting date.

There is another point worth considering.

De Boer was right when he said that the early use of logic by the people of Basra was no accident.[^V2-587]

The influence of philosophical schools genuinely did appear in Basra before it appeared elsewhere.

Many of Basra’s grammarians were Shiʿis and Muʿtazilites, and they opened the way for “foreign wisdom” to influence their theological doctrines.[^V2-588]

But this raises another question.

Why did the influence of philosophical schools appear in Basra before it appeared elsewhere?

Why were the Shiʿi and Muʿtazilite grammarians of Basra the first to open the way for “foreign wisdom to influence their theological doctrines,” even though the Shiʿa were more numerous and more concentrated in Kufa, where there were also grammarians and theologians just as there were in Basra?

And why did the Muʿtazila arise in Basra rather than in Kufa?

Earlier in this study, when discussing the problem of predestination, we laid the basis for answering these questions. Basra was the first centre in which that debate took root.

The point can be summarized by saying that throughout the Umayyad period, Basra was distinguished by two major features.

The first was that, more than any other Muslim city at the time, it contained a dense concentration of social forces and political parties both opposed to Umayyad rule and supportive of it, together with the competing intellectual movements that expressed these forces and parties.

This situation rested above all on the fact that Basra and its surrounding region had become a major centre in which large groups of working people were concentrated, including peasants, slaves, small traders, the destitute, and workers employed in craft industries. In Kufa, by contrast, we find the great merchants, major investors in land and agriculture, and the ruling aristocracy.

The second feature was this: because Basra brought together such sharply opposed social groups, it experienced some of the harshest forms of repression. This repression fell both on the forces of political opposition and on the poor and vulnerable working groups within society.

These social and political conditions made Basra especially ready—earlier and more strongly than other places—to absorb ideas and sciences that offered new ways of looking at society, nature, and thought. Such ideas made it possible to approach these questions with a more advanced kind of awareness. They also gave people an ideological weapon against the ideology of the Umayyad state, which insisted that there was only one path to knowledge and truth, and only one source of them. That approach left little room for people to use their own powers of understanding, especially human reason.

Logic therefore became the tool that organized the use of this new ideological weapon: the new philosophical ideas entering Umayyad society through the broad social and cultural interaction taking place within an empire made up of many different peoples.

But logic was also an ideological weapon in its own right. It offered a rational way of organizing the relationships between subjects and propositions and of reaching conclusions through the independent use of reason. Used in thinking, deduction, and the formation of general judgments, logic therefore became an indirect class weapon against another kind of weapon: transmitted texts and ready-made generalizations. The state used these to impose its absolute authority over the different forces within society and to fight both its political and its class opponents.

This was the ideological meaning of using logic in the Umayyad period, and the same basic meaning applied to philosophical thought more generally.

We therefore cannot imagine philosophical thought reaching the Arabs during the Umayyad period, as the historical evidence indicates that it did, while remaining separate from logic. The social and cultural channels through which philosophy reached them already combined philosophy and logic.

These channels included the Nestorian and Jacobite schools of Syria and Mesopotamia, the school of Alexandria, the mixing of civilizations among the peoples of the Arab empire, religious and intellectual debate, and the way material interests both came together and came into conflict within the concrete historical structure of material production. All of these social and cultural conditions carried philosophical thought and logic together. They did not bring one without the other.

As *kalām* gradually took shape, grew, and developed during the first and second centuries AH—first through the Qadarites, and later through their Muʿtazilite heirs—this development took place in the presence of both philosophical thought and its main rational tool at the time: logic.

The historical sources still do not tell us exactly how logic reached Arab thought during the Umayyad period or through what channel it arrived. But the loss of this particular historical link does not leave us without a method for reconstructing much of the path Arab thought was following as it developed alongside Arab society itself after the rise of Islam and the great conquests.

At the same time, we should not say that the historical sources deny that logic had reached Arab thought in this period. Nothing in them supports such a denial. Logic could already have had a direct and concrete effect on methods of thinking and on the development of Arab sciences, just as it could help arm political and class opposition with a new intellectual weapon in the ideological struggle.

As we have already seen in this chapter, the sources provide more than a few clues from which this can reasonably be inferred. For that reason, it is no longer very important for our argument whether logic reached Arab-Islamic thought through direct translation, through the spontaneous mixing of civilizations, or through a looser and less organized form of intellectual exchange.

### 3 — The Role of Logic in Arab-Islamic Thought

Earlier in this chapter, we tried to shed some light on the relationship between Arab-Islamic thought and Aristotelian logic, as part of the wider development of its relationship with Greek philosophical knowledge.

Seen in this light, we can perhaps understand the social and ideological meaning of that relationship. It formed part of a much larger historical change: the movement of Arab thought away from the conditions of its earlier stage in the pre-Islamic period—a stage of simple, direct, and spontaneous thinking—and toward its first forms of combined, analytical, abstract, and more complex thought. In other words, toward the first beginnings of philosophical awareness.

During the long course of this change, throughout the first two centuries AH, Arab thought gradually developed a need for a clear rational method.

It was encountering many kinds of knowledge that were new to it, differing in form, subject, and cultural origin. It needed a method that could guide its use of this knowledge, help develop it, and enrich it through its own experience.

This was necessary in order to meet the needs of a large and rapidly changing new society. Many different social forces were developing within it, including active forces located in the society’s material production. Here we are especially concerned with those who worked the land and those involved in craft production.

This society, with its predominantly feudal but distinctive character, increasingly required more advanced techniques in these crafts. It also demanded new and technically sophisticated products to satisfy the growing luxury of the aristocracy, represented increasingly by state officials at the many levels of the political and administrative hierarchy.

All these needs together helped produce the organized and openly sponsored translation of philosophical and natural sciences, mathematics, and medicine at the beginning of the third century AH, the ninth century CE. The state itself now supported this movement.

It was almost an explosion of activity after the long period of preparation that had taken place during the previous two centuries. And, as historians of the translation movement generally agree, almost the whole of Aristotle’s logical tradition stood at the forefront of it.

Against this historical explanation, Ibn al-Nadīm gives us an idealist and highly personal explanation in the *Fihrist*. Some historians later repeated it without question.

According to the author of the *Fihrist*, the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn:

> “Saw Aristotle in a dream and asked him a number of questions. When he awoke, he ordered that Aristotle’s books be translated. He wrote to the Byzantine emperor asking permission to send for whatever books of the ancient sciences he wished to obtain from Byzantine lands. The emperor eventually agreed after first refusing. Al-Maʾmūn then sent a group that included al-Ḥajjāj ibn Maṭar, Ibn al-Biṭrīq, Salm, the head of the House of Wisdom, and others. They took what they found and selected what they wanted. When they brought the books back to him, he ordered them to translate them, and they did.”[^V2-589]

A similarly crude explanation is often given for the scientific translation movement under al-Manṣūr Abū Jaʿfar.

Even many modern historians explain his use of the school of Jundishapur, its doctors, and its teachers—and the growing demand for relatively advanced medicine, trained physicians, and further translations of Greek and Arabic medical books—by pointing to an illness suffered by the caliph himself.

They tell us that al-Manṣūr developed a stomach disorder and that his doctors advised him to summon Jurjīs ibn Bukhtīshūʿ, the Syriac head of the physicians of Jundishapur, to treat him. He was dramatically brought to court, as the story is usually told. When his treatment succeeded, al-Manṣūr persuaded him to remain in Baghdad permanently. This then supposedly became the beginning of a vigorous new movement in medical treatment, medical research, and medical writing—and so the story continues.[^V2-590]

In reality, all the scientific translation and intellectual and cultural activity that took place under al-Manṣūr and al-Maʾmūn, as well as before and after them, was part of the wider development of society.

It reflected historical necessities that had been maturing within that society itself. The internal and external conditions needed for these developments were gradually coming together.

### 4 — Aristotle’s Logic

We have said that Aristotle’s logical works stood at the forefront of the translation movement in philosophy, natural science, and mathematics during the Abbasid period of al-Maʾmūn. Historians of this movement are generally agreed on this.

Does this mean that Arab-Islamic thought consciously chose Aristotle’s logic as the method it needed at this stage of development—a method that could guide the organization of its different intellectual activities and provide what al-Fārābī described as:

> “The laws whose function is to correct the mind and guide a person toward what is right and true in everything where reason may fall into error; the laws that preserve and protect the mind from mistakes, slips, and errors in matters of reason; and the laws by which we test conclusions where we cannot be sure that someone has not made a mistake…”?[^V2-591]

It is not easy to answer this question with certainty.

There can be no doubt that Aristotle’s logic had a deep influence on the development of Arab-Islamic thought as it moved toward philosophical awareness and later began to construct its own philosophical systems.

But there is equally little doubt that Arab-Islamic thinkers—especially those working in philosophy, natural science, and mathematics—continually adapted this logical system to the questions placed before them by their own complex and changing society.

Different groups adapted it according to their different positions on these questions, and those positions were in turn shaped by their social locations.

These adaptations did not, however, change the basic general laws or the fundamental structure of Aristotle’s logical system.

Some thinkers concentrated on only one part of Aristotelian logic. Traditionalist theologians, most of them Ashʿarites and above all al-Ghazālī, focused mainly on its formal side while setting aside its ontological side—its concern with reality itself.[^V2-592]

But there was also another kind of adaptation.

Arab-Islamic thought changed Aristotle’s logic in much the same way that it changed Aristotle’s philosophy, Greco-Roman philosophy more generally, and Neoplatonism in particular.

By this “other kind” of adaptation, we mean the changes Arab-Islamic thought made to logical, philosophical, and intellectual systems that had come from outside.

These changes were not simply deliberate or subjective choices. They arose objectively from real differences between two historical worlds. Arab-Islamic thinkers lived within social relations very different from those of the ancient philosophers. They also lived at a different stage in the historical development of human knowledge.

This second kind of change appeared especially among the philosophers.

Their engagement with Aristotle’s logic was dialectical. It followed what Marxist thought calls the law of the **negation of the negation**. This does not mean completely destroying or rejecting what came before. It means removing what has become negative or historically exhausted while preserving what remains valuable and capable of continuing in a new form.

Before looking more closely at the different attitudes toward Aristotle’s logic, we should stress one point.

The role Aristotle’s logic played in this period of historical transition was positive and progressive.

For rationalist thinkers, it offered both a theoretical and a practical way of strengthening the idea that human reason itself could be used to gain knowledge. It also helped them challenge the claim that knowledge must come from one source alone.

Aristotle’s logic could play this role because it was not purely formal, despite the way some medieval thinkers in both the East and Europe tried to understand it.

It dealt with the laws of thought in both their form and their content.

We can see this clearly in Aristotle’s division of his logical works into the *Prior Analytics*, which deals with the formal laws of thought, and the *Posterior Analytics*, which deals with the practical laws of logical demonstration.

Aristotle did not reduce logic to a technique for using terms correctly. He also analyzed the forms of thought and repeatedly tried to connect those forms with the natural relationships reflected in thought.

Lenin drew attention to this important feature of Aristotle’s logic in his *Philosophical Notebooks*. He noted that Aristotle looks for the ontological content of logical operations and repeatedly brings subjective and objective logic together, so that objective logic—the logic of reality itself—remains visible.[^V2-593]

Lenin made another observation about Aristotle’s logic while commenting on a passage from Hegel about a purely formal understanding of logic.

Hegel wrote:

> “Even if you see nothing in logical forms except the formal functions of thought, that alone makes them worth examining to see how far they correspond to truth. A logic that does not concern itself with this question can at best claim the value of a natural-historical description of the phenomena of thought.”

Lenin commented:

> “This is precisely Aristotle’s immortal achievement.”

Then he added:

> “But we must go further.”[^V2-594]

In short, Aristotle’s importance lies in the fact that he did not believe his task ended with simply recording forms of thought and forms of analysis. He also tried to establish principles that could lead toward scientific knowledge.

When he studied different forms of logical reasoning, he examined them in relation to the outside world and to practical sciences, especially the natural sciences.

The same is true of his classification of the five universals: genus, species, differentia, property, and accident. He arrived at this classification through his study of the worlds of plants and animals.

It seems to us that this major strength of Aristotelian logic found a particularly receptive audience within Arab-Islamic thought.

That is why it gained an important place and influenced many of the processes taking place as Arab-Islamic thought developed historically.

We mean the rise of Arab-Islamic science, followed by the rise of philosophical inquiry into religious belief, nature, and society. This development moved at a remarkably rapid pace. In less than roughly a century, and through *kalām*, it moved from a mainly theological direction toward philosophical systems that achieved a considerable degree of independence from theology.

We do not mean to give Aristotelian logic a larger place in the history of medieval Arab-Islamic thought than it really had.

Our aim is simply to recognize its real importance without either minimizing or exaggerating it.

That brings us to several materialist elements in Aristotle’s logic that some Arab thinkers of the period were able to recognize.

The first appears in Aristotle’s *Categories*, in his discussion of knowledge and the object of knowledge.

Here Aristotle takes what can be called a materialist position. He argues that the object we know must exist before our knowledge of it. Knowledge can arise only if there is first something there to be known.

He says that knowledge and the object of knowledge do not necessarily come into existence at the same time.

If the object of knowledge disappears, then knowledge of it must also disappear. But the disappearance of our knowledge does not necessarily mean that the object itself disappears.

Take, for example, the squaring of the circle. Knowledge of it does not yet exist, Aristotle says, but the squaring of the circle still exists as something that could potentially be known.

In this idea, Aristotle accepts the priority of what exists over consciousness. On this particular question, then, he takes a materialist position.

There is another part of Aristotle’s logic that also expresses a materialist position.

When Aristotle discusses the concept, or essence, he argues that the universal is not some separate spiritual reality existing beyond individual things or beyond the material world, as it is in Plato’s world of Forms.

Instead, the universal exists within particulars—the general within the particular.

The universal cannot exist without individual things. Nor can we come to know a universal without first encountering individual things repeatedly.

There is, however, a difference between knowing an individual thing and knowing the universal concept. We know the individual through the senses. We know the universal through reason, by mental abstraction.

Aristotle’s understanding of the relationship between concepts and reality therefore also represents a materialist position.[^V2-595]

Because of these and similar features in Aristotle’s logic, and because major Arab-Islamic thinkers were able to recognize them, Aristotelian logic could play the positive and progressive role we have described.

It did so in three main ways.

First, it helped the scientific tendency mature within the wider cultural activity of Arab-Islamic society.

Second, it provided an effective way of directing productive intellectual abilities toward mental abstraction—in other words, toward moving thought from simpler to more complex forms.

Third, Aristotle’s logic helped strengthen the rationalist current that led the intellectual and ideological opposition to the idea that knowledge had only one source: a supernatural one.

### 5 — Different Attitudes Toward Aristotle’s Logic

The positive features of Aristotle’s logic were visible to all the major intellectual and ideological currents of the period.

Their attitudes toward it therefore differed according to their wider intellectual and ideological positions.

#### A — The Position of the Extreme Traditionalist Current

This current took a hostile position toward Aristotle’s logic and philosophy for both religious and social reasons.

It attacked them fiercely, persecuted those who studied them, and encouraged their persecution in the name of religion.

Hostility toward Aristotelian logic and philosophy began to become especially visible after the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil came to power in 232 AH/846 CE and began persecuting the Muʿtazila and their doctrine.

But the larger wave of hostility toward philosophy and logic came later, with the campaign of intellectual terror led by theologians and Ashʿarites.

They themselves used the methods of logic, but mainly in its rigid and purely formal form.

The most famous Ashʿarite scholar, and the one who had the greatest influence on religious public opinion, was Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī (1059–1111). He became the leading figure in this campaign.

For generations afterward, his thought continued to cast a shadow of fear over philosophy and philosophers.

This influence reached every region in which Arab-Islamic intellectual life was active, in both the eastern and western Islamic worlds. But its weight appears to have been even greater in the West.

This may have been connected with the dominance there of the Mālikī school of law, which had a particularly conservative and traditionalist character and placed especially strong emphasis on inherited texts.

The rulers of the *ṭāʾifa* kingdoms, princes, and other political authorities in al-Andalus and North Africa made use of the influence enjoyed by Muslim theologians.

They needed the support of religious scholars who held great intellectual influence over public opinion, while those religious figures in turn supported rulers in suppressing free thought, which at the time was represented above all by philosophy and logic.

Books and entire libraries were burned more than once. Thinkers were imprisoned, exiled, persecuted, or stoned after rigid and reactionary jurists stirred rulers and the public against anyone they suspected of departing from their traditionalist way of thinking through an interest in philosophy or logic.

One Andalusian thinker of the period described this historical reality as follows:

> “I saw the art of logic rejected among them and cast aside. They paid it no attention and gave it no importance. More than this, the people of our time recoil from it and accuse anyone learned in it of heresy and unbelief.”[^V2-596]

The wave of intellectual terror associated with al-Ghazālī weakened for a time with the appearance of Ibn Rushd, the great philosopher of the Islamic West.

Ibn Rushd defended philosophy and directly attacked al-Ghazālī’s hostility toward it. He wrote *The Incoherence of the Incoherence* in reply to al-Ghazālī’s *The Incoherence of the Philosophers*.

But Ibn Rushd was able to lift this dark shadow from philosophical thought only briefly.

Before long, it descended on Ibn Rushd himself, despite his high scientific and social standing throughout al-Andalus and the Islamic West.

Muslim theologians turned the ruler of the country[^V2-597] against him, claiming that he had written works showing corruption in his religion and beliefs.

The great philosopher was put on trial before the ruling prince in the presence of leading theologians who held enormous influence over the religious thinking of the Muslim population.

He was sentenced to exile. A number of other free-thinking intellectuals of his time were punished with him.[^V2-598]

The punishment was lifted only shortly before Ibn Rushd died in 1198.

After Ibn Rushd, the wave of intellectual repression associated with al-Ghazālī again came to dominate philosophical thought almost completely, and its creative movement stagnated.

During the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, the pressure became even heavier. Hostility toward philosophy and logic was one of the dominant features of the period.

The young philosopher and mystic Shihāb al-Dīn al-Suhrawardī had already been killed near the end of the twelfth century, in 587 AH/1191 CE, after being accused of philosophy and unbelief.

After him came two major leaders of rigid traditionalist religious thought who expressed the hostility of conservative forces toward logic and philosophy in particularly aggressive language.

The first was Abū ʿAmr Taqī al-Dīn al-Shahrazūrī, better known as Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ (d. 643 AH/c. 1244 CE).

The second was the figure known as Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyya (d. 728 AH/1328 CE).

Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ issued the famous ruling known historically as the “Fatwa of Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ,” which prohibited both teaching and studying logic and philosophy.

He wrote:

> “…As for logic, it is the gateway to philosophy, and the gateway to evil is itself evil.”

From these premises he went on to support harsh action against those who studied philosophy and logic. He called for their persecution in every area of life, even for cutting off their means of livelihood and depriving them of life itself.[^V2-599]

Ibn Taymiyya waged a similar war against philosophical thought.

He prohibited the reading of books by philosophers and logicians, accused Ibn Sīnā of teaching union with God in his *Majmūʿat al-Rasāʾil al-Kubrā* (Cairo edition, p. 138), and wrote a separate work attacking the views of theologians, logicians, philosophers, and Sufis.

In the fourteenth century, the religious leader known as Imam al-Dhahabī followed the same path.

He declared that there was no “remedy for the sciences of philosophy, or for those who carry and practice them, except burning and removing them from existence.”[^V2-600]

Sectarian intolerance and intellectual rigidity alone do not explain this hostility toward logic.

Behind both, we need to look for something deeper.

We need to ask about the social position of these intolerant thinkers and the ideological basis of their attitudes.

Conservative jurists undoubtedly understood how strongly Aristotle’s logic could help philosophical thought develop and how it could bring out materialist positions among some philosophical thinkers.

#### B — The Traditionalist Current That Made Use of Aristotelian Logic

This hostility toward Aristotle’s logic does not mean that every traditionalist opposed it in exactly the same way.

Nor does it mean that they avoided using logic in their own theological writings or escaped its influence on their own methods of thought.

In reality, the influence of logic had become too deep and too firmly established for anyone working seriously in questions of thought or science—whatever kind of science—to remain completely outside it, regardless of their intellectual or ideological position.

For that reason, especially among later traditionalists, we find another form of hostility toward Aristotle’s logic.

It differed from the open and rigid hostility described in the previous section.

These thinkers separated Aristotle’s logic from its substantive meaning—from its relation to knowledge—and reduced it to one aspect alone: pure form.

This was a distortion.

The great social philosopher Ibn Khaldūn clearly recognized this kind of “change” in Aristotle’s logic, as he called it.

After reviewing the contents of Aristotle’s eight logical works, discussing their translation “within the Islamic community,” and describing how Muslim philosophers circulated them through commentaries and summaries, Ibn Khaldūn wrote:

> “…Then the later scholars came and changed the terminology of logic.”

He then identified the exact point where this change had taken place:

> “…They discussed the syllogism only in terms of its general ability to produce conclusions, without regard to its subject matter. They removed the study of the syllogism according to its material content—that is, the five books on Demonstration, Dialectic, Rhetoric, Poetics, and Sophistics. Some of them may touch on a little of this, but only briefly. They neglected these works almost as though they did not exist, even though they are the most important and essential part of the discipline.”[^V2-601]

Whatever position this group of traditionalists took toward Aristotle’s logic, they still used it, even in their attacks on philosophy and philosophers.

They used mainly its purely formal side.

Al-Ghazālī himself is the clearest example.

Despite his famous hostility toward philosophy and philosophers and his historical campaign against them, he not only wrote several works devoted specifically to formal logic. He also placed a purely logical introduction at the beginning of his *al-Mustaṣfā*.

There, in very firm language, he states that anyone who does not understand the logical questions covered in that introduction cannot be trusted in his knowledge.[^V2-602]

Before al-Ghazālī, Imam al-Ḥaramayn, one of the leading early Ashʿarites (d. 478 AH), had already used Aristotelian logic in his discussions of the principles of Islamic law, despite disagreeing with parts of that logic.[^V2-603]

Among later thinkers of this traditionalist current were Najm al-Dīn al-Rāzī (d. 606 AH/early thirteenth century) and Afḍal al-Dīn al-Khūnajī[^V2-604] (d. 646 AH/mid-thirteenth century).

Both gave considerable attention to logic in their writings, but in the way Ibn Khaldūn described above.

The Andalusian thinker Ibn Ḥazm (d. 456 AH/c. 1064) took a similar position toward Aristotle’s logic.

Although his Ẓāhirī school made him a strict traditionalist, he defended logic and wrote the well-known work *Approximation to the Limits of Logic and an Introduction to It through Everyday Examples and Juristic Expressions*.[^V2-605]

His book was, in practice, an answer to the hostility shown toward logic by the jurists and later theologians of his time.

#### C — Theoretical Differences Between Two Kinds of Logic

Alongside these two positions, there were also specific theoretical differences between Aristotle’s logic and the logic used by some schools of jurisprudence, *kalām*, and mystical philosophy.

These differences were another form of the adaptation that Aristotle’s logic—and ancient logic more generally—underwent through cultural interaction within the historical conditions of the period.

Here are several examples.

**First — Definition (*ḥadd*, or “term”):**

On this question, Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, for example, rejects the idea that a definition must be made up of a genus and a differentia.[^V2-606]

This goes against Aristotle’s understanding of definition.

An Aristotelian definition is made up of genus and differentia[^V2-607] because its purpose is to answer the question “What is it?”—that is, to explain “the essence of the thing and its true nature.”[^V2-608]

Al-Rāzī’s position comes from his complete denial that universals exist outside the mind.

Most Ashʿarite theologians took the same position.

For them, universals were nothing more than “conventional names.”

ʿUthmān Amīn argues that they derived this view from Stoicism.[^V2-609]

Can we see a connection here between this position and the nominalism known in medieval Europe?[^V2-610]

One reason for thinking so is that thinkers who agreed with al-Rāzī in rejecting Aristotle’s theory of definition also argued that a definition does no more than explain the meaning of a name. It does not reveal the essence of the thing being defined, as it does in Aristotelian logic.

One leading traditionalist theologian[^V2-611] wrote:

> “…The most rigorous theoretical thinkers know that the purpose of a definition is to distinguish the thing defined from other things, just as a name does. Its purpose is not to form a conception of the thing or reveal its true nature. Only the followers of Greek logic, the followers of Aristotle, make that claim…”

We find another position on definition in the philosophy of the Illuminationist mystic al-Suhrawardī, known as “the slain young man.”

He too opposed Aristotle’s theory of definition, but for a different reason.

In al-Suhrawardī’s view, an Aristotelian definition is not a productive tool for gaining knowledge, because the property[^V2-612] used to distinguish the thing being defined does not actually reveal its true nature.

Take a horse.

Using the Aristotelian method, we might define it as an animal—the genus—that neighs—the distinguishing property.

But while we already understand what an animal is, “neighing” is still not understood if it exists only in the very thing we are trying to define: the horse.

For someone who has never seen a horse, saying that a horse is “an animal that neighs” therefore tells them very little.

Al-Suhrawardī concludes that a proper definition must list all the essential characteristics which, taken together, belong only to the thing being defined.[^V2-613]

The Arab-Islamic philosophers, by contrast—especially the most famous among them, al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and Ibn Rushd—accepted Aristotle’s theory of definition.

The main reason was that they accepted the existence of universals.[^V2-614]

They believed that universals explain the true nature and essence of things. For them, universals were therefore not merely conventional names.

Ibn Sīnā, for example, bases his treatment of the five universals—genus, species, differentia, property, and general accident—on the fact that they answer the question “What is it?”

In other words, they belong directly to the definition of a thing’s true nature and essence.

He writes:

> “Every universal predicate said of what falls under it in answer to the question ‘What is it?’…”[^V2-615]

And on the meaning of definition itself, he writes:

> “A definition is a statement that indicates the essence of a thing. There is no doubt that it must contain all the elements that constitute that essence, and so it must necessarily be made up of its genus and differentia…”[^V2-616]

But Ibn Sīnā did not limit definition to this Aristotelian form.

He also described three other kinds: definition by indication, definition by wording, and definition through a necessary or accompanying property—the last of which is known as *rasm*.

This kind of definition is based on “necessary attributes that constitute the thing’s existence, even if they do not constitute its essence or concept.”[^V2-617]

Unlike the Aristotelian definition, this last kind relies on induction.

This was Ibn Sīnā’s addition to Aristotle’s theory.

**Second — The question of the excluded middle:**

Aristotelian logical demonstration rests on two basic principles.

The first is the principle that two contradictory propositions cannot both be true.

The second is the principle that two contradictory propositions cannot both be false. This is also known as the **law of the excluded middle**.

Arab logicians did not disagree with the first principle.

But some did reject the second.

One example was Abū Sulaymān al-Sijistānī the Logician (d. 380 AH/990 CE), the teacher of Abū Ḥayyān al-Tawḥīdī.[^V2-618]

While trying to prove the existence of God, al-Sijistānī argued that the only possible path was to deny an attribute of God and also deny the absence of that attribute; to deny a limit and also deny the absence of a limit.

He realized that this would provoke the objection that he was combining contradictions.[^V2-619]

His answer was that two propositions count as contradictory only when one is affirmative and the other negative.

That condition, he said, did not apply here, because both propositions were negative.[^V2-620]

There is therefore no contradiction, he argued, between saying “not described” and “not not-described.”

The contradiction would be between “described” and “not described.”

Al-Sijistānī finally wrote:

> We have not combined two contradictions by saying that God is living and not living. We have instead rejected both sides and said: neither described nor not-described.[^V2-621]

Al-Sijistānī therefore defended himself against the charge of accepting two contradictions at once.

But he openly accepted the possibility of rejecting both sides of a contradiction, and he saw nothing problematic in doing so.

He therefore directly rejected the principle that both contradictory alternatives cannot be excluded—the principle of the excluded middle.

**Third — The law of causality:**

In Aristotle’s logic, causality is one of the basic principles underlying demonstrative reasoning.

The relationship between cause and effect in the existence of things, events, and people is treated as necessary and self-evident to reason.

The validity of logical demonstrations depends on this necessary and rational connection.

On this question, the Ashʿarites and some Muʿtazilite theologians rejected the law of causality at its foundation.

Their position differed from that of the best-known Arab philosophers, who relied on causality in their studies of both logic and philosophy.

Ibn Rushd, for example, wrote:

> “Whoever denies causes denies reason itself. The discipline of logic assumes that causes and effects exist, and that complete knowledge of effects is possible only through knowledge of their causes. To deny these things is to destroy knowledge and abolish it.”[^V2-622]

The disagreement here was not merely theoretical.

At its core, it was ideological.

To deny the law of causality is, as Ibn Rushd said, one form of denying reason. It also means denying reason’s role in the development of science. And denying the development of science ultimately means denying the development of society.

The Ashʿarites generally believed that accepting causality as a rational and logical law would threaten their belief that God continually creates human actions, natural events, and natural things anew at every moment.

In their view, these actions and events can be divided into separate parts with no necessary causal connection between them.

God creates each part separately and independently.[^V2-623]

They explained that what appears to us to be a logical sequence between these separate events is not really a logical sequence at all.

It is not a causal connection.

It is a “chance” phenomenon—a kind of coincidence.

To soften this idea of coincidence, the Ashʿarites developed their well-known theory of **habit**.

They used it to explain why things and events appear to be causally connected.

Take the connection between touching fire and being burned.

The Ashʿarites argued that this connection is only apparent, not real.

We think it is causal because we have repeatedly seen the two events occur together. Habit then leads us to judge that fire is the cause of burning.[^V2-624]

The theory of habit was not only a defense of the idea of continuous renewed creation. It was also a defense of divine miracles.

The law of causality creates a problem for the idea of miracles because it rejects the possibility that things and events can occur in ways that break the general laws of the universe and nature.

The Ashʿarites therefore denied this law in order to leave room for miracles.

It is well known that denying causal relationships between the phenomena of the material world has been one of the positions adopted by idealist philosophers in many different periods.

In modern philosophy, examples include Malebranche (1638–1715), Berkeley (1685–1753), and David Hume (1711–1776).

Malebranche explained the relationship between body and soul in much the same way that he explained two clocks showing the same time: God moves both clocks together at every moment.

In Malebranche’s view, then, there is no necessary connection in the universe and no true cause within it.

There is only one real cause: God.[^V2-625]

This divine presence in the actions of created things closely resembles the Ashʿarite idea of continuous renewed creation.

Berkeley explains causal relationships between the phenomena of existence from the same subjective idealist position. He says that the pain I feel when I touch fire is not caused by the fire itself. Rather, the cause is a divine sign warning me that pain may follow. He then asks: Why are pain and burning always associated with fire? His answer is that this happens because God acts according to fixed and lasting rules. We call these rules laws of nature, but in reality they are God’s laws.[^V2-626]

The problem of causality also plays a major role in Hume’s philosophy. He asks, for example: What is the causal relationship between events? Or what is necessity? Hume answers that when we repeatedly observe two events occurring together and following one another, we become used to expecting the same pattern every time. From this, he concludes that the only reality we can be certain of is the repeated succession of two perceptions. This repetition creates in us a firm expectation that the same sequence will continue. We call this expectation a “law.” Imagination also plays a part here, and what imagination adds is what we call “causality.”[^V2-627] Hume later goes on to argue that the law of causality has only a hypothetical character.

The partial similarity between the Ashʿarites and philosophers of this kind in the way they explain relationships between events in the universe comes, in turn, from a partial similarity in their subjective idealist and metaphysical positions.[^V2-628] From everything discussed above, we can finally conclude that the Ashʿarites—above all al-Ghazālī—came close to the position later taken by Hume: that the necessity we observe between cause and effect is only an empirical necessity, not a logical one.[^V2-629]

### 6 — The Name “Logic” and Its Theoretical Meaning

The fact that this science is called *manṭiq* in Arabic points to a sound understanding of the relationship between the linguistic meaning[^V2-630] of the Arabic word and its intellectual meaning. In one way or another, those who chose this Arabic name must have understood the basic ontological and dialectical relationship between language and thought.

Language is the spoken form of thought, while thought is the content that language expresses through that form. Because of this, language and thought affect one another in a dialectical process.[^V2-631]

This does not mean, however, that there was no connection between the Arabic name *manṭiq* and the name of the same science that originally came from Greek, *Logic*.[^V2-632] Those who chose the Arabic term may well have known the derivation of the word *Logic*: that it came from *Logiche*, meaning speech, which in turn was derived from the Greek word *Logos*, meaning “the core and essence of thought.”[^V2-633]

So we cannot rule out the possibility that the Arabic name was inspired by this Greek derivation. But that does not mean Arab thinkers were unaware of how precisely the term, in both languages, expressed the ontological and dialectical relationship between thought and language. Quite the opposite. Arab writings on logic show that they understood this relationship deeply.

There are several signs of this.

First, they explicitly discussed this relationship in their works on logic. The fullest, clearest and most precise statement of it, in our view, comes from Abū Naṣr al-Fārābī. In a chapter devoted to logic, he explains that the subjects of this science are:

> “The concepts of the mind insofar as words point to them, and words insofar as they point to those concepts.”

Elsewhere in the same discussion he says:

> “For this reason, we need rules that protect us both in our concepts and in the way we express them, and that guard us against error in both. The ancients called both of these—that is, the concepts and the statements through which they are expressed—‘logic and speech.’ They called the concepts ‘speech’ and ‘inner logic rooted in the soul,’ while the speech through which they are expressed is ‘outer logic voiced aloud.’ What enables a person to correct an opinion within himself is the speech rooted in the soul, while what enables him to correct it in another person is speech expressed aloud. The ancients called any speech whose purpose is to establish the correctness of an opinion a ‘syllogism,’ whether that speech remained within the soul or was expressed aloud.”[^V2-634]

We have quoted this passage at length because it shows, with unusual clarity and precision, how deeply al-Fārābī understood the relationship between thought and language.

Abū Ḥayyān al-Tawḥīdī also has an interesting discussion of the relationship between logic and grammar, which is itself one form of the relationship between thought and language. In it he gives this brief and striking formulation:

> “Grammar is Arabic logic, and logic is rational grammar.”[^V2-635]

Second, Arab logicians added new discussions to Aristotle’s logic in the section dealing with concepts. They called these “discussions of words.”

They understood a concept, in the logical sense, as the mind’s grasp of a single term. Since that single term is expressed through a word, they began to study words in terms of the meanings they convey, rather than simply as words in themselves.

This gave rise to a whole set of discussions about language that went beyond what was found in Aristotle’s logic. In Arabic works on logic, the study of concepts therefore became richer through a variety of classifications of words, reflecting the different relationships involved in expression.

Words were classified according to how they signify meaning,[^V2-636] according to how general or specific their meaning is,[^V2-637] according to whether they are single or compound,[^V2-638] according to the word itself,[^V2-639] according to its relationship with its meaning,[^V2-640] and in several other ways.

At first sight, these discussions may seem purely linguistic. But Arab logicians gave them a logical character as well.[^V2-641] They did so because, as we said earlier, they had a sound understanding of the real dialectical relationship between thought and language.

We therefore find here another Arab-Islamic response to Aristotle’s logic. This time it was a constructive one. Arab thinkers developed some of the relationships between words already present in Aristotelian logic and enriched logic with new areas of study.

At the same time, these developments opened new theoretical possibilities for Arab-Islamic disciplines such as the principles of Islamic law, *kalām*, Qurʾānic interpretation, grammar, philology and rhetoric.

### 7 — The Categories

Logic has been closely tied to philosophy for a very long time.

We can already see the beginnings of this connection in Plato’s philosophical classifications, which had an early logical character. It continued with the birth of Aristotle’s logic within his philosophical system, then with the appearance of the *Isagoge* in the setting of Neoplatonism.

Logic and philosophy later reappeared together as Arab-Islamic thought developed in the Middle Ages. They then continued to change together through the great scientific transformations of the European Renaissance and the modern period, until the rise of Marxist philosophy and its dialectical logic.

This historical connection has a theoretical basis in the nature of both logic and philosophy.

Philosophy, as we all know, is the highest form of abstraction. It is, in fact, the language of concepts—concepts understood as universals or essences. But we cannot speak in the language of concepts, which is the language of abstraction, without using categories, and categories stand at the center of the study of logic.

Categories are simply expressions of species and genera arranged according to increasing degrees of generality. We move upward until we reach the highest genus: the most general and inclusive form of being.

Categories, then, are existing things expressed as abstract concepts or universals—that is, as species and genera.

Aristotle, the father of logic, held that there were ten highest genera. These were his ten categories. At their head, and serving as the point of reference for the others, stood the category of substance. Substance was also the central subject of Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, or what he called “first philosophy.”

The other nine categories were quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action and being acted upon.

Aristotle treated these categories as general and universal conceptual features of things that form part of what those things are. In other words, he treated them as species or genera of existing things.

For this reason, Aristotle sometimes calls the categories “kinds of being”[^V2-642] and also “general genera” (*Summa general*).[^V2-643]

This way of understanding the categories gives them real content and shows that they are originally connected with things that exist outside the mind. In that sense, they have a material significance.

Arab logicians and philosophers approached the categories on the same basis and in the same spirit.

We can see this from the disagreement among them over whether the categories belonged to logic or to metaphysics. In practice, this disagreement had little effect on how they treated their content. Almost all of them discussed the categories within logic, even those who believed that the subject also had a metaphysical side.

Ibn Sīnā himself believed that the categories properly belonged to metaphysics, yet he still included them in the logic section of *al-Shifāʾ*. In fact, his discussion of the nature of judgments, or logical categories, is one of the most valuable parts of his work.

More broadly, much of the importance of Ibn Sīnā’s logic comes from the fact that he dealt with the content of logical categories, one of the most difficult problems in philosophy.

Since Aristotle, one of the central problems of both logic and philosophy had been the structure of concepts, judgments and conclusions.

Ibn Sīnā begins above all with the problem of judgment. He sees a judgment as establishing a connection between two things, and this is itself a logical category.

A judgment therefore determines a particular subject. When we want to determine what a subject is, we first identify the genus to which it belongs and then add the characteristics that distinguish the individual thing. The genus through which we identify the subject is itself a logical category.

Judgments can therefore be classified according to the logical category on which they are based.

Ibn Sīnā accepts ten categories, just as Aristotle does. For that reason, he distinguishes ten types of judgment, since every judgment rests on a logical category.

Among these are the definitive judgment, which is based on the category of essence; the hypothetical judgment, which is based on the category of cause; and the certain judgment, which is based on the category of necessity.[^V2-644]

Ibn Rushd, by contrast, never hesitated over whether the categories belonged to logic rather than metaphysics. He placed them in his discussion of Aristotle’s logic, not in his discussion of Aristotle’s metaphysics, and treated them purely as logical categories.

Only later Muslim logicians and theologians removed the categories from the heart of logic. These were thinkers with conservative, traditionalist tendencies who tried to strip Aristotelian logic of its concern with content and confine it to purely formal reasoning, as Ibn Khaldūn later pointed out.[^V2-645]

Plotinus, however, also had a system of ten categories, presented in the seventh section of the *Enneads*. He arranged them differently, in a way that reflected the idealist outlook of Neoplatonism.

He divided them into two groups.

The first consisted of five categories belonging to the intelligible world. The second consisted of five belonging to the sensory world.

The first five were substance, rest, motion, identity and difference (*L’identité et la différence*).

The second five were substance, relation, quantity, motion and quality.[^V2-646]

Plotinus then reduced the last three of these to relation.[^V2-647]

Did Arab logicians, theologians or philosophers come under the influence of this Plotinian classification?

We have no source that clearly says so. The only relevant evidence we know of comes from al-Tahānawī, who reports that some thinkers reduced the categories to four: substance, quantity, quality and relation—or possession—which they believed included the remaining seven categories of the traditional ten.

He also says that “the slain shaykh,” meaning al-Suhrawardī, “made them five by treating motion as a category in its own right.”[^V2-648]

Neither of these later classifications, however, gives us clear evidence that their authors were following Plotinus in limiting the number of categories.

### 8 — Methods of Reasoning

Aristotle’s logic relies on demonstration as the way to acquire knowledge.

He recognizes two kinds: syllogism and induction. Aristotle calls the first syllogistic, or deductive, demonstration, and the second inductive demonstration.

In his view, the difference is that the first gives scientific certainty, while the second gives only probable knowledge.

The reason is that a demonstrative syllogism reaches knowledge by relying on first principles of reason. These first principles cannot themselves be demonstrated because they are self-evident.

Inductive demonstration, by contrast, begins with individual cases and moves from them to the universal that includes them all,[^V2-649] meaning the essence they are all understood to share.

For Aristotle, induction can be scientifically certain only if it is complete—that is, only if it includes every individual case before reaching the general law that covers them.

But it is impossible to include every case. Induction therefore remains incomplete, and incomplete induction cannot produce certainty.

Aristotle built his entire logical system around the problem of how demonstration is constructed.

He first concluded that demonstrations must be made up of propositions. He then concluded that propositions are made up of words or terms.

He therefore organized the general structure of logic around two basic areas. The first was the study of terms, which he called the study of concepts. The second was the study of propositions made up of those terms, which he called the study of judgments.

In his discussion of propositions, however, Aristotle dealt only with categorical propositions. He did not examine conditional propositions, whether connected or disjunctive.

The study of definition was also part of the foundation of Aristotle’s logical system because it served the same ultimate aim as demonstration: acquiring knowledge.

For Aristotle, definition is one of the ways we reach knowledge because it allows us to understand the essence of things.

This is the basic outline of demonstration in Aristotle’s logic. We have presented it here as a starting point for examining the changes it underwent among medieval Arab thinkers.

The first thing that stands out is how much they expanded the study of syllogism beyond what we find in Aristotle.

This expansion appeared in two main areas.

First, in their treatment of propositions.

Second, in their treatment of the different figures of the syllogism.

In the case of propositions, Arab logicians discussed not only categorical propositions but also different kinds of conditional propositions.[^V2-650] Here they benefited from additions made by later Greek commentators on Aristotle’s logic, especially Alexander of Aphrodisias and Porphyry of Tyre, the author of the *Isagoge*.

As for the figures of the syllogism, Arab logicians also discussed a fourth figure. Aristotle had either ignored this figure or had at least not stated it explicitly, since his attention was limited to the first three.

In the fourth figure discussed by Arab logicians, the middle term is the subject in the minor premise and the predicate in the major premise.

Ibn Rushd attributes the invention of this fourth figure to Galen after Aristotle.

But the fact that Arab logicians discussed the fourth figure does not mean that they actually used it in demonstrative syllogisms, that they regarded it as equal in value to the other three, or that they all took the same position toward it.

Some, including Ibn Sīnā and al-Sāwī, discussed the fourth figure but explicitly said that they did not rely on it because it was “remote from natural reasoning.”[^V2-651]

Al-Ghazālī mentioned it when classifying syllogisms according to the position of the middle term. But when he turned to the figures produced by this classification, he did not discuss the fourth figure at all.[^V2-652] This effectively meant that he rejected it as a method of reasoning.

Later Arab logicians, however, gave the fourth figure much more attention and added new forms of it that there is no need to discuss here in detail.

#### Induction

Arab thinkers treated inductive demonstration on an essentially Aristotelian basis, without changing it.

They regarded induction as a probable form of demonstration that could not produce certainty. Their reason was the same as Aristotle’s: complete induction is impossible, while incomplete induction is not enough to give certain knowledge.[^V2-653]

#### Analogy

Aristotle also treated analogy as a method of reasoning. Arab thinkers adopted the idea as well, although they did not agree either on how to understand it or on how much value to give it.

Reasoning by analogy means moving from one particular case to another particular case. It is defined as “giving one particular case the same judgment as another particular case because the two share a common feature.”[^V2-654]

Ibn Sīnā, however, does not justify the judgment simply by treating the similar case as an “original” and the new case as a “branch,” as others do.

Instead, he bases the judgment on the “common feature,” which he identifies as “the cause or the sign”—in other words, on the cause shared by both cases.[^V2-655]

Here Ibn Sīnā rejects the idea that analogy works simply through formal comparison and instead grounds it in causality. In this, he was influenced by Shīʿī legal thought, since Shīʿī jurisprudence does not accept *qiyās*, or legal analogy.

Theologians and scholars of legal theory, meanwhile, used a principle they called “reasoning from the seen to the unseen.”[^V2-656]

This resembles Aristotelian analogy because both move from one particular case to another.

But theologians and legal theorists used this method in the belief that it could lead to certainty, whereas Aristotle regarded analogy as only probable.

They also based their form of reasoning on both the law of causality and the principle of regularity.

The idea is this: a judgment in the observed case was established because of a particular cause. If the same cause is found in an unseen or unknown case, under conditions similar to those found in the observed and known case, then the same effect follows. The same judgment is therefore applied to the unseen case by analogy with the observed one.

The traditional example is wine.

If we know that wine is forbidden because it causes intoxication, then the same cause must apply consistently to every drink that resembles wine in this respect. We should therefore judge every intoxicating drink to be forbidden, because the same cause must produce the same judgment wherever it occurs.[^V2-657]

The Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites, however, understood the idea of cause in fundamentally different ways.

The Muʿtazilites believed that causes are objective. In other words, causes exist in things themselves without the need for outside intervention.
