This view follows from their rationalist doctrine. On the same basis, they argued that reason itself can recognize good and evil: that good things are objectively good and bad things objectively bad.

The Ashʿarites, as we have already seen, denied that causality exists objectively in things and events.

For this reason, when they spoke of a “cause” in reasoning from the seen to the unseen, they used the term figuratively rather than literally. Their idea of cause was idealist and far removed from a materialist concept of causality.

They explained the cause used in this kind of reasoning as something that God had made into a cause. If God had not made it one, it would not have been a cause at all.[^V2-658]

## Summary of Chapter Seven

### 1 —

At the beginning of this chapter, we tried to identify the period when Arab-Islamic thought first came into real contact with Aristotle’s logic, or with Greek logic more generally.

During the discussion, we found several historical signs suggesting that this contact began in the first century AH—the seventh century CE—during the Umayyad period.

Among these signs were the following:

1. There was growing intellectual contact between representatives of Arab thought under the Umayyads and members of non-Muslim religious schools in Syria and Mesopotamia. These included Jacobite, Nestorian and Sabian schools, where Aristotelian logic was taught alongside the rest of the Greek philosophical tradition.

We considered it highly unlikely that such broad intellectual contact—especially in religious debate between Christian and Muslim beliefs—could have taken place without Arab thinkers being influenced by logic, particularly since members of these schools used logic themselves when debating Muslims.

2. Al-Shahrastānī says of early theologians who lived across the first and second centuries AH, such as Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, that they “read the books of the philosophers” (*al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal*, vol. 1, p. 58).

Al-Suyūṭī, quoting Ibn Kathīr in *Ṣawn al-Manṭiq* (p. 12), likewise says:

> “The sciences of the ancients entered Muslim lands in the first century AH when the Muslims conquered the lands of non-Arabs. But they did not become widespread among them because the early generations forbade people from entering into them.”

Arab historians used the expression “the sciences of the ancients” to mean the sciences of Greek philosophy, including logic.

Here too, we considered it unlikely that theologians in the first Islamic century could have read philosophical books without encountering logic, or that these sciences could have entered Muslim lands without creating some contact with logic.

Indeed, according to al-Suyūṭī’s own statement, attempts to forbid the study of these sciences could hardly have happened unless they had already spread to some extent and begun to influence Muslims. Otherwise, the authorities would have had little reason to fear that they might weaken accepted Islamic beliefs among educated Muslims.

### 2 —

But if these historical signs show that Arab contact with logic began in the Umayyad period, historians also tell us that works of logic were not translated into Arabic until the Abbasid period.

So how did this contact take place under the Umayyads?

The sources are confused and inconsistent on this question, which makes it difficult to identify exactly when contact with logic began and what form that contact first took.

We therefore asked why the sources are so uncertain.

We rejected De Boer’s explanation that the problem was simply caused by the loss of many translations produced in the eighth century CE (*History of Philosophy in Islam*, p. 29, Arabic edition).

If loss alone were the explanation, we would still have to explain why every eighth-century translation of logic disappeared while many translations from other fields, including literature, survived.

So the question remains: how did Arab thinkers become familiar with logic during the seventh and eighth centuries?

The development of Arab-Islamic society during these two centuries gives us clear evidence that Arab thought knew some of the main questions and basic rules of Aristotelian logic before the eighth century.

Besides the historical signs already mentioned, we can point to a well-known cultural phenomenon: the new Arab sciences that began developing under the Umayyads were already strongly influenced by logical questions.

Arabic grammar, for example, often based its rules on principles that had an Aristotelian logical character.

This close relationship between grammar and logic later appeared in the difference between two major historical schools: the Basran and Kufan schools.

The Basran school became known for its rational and logical approach, and Basran grammarians were even given the title “the people of logic.”

There is really only one way to explain this.

After the Arab conquests, a wide and deep cultural interaction took place with countries that possessed rich and varied intellectual traditions. In those historical conditions, ideas and forms of knowledge that were still alive and developing in those societies naturally entered the growing Arab culture.

Communication between educated people in the conquered lands and Arab intellectuals was active and relatively easy, while debates over religious beliefs were almost part of everyday life.

This is how Greek logic entered the rapidly developing movement of Arab thought.

Its arrival, together with other sciences and forms of knowledge, helped produce important qualitative changes in Arab intellectual life, both in the kinds of knowledge being developed and in the methods used to develop it.

### 3 —

Because we had described the Basran school of grammar as especially rational and logical in its method, we also needed to explain the social factors behind this historical fact.

We showed that Basra in the Umayyad period had two important features.

First, it contained a dense concentration of social groups divided by class, along with strong political parties opposed to Umayyad rule.

Second, because of these sharp social and political conflicts, Basra was subjected to particularly severe forms of social and political repression.

This encouraged the rise of powerful intellectual currents that expressed these conflicts on the one hand, and an ideological opposition to the thought and ideology of the ruling group on the other.

The rational method became the main form taken by this ideological struggle, while logic provided an organized method for using the ideological weapons directed against the rulers.

In the same discussion, we saw that *kalām*, which developed step by step during the first and second centuries AH—first through the Qadarites and then through the Muʿtazilites—grew along the path of philosophical thought and made use of its rational instrument: logic.

### 4 —

We then tried to deal with another important question: what role did logic play in the development of Arab thought?

We argued that logic entered Arab intellectual life at a time when Arab thought was beginning to move beyond a simple, direct and spontaneous view of the world toward an increasingly complex, abstract and systematic way of understanding it.

In other words, it was entering the first stages of philosophical awareness.

As this happened, the need for a clear rational method gradually became stronger. Logic was the method that could meet this need.

Arab thinkers used it to develop their knowledge and enrich it through their own experience, while responding to the needs of the new society that had emerged after the conquests.

Many different social forces were developing within this society, especially the productive forces working in agriculture and craft production.

The feudal and commercial relations of the period increasingly required these groups to develop new and relatively advanced techniques. These techniques were needed both to satisfy the growing demand for luxury among the newly developing landed and commercial aristocracies of the Umayyad state, and to develop the productive sectors themselves: agriculture, crafts and trade.

Under the influence of these social conditions, the need matured for the great historical movement of translating philosophical, natural, mathematical and medical sciences into Arabic.

Logic became the method used throughout this movement, which translated almost the entire Aristotelian logical tradition together with its later commentaries.

Older Arab historians, and some modern historians as well, offered subjective idealist explanations for the movement that translated sciences from Syriac, Greek and Persian into Arabic.

In this chapter we presented two examples of these idealist explanations in order to show why they were mistaken and to replace them with what we regard as the real historical-materialist explanation.

### 5 —

At this point we had to ask another question: Was Aristotle’s logic the only method Arab thought adopted?

Our discussion showed that although Aristotle’s logic played a major role in the development of Arab thought, it did not remain completely Aristotelian and unchanged.

It was adapted to the conditions of a new society and a new historical period—one that differed from Aristotle’s society and age both in its social relationships and in the level of human knowledge.

We saw that Aristotle’s logic underwent different kinds of adaptation, reflecting the different intellectual positions that grew out of different social and ideological positions.

At the same time, these adaptations did not alter the most basic general laws or the fundamental structure of the Aristotelian logical system.

Before examining the different positions taken toward Aristotle’s logic in Arab thought, we tried to explain the positive and progressive role that this logic played.

The first sign of this positive role was that Aristotle’s logic gave rationalist thinkers both a theoretical and a practical tool for strengthening the idea that human reason should play a central role in acquiring knowledge.

It also helped them resist attempts to reduce all knowledge to a single source.

This was possible because Aristotle’s logic was not purely formal. It was a broad system that dealt with the laws of thought both in their formal structure and in relation to their content.

Here we referred to Lenin’s comment in his *Philosophical Notebooks* that Aristotle looked for the ontological content of logical processes.

Aristotle did not reduce logic to a technique for manipulating terms. He analyzed different forms of thought and repeatedly tried to connect those forms with the natural relationships reflected in human thinking.

He also tried to establish principles for advancing toward scientific knowledge.

Because of these strengths, Aristotle’s logic had an important and positive influence on Arab-Islamic thought during its period of growth and development in the eighth, ninth and tenth centuries CE.

Aristotle’s view of the object of knowledge, and of the role played by material objects outside the mind in acquiring knowledge, also contributed significantly to some of the materialist tendencies that appeared in Arab-Islamic thought, especially in philosophy.

### 6 —

These positive features of Aristotle’s thought and logic appear to have played an important role in producing the many different attitudes toward Aristotelian logic.

Those attitudes varied according to different intellectual and ideological currents and different social positions.

In Chapter Seven, we identified three main positions.

First came the position of the conservative tendency that we consistently call “Salafi” in this study.

This tendency opposed Aristotle’s logic and philosophy for both religious and social reasons.

The Ashʿarite theologians represented this position, even though they themselves were armed with the methods of Aristotelian logic.

This campaign against Aristotle’s logic began after the defeat of the Muʿtazilites under the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil in 232 AH/846 CE.

People who studied or taught Aristotle’s logic were persecuted, and some religious scholars even issued rulings saying that Islam prohibited both teaching and studying it.

Second came another conservative position.

This tendency also opposed Aristotelian thought, both philosophy and logic, but its opposition took a different form.

Its representatives could not free themselves from the influence of Aristotelian logic and continued to use it in their own works.

But they took only its purely formal side and rejected its content and its positive features.

The most important example was Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī (1059–1111), the leading Ashʿarite scholar and the one who had the widest influence on Muslim religious opinion.

Third came a set of theoretical disagreements with particular parts of Aristotelian logic. These appeared among some schools of Islamic law, some theological schools, and some traditions of Sufi philosophy.

Their disagreements with Aristotle’s logic concerned several specific points.

Among them were the following:

(a) Definition

Some theologians rejected Aristotle’s theory of definition, according to which a complete definition is built from genus and differentia—that is, from the broader class to which something belongs and the feature that distinguishes it—in order to identify its essence.

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī[^V2-659] represents this opposing tendency.

He argues that a definition cannot validly be constructed from genus and differentia.

The basis of this view is the denial that universals exist at all, since both genus and differentia are universals.

Thinkers of this tendency hold that universals are nothing more than conventional names and that a definition does nothing more than explain the meaning of a word.

On this basis, we might say that there is some relationship between this tendency and the doctrine of “nominalism” known in medieval Europe.

But the similarity is only formal. This Arab tendency did not contain the materialist position that was present in nominalism.

(b) The Law of the Excluded Middle

This question is also known as “the principle of the excluded third.”

Although this principle is one of the basic principles on which Aristotelian logical demonstration rests, there was a major logician in medieval Arab-Islamic thought who disagreed: Abū Sulaymān al-Manṭiqī al-Sijistānī (d. 990 CE). We have already quoted a clear passage in which he argues that it is not impossible for both sides of a contradiction to be false. In fact, his wording suggests that he regarded this as quite straightforward. But he still believed that two contradictory statements could never both be true at the same time.

C — The Law of Causality

The law of causality is one of the basic principles of demonstrative reasoning in Aristotelian logic. In Aristotle’s system, the validity of a proof depends on the assumption that there is a self-evident connection between cause and effect.

The Ashʿarites, along with some Muʿtazilite theologians, rejected this law at its foundation. Arab-Islamic philosophers, by contrast, relied on causality throughout their logical and philosophical work.

Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī was one of its leading critics. He wrote extensively against the principle of causality and argued that what people call cause and effect is really a matter of habit. People repeatedly see two things or two events occurring together, he says, until they come to “imagine that the connection between them exists because one is the cause of the other.”

This view is similar to positions later taken by modern philosophers such as Malebranche, Berkeley, and Hume.

### 7

In Chapter Seven, we examined the relationship between language and thought. We argued that even the Arabic name for the science of logic, *manṭiq*, gives evidence that Arab thinkers understood this relationship as both ontological and dialectical. We also quoted passages from their writings on logic that show how deeply they understood it.

Because of this, they added new discussions of how words convey meaning. These additions enriched the part of logic concerned with concepts. And although these discussions may look linguistic on the surface, Arab logicians succeeded in giving them a genuinely logical character.

### 8

We also examined the categories in relation to both logic and philosophy.

The categories are abstract concepts, and they helped philosophy develop and use the language of abstraction. This language is essential to philosophy because philosophy represents the highest form of abstraction.

We saw that Aristotle treated the categories as general and universal attributes of existing things—in other words, as their kinds and genera. We then showed that this basis reveals the material content of the categories.

Arab logicians and philosophers approached them on the same basis. We pointed in particular to the positions of Ibn Sīnā, al-Fārābī, and Ibn Rushd.

Our study showed that the Aristotelian approach remained the dominant one in Arab discussions of the categories. Only a small number of thinkers removed the categories from logic and placed them instead within metaphysics.

### 9

At the end of the chapter, we examined Aristotle’s different forms of reasoning and the different ways knowledge can be reached: syllogistic proof, induction, definition, and analogy.

We found that Arab logicians greatly expanded the study of propositions and the forms of the syllogism. Alongside categorical propositions, they developed the study of conditional propositions, which Aristotle’s logic had not examined. They also added the fourth figure of the syllogism, which Aristotle had left out of his own logical system.

When it came to induction, however, we found that Arab logicians added nothing substantial to what Aristotle had already discussed.

They explained this limitation by pointing to the level reached by the natural sciences in both the Greek and medieval periods. Scientific tools and methods had not yet developed far enough to let logicians and philosophers examine a sufficiently large number of individual cases and then move from them to general laws with certainty rather than probability.

That is one side of the matter.

There was another problem as well. Logic had been restricted largely to the service of Islamic and Christian theology. This prevented the law of causality from being fully used in induction—or in inductive proof—to discover general laws of nature and society with certainty.

We also found an important difference between Aristotle’s use of analogy and the Arab understanding of reasoning by analogy.

For Aristotle, analogy meant reaching a judgment by relying on a direct similarity between one particular case and another.

Arab thinkers, however, based the similarity between two particular cases on the idea of causality. They tried to discover a cause for the judgment that was shared by two things with similar qualities and circumstances.

There was, of course, a fundamental difference between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites in what they meant by “cause.”

[^V2-8]: A person who deliberately breaks the fast during Ramadan must make expiation in one of three ways: fast for two consecutive months, free a slave they own, or feed sixty poor people. Freeing a slave is also required as expiation for a false oath and for accidental killing.

[^V2-9]: For a detailed account of this revolt, see al-Masʿūdī, *Meadows of Gold*, vol. 3.

[^V2-10]: The name “Murjiʾa” is connected with the history of the group’s emergence after the Battle of Ṣiffīn between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya. When the Khārijites broke away from ʿAlī’s army because they rejected his acceptance of arbitration, they declared both ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya unbelievers. Most Muslims rejected this view. At that point, some argued that judgment on the matter should be “deferred” (*irjāʾ*) to God alone. In practice, this was a political position presented as neutrality. Those who held it therefore became known as the Murjiʾa. See al-Ashʿarī, *Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn*, Cairo, 1950, p. 197.

[^V2-150]: The point is this: before a thing exists, God’s knowledge of it is knowledge of what **will** exist. Once the thing actually exists, however, knowledge that it “will exist” would no longer match reality, because the thing can no longer correctly be described as something that will exist. Correct knowledge would now have to be knowledge that it **has** come into existence. So once the thing has been created, the original object of the first knowledge has disappeared. That knowledge should therefore disappear too and be replaced by new knowledge whose object is the thing that “has come into existence,” not the thing that “will come into existence.” If the first knowledge remained unchanged, it would no longer match reality and would therefore amount to ignorance.

[^V2-151]: In other words, if the first knowledge—knowledge of “what will exist”—changes into knowledge of “what has come into existence,” then God’s knowledge has changed.

[^V2-152]: The argument is that if God’s knowledge changes, then it has undergone something that happens to every created, non-eternal thing: change. Since what is eternal does not change, God’s knowledge would therefore have to be non-eternal.

[^V2-153]: The point is that if God’s knowledge comes into existence within God’s own being, two problems follow. First, God’s being itself would have changed: it was previously without this knowledge and then became the bearer of it once the knowledge arose. But God’s being is eternal, and what is eternal cannot change. Second, this would make God’s being a place in which new events occur. That too is impossible, because anything that serves as a place for events is spatially limited, whereas God is not limited by space.

[^V2-154]: In other words, since God’s knowledge cannot be said to arise within God’s own being for the two reasons just given, it must arise in some locus other than God’s being.

[^V2-155]: That is, if we say God’s knowledge arises in some locus, then that locus becomes characterized by this knowledge: the knowledge becomes an attribute of the locus in which it arose. We would then have to call that locus “knowing,” even though it is God who is “the Knower.”

[^V2-156]: Since, as the argument has shown, God’s knowledge cannot arise either within God’s own being or in some particular locus outside it, we are left with one unavoidable conclusion: God’s knowledge has no locus.

[^V2-295]: Historians of Greek philosophy generally believe that Leucippus was a contemporary of Empedocles and Anaxagoras in the fifth century BCE. Democritus was born in Abdera, in Thrace in northern Greece, late in the fifth century BCE. He lived to a great age, and some accounts say he lived for more than a hundred years. He travelled to Egypt, Babylon, and Persia, and even reached India, gaining much from these journeys through the East. His works have not survived in their original form. What remains are relatively short fragments, most of them preserved in quotations by Aristotle. These quotations and the historical evidence suggest that his largest work was *The Great World-System*, in which he set out his view of the structure of the universe.

[^V2-299]: Science in later centuries confirmed this hypothesis of Democritus. Torricelli’s experiment in 1643 demonstrated that a vacuum really exists, finally overturning the Aristotelian mechanics that held that nature abhors a vacuum. Modern science has also established the principle that nothing comes from nothing, that no existing thing can simply vanish into nothing, and that changes in matter occur through the joining or separation of particles. This was already part of Democritus’s conception when he developed his atomic theory. It also contains the basis of the modern physical principles of the conservation of matter and energy.

[^V2-300]: Some ancient historians report that Plato intended to burn every work of Democritus he could collect, but abandoned the plan because Democritus’s ideas had already spread so widely that burning his books would achieve nothing. See Lange, *History of Materialism*, Fischer Library ed., Paris, 1910, vol. 1, p. 441.

[^V2-490]: Some of these uprisings had a social, and even a class, character. Examples include the revolt of enslaved people in Syria at an earlier stage (al-Masʿūdī, *Meadows of Gold*, vol. 3), the revolt in Basra during the time of al-Ḥajjāj (al-Balādhurī, *Ansāb al-Ashrāf*, p. 303), and the uprisings of poor commoners and Turkic peasants in Central Asia in 73 AH.

[^V2-491]: After the killing of ʿUthmān, the political split into two main camps—supporters of the Umayyads and their opponents—was reflected in legal and theological thought. Jurists and theologians disagreed over a basic question: must people patiently endure the injustice of an oppressive ruler, or must they resist him? The Imamis, Muʿtazilites, and Khārijites held that such a ruler had to be opposed and resisted. See Shaykh Muḥammad Jawād Mughniyya, *Landmarks of Islamic Philosophy*, Beirut, 1960, p. 21. The Sunnis, by contrast, held that ideally the imam should be virtuous, just, and benevolent; but if he was not, patient obedience to an unjust ruler was preferable to rebelling against him. See the same source, quoting Shaykh Abū Zahra, *Islamic Schools*.

[^V2-492]: We can see this in the different names given to these theological discussions before *kalām* became an independent discipline. They were sometimes called “the principles of religion” (*uṣūl al-dīn*), sometimes “understanding religion” (*al-fiqh fī al-dīn*). Abū Ḥanīfa (d. 150 AH/767 CE) called them “the greater jurisprudence” (*al-fiqh al-akbar*). They were also called “the science of divine unity,” “the science of divine unity and attributes,” and “the science of religious laws and rulings.” See al-Tahānawī, *Kashshāf Iṣṭilāḥāt al-Funūn*.

[^V2-497]: There are several views about why the discipline came to be called *ʿilm al-kalām*. Al-Nasafī, for example, says in *al-ʿAqāʾid al-Nasafiyya*, pp. 10–11, that it was called *kalām* because, like logic and philosophy, it gives a person the ability to speak effectively in establishing religious doctrines and compelling opponents to accept the argument. Al-Shahrastānī gives another explanation in *al-Milal*, vol. 1, p. 33, printed in the margin of Ibn Ḥazm’s *al-Fiṣal*. He says that after leading Muʿtazilites studied the philosophers’ books “when they were translated in the days of al-Maʾmūn, they mixed the philosophers’ methods with those of *kalām*, made it a separate branch of knowledge, and called it *kalām*. This may have been because the most prominent question they discussed and fought over was the question of the *kalām* [speech] of God, so the whole discipline was named after it. Or it may have been because they were answering the philosophers, who called one branch of their knowledge *manṭiq* [logic]. *Manṭiq* and *kalām* can both mean speech.”

[^V2-498]: Historians of the period before the great flourishing of authorship under the Abbasids mention many writers and books from that earlier time. For example, al-Maqrīzī (*al-Khiṭaṭ*, vol. 2, p. 345) says that Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ wrote a book titled *The Intermediate Position*. They also mention a book by the Muʿtazilite ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd refuting those who upheld predestination, as well as works by Imami, Khārijite, and other theologians. See Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq, *Introduction to the History of Islamic Philosophy*, p. 288.

Second, Cahen argues that al-Maʾmūn’s support for the Muʿtazilites was implicitly an attempt to win over the Zaydis, who were among the strongest followers of Muʿtazilism. See Claude Cahen, *History of the Arabs and the Islamic Peoples*, Beirut, 1972, vol. 1, p. 110. This explanation has a basis in reality, but it stays at the surface of the phenomenon and does not take account of the more powerful social factor.

[^V2-524]: Sunni Islamic law requires Muslims to obey the caliphs, based on the command in the verse: “O you who believe, obey God, obey the Messenger, and those in authority among you” (Qur’an 4:59). Jurists interpreted “those in authority” as meaning rulers.

Al-Mutawakkil was not “the first Abbasid caliph to love luxury.” Luxury had already accompanied the lives of Abbasid caliphs before him, just as it had accompanied the Umayyad caliphs before them. This was natural: it was an objective social phenomenon, though there were differences and exceptions, such as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and al-Manṣūr. What distinguished al-Mutawakkil was that his love of luxury was more extravagant and excessive than that of others.

[^V2-595]: We regard this position as a positive one, while still recognizing that Aristotle also wavers on this issue toward an idealist basis, or toward remnants of Platonism in his thought. When he tries to solve the basic problem of the relation between the concept and reality—that is, between the universal and the particular—he introduces a Platonic element. He argues that the soul grasps the concept intuitively after repeatedly observing particular things. Aristotle could not solve this problem because the level of knowledge in his time did not allow him to bring practical activity into the solution. The problem is solved by uncovering the dialectical relationship between the universal and the individual, as dialectical materialism later did.

[^V2-623]: The Ashʿarite idea of repeated creation rests on the principle that an accident does not last for two moments, while creation itself is an accident. Creation must therefore be continually repeated. This idea contains an unintended materialist implication because it leads to the eternity of the world. If creation is continually repeated, the world exists for as long as God exists. If the world came to an end, that would mean God had ceased to be a creator. The Ashʿarites, of course, cannot accept that conclusion. They therefore face a contradiction with only two possible solutions: either accept the eternity of the world, in keeping with belief in God’s eternity, or reject the idea of continuous repeated creation.

[^V2-624]: Detailed explanations of the Ashʿarite position on this question can be found in the works of major Ashʿarite thinkers, especially Abū Bakr al-Ṭayyib al-Bāqillānī, or Ibn al-Bāqillānī (d. 403 AH/1012 CE), in *al-Tamhīd fī al-Radd ʿalā al-Muʿaṭṭila wa-l-Rāfiḍa*, and Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī, especially in *The Incoherence of the Philosophers*.

[^V2-628]: By “metaphysical” here, we mean the opposite of “dialectical.” Denying causality in the relationships between natural and social phenomena amounts to treating the universe as static. It also means denying the law of development, which is connected to a chain of causes, conditions, and chance events produced by the dialectical motion of matter in the universe. The static character comes from the idea that, at every moment and in every part of their existence, things require outside intervention through the process of continual renewed creation. Existence in itself is therefore motionless and cannot move for even a moment without an external mover. This is so even though, as noted earlier, the idea of continuously renewed creation can also lead in another direction to a materialist position.

Ibn al-Sikkīt, for example, called his book *Iṣlāḥ al-Manṭiq*, meaning the correction or refinement of expression and eloquent speech. In most later usage, however, the word came to mean the “science of logic” (*Logic*).

Hegel continues: “That is a delight for thought.” Lenin then writes in the margin: “History of thought = history of language.” See the Arabic edition of *Philosophical Notebooks*.

[^V2-649]: As noted earlier, Aristotle was unable to solve the problem of how thought moves from individual cases to the universal that includes them. In other words, he could not explain the real relationship between the universal and the individual, or establish how the connections between concepts correspond to the connections found in the sensory world. In fact, this problem remained unresolved until Marxist philosophy found its answer by discovering the active social essence of human beings. Through practical activity, within people’s social life, the relationship between the universal and the individual becomes clear. A human being is a social being, and each individual human is both an individual and a member of the universal or general category. The universal therefore exists in the individual: the existence of the individual contains the existence of the universal. The individual comes first, and the universal arises on the basis of individual existence. Darwin’s theory can provide a scientific and practical example of how a “universal” arises in a new biological species of animal or plant. According to Darwin’s theory, accidental changes occur in a group of individual organisms. From these changes a new species emerges, and with that species comes the general concept that refers to it.

[^V2-650]: One Arab logician tried to explain why Aristotle did not discuss conditional propositions. [^V2-652]: al-Ghazālī, *Miʿyār al-ʿIlm*, Cairo, 1341 AH, p. 79.

[^V2-653]: Ancient logic, and later medieval logic, relied on deductive demonstration rather than induction for an objective reason: the level reached by the natural sciences in those periods. Science had not yet developed far enough for researchers to examine a sufficient number of individual cases and use them to form a general law known to apply to the remaining cases as well. There was another objective reason. Medieval philosophers, especially the Arab philosophers, knew the law of cause and effect but did not use it in inductive reasoning. Had they done so, they could have examined a number of individual cases, identified a cause governing the relationship between them, and concluded that the same relationship also existed in the cases they had not examined. They failed to apply causality in this way to nature and society because, during the Middle Ages, logic was largely confined to serving theological thought—Islamic theology in the East and Christian theology in Europe. Causality was therefore applied only in theological discussions.
